Statistical analysis was performed using two-sided Welch’s t-tests (b, d, e and m) and two-way ANOVA followed by Šídák’s multiple-comparison test (f and g). For d, P values were corrected using the Holm–Šídák method. Only peak values were tested in b and m. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. The diagrams in a, g, l and n were created using BioRender; Jiang, Z. https://BioRender.com/rr7rsxf (a), https://BioRender.com/ht8s5kb (g), https://BioRender.com/bwofnm2 (l), https://BioRender.com/jm782f8 (n) (2026).

On secondary IMQ challenge, however, HFDDODO mice developed a markedly more rapid and severe disease recurrence, with around twofold greater ear thickening, elevated TH17 cell numbers, enhanced neutrophil accumulation and sustained IL-1R1 expression in conventional CD4+ T cells compared with the LFD-fed control mice (Fig. 4b–f). This enhanced response in HFDDODO mice was durable: mice that were allowed to recover for 6.5 months after the initial flare continued to exhibit exaggerated ear thickening after rechallenge (Extended Data Fig. 9e). Importantly, transient HFD in the absence of IMQ did not confer durable effects: such mice responded like the LFD-fed control mice on rechallenge (Extended Data Fig. 9f). Moreover, when mice that had recovered from initial disease were rechallenged, only the previously inflamed ears—not contralateral naive ears—exhibited exaggerated recurrence in HFDDODO animals (Extended Data Fig. 9g), indicating that the long-term immunomodulatory imprint of DODO is localized and tissue specific. We further found that obese mice maintained on HFD at disease onset developed recurrence equivalent to lean mice that were exposed to HFD at disease onset, underscoring that dietary context coincident with the inflammatory trigger, rather than previous obesity or dietary history, dictates the establishment of diet-induced inflammatory memory (Extended Data Fig. 9h–j). In addition, blocking lymphocyte egress with FTY72039 during the second flare did not prevent HFDDODO-induced exaggerated inflammation, further suggesting a tissue-resident immune response (Extended Data Fig. 9k,l).

We next examined whether skin-resident immune cells mediated these durable effects. To address this, we profiled previously inflamed (left) and unchallenged (right) ears of recovered mice before secondary challenge. In HFDDODO mice, previously inflamed ears contained around 2.3-fold more CD4+ tissue-resident memory (TRM) cells40 compared with LFD-fed controls, whereas unchallenged ears showed no differences (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 9m). Consistent with the flow cytometry findings, thick-section imaging of back skin 45 days after IMQ withdrawal revealed a greater accumulation of CD4+ T cells (red) in HFDDODO mice (Fig. 4h), concentrated around the hair follicle near the sebaceous gland—a region where follicle-associated immune niches have previously been described41,42. To further resolve the CD4+ T cell compartment, we sorted CD4+ T cells from recovered ears and performed single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC–seq; Fig. 4i). Dimensionality reduction revealed marked chromatin heterogeneity, including multiple clusters with features consistent with TRM cells (Extended Data Fig. 10a). Notably, one population (cluster 8) was selectively enriched in HFDDODO mice relative to LFD-fed control mice (Fig. 4j). This cluster exhibited increased chromatin accessibility at loci encoding key inflammatory signalling receptors, including Il1r1 and Il23r (Fig. 4k), alongside accessibility at Hlf, a transcription factor that was recently implicated in CD4+ TRM programming43, Il21, Ccl20 and Tnfsf4 (Extended Data Fig. 10b). By contrast, cluster 8 showed reduced accessibility at Ikzf2, a regulator associated with regulatory T cell identity, as well as Tox and Il6st (Extended Data Fig. 10c). Together, these features define cluster 8 as a distinct CD4+ TRM-like population epigenetically poised for IL-1 and IL-23 responsiveness. These findings indicate that transient HFD exposure durably reshapes the chromatin landscape of skin-resident CD4+ T cells, biasing inflammatory recall responses long after dietary normalization.

To formally establish the functional significance of CD4+ T cells in mediating dietary inflammatory memory, we administered CD4-depleting antibodies or isotype controls to recovered mice and then rechallenged them with IMQ (Fig. 4l). HFDDODO mice treated with isotype control antibodies developed exacerbated recurrent disease, whereas anti-CD4 treatment abolished the difference between the HFDDODO and LFD groups (Fig. 4m). Thus, the CD4+ cell compartment is required for the expression of durable inflammatory memory induced by transient HFD feeding. Further supporting this mechanism, topical administration of the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 during the initial challenge reduced the exaggerated recurrence observed in HFDDODO mice, whereas identical treatment during recurrence conferred no benefit (Extended Data Fig. 9n). These results indicate that local NLRP3 activation during the initial inflammatory episode is required to establish diet-induced inflammatory memory, which is subsequently mediated by CD4+ T cells.

A defining feature of tissue-resident memory is the persistence of the memory response after transplantation. To test whether diet-induced inflammatory memory was similarly tissue intrinsic, we transplanted previously inflamed back skin from recovered HFDDODO or LFD mice—pretreated with either IgG isotype control or anti-CD4 antibodies—onto naive recipients and subjected them to IMQ challenge (Fig. 4n). Grafts from IgG-treated HFDDODO donors displayed markedly increased pathology compared with the IgG-treated LFD controls, including prominent scaling and surface roughening (Fig. 4o) as well as epidermal thickening and elevated leukocytic infiltration in the dermis (Fig. 4p). Thus, transient HFD exposure during disease onset is sufficient to imprint a CD4+ T-cell-dependent, tissue-intrinsic program that amplifies inflammatory recall responses after recovery.

Transient exposure to HFD during a narrowly defined peri-initiation window durably reshapes tissue immunity without requiring obesity. The consequence is not merely heightened acute pathology but a lasting change in local immune responsiveness that becomes evident months later after rechallenge, after return to LFD. These experiments identify dietary state, rather than accumulated adiposity, as the proximate determinant of disease amplification. Three compositionally distinct fat-enriched diets—HFD, MFD and WD—each amplified IMQ-induced type 17 skin inflammation, whereas glucose water alone did not. Conversely, transiently switching persistently obese mice from HFD to LFD during a corresponding four-day peri-initiation window attenuated disease. Semaglutide further sharpened this dissociation: GLP-1 receptor agonism improved glucose handling, reduced body weight and adiposity, and lowered circulating insulin and leptin, but did not attenuate HFD-amplified inflammatory responses. Although longer-term treatment with GLP-1 receptor agonists and related incretin-based therapies may improve established psoriasis in patients with obesity or type 2 diabetes44,45,46,47, our experiment addressed the distinct question of whether short-term semaglutide treatment blocks the additional amplification imposed by coincident HFD exposure. It did not, indicating that systemic metabolic improvement and diet-primed inflammatory susceptibility are separable. Whereas prolonged high-fat or Western-style feeding has previously been shown to exacerbate IMQ-induced and IL-23-driven inflammation48,49,50 and, with sustained exposure, promote spontaneous dermatitis23,24, as little as 4 days at inflammatory onset was sufficient here. HFD alone did not confer durable susceptibility to a later inflammatory challenge, indicating that dietary exposure must intersect with tissue inflammation to imprint the long-term phenotype. Our findings may also help explain a previous observation that leptin-deficient ob/ob mice did not exhibit increased IMQ susceptibility despite profound adiposity49. As leptin supports optimal TH17 differentiation51, its absence may limit engagement of the IL-1β–TH17 axis. Consistent with this possibility, transient peri-initiation HFD amplified IMQ-induced inflammation in WT but not ob/ob mice (Extended Data Fig. 2o).

Mechanistically, the data support a model linking neutrophil-dependent inflammatory signalling to durable tissue immune memory (Extended Data Fig. 10d). Brief HFD increased neutrophil accumulation in skin before overt disease; after inflammatory challenge, Nlrp3 and Il1b were expressed predominantly in neutrophils, and NLRP3–IL-1β signalling licensed IL-1R1+CD4+ T cell responses. NLRP3 inhibition was effective during the initial challenge but not at rechallenge, whereas tissue-resident CD4+ T cells mediated recall, distinguishing memory establishment from memory expression. Skin transplantation further showed that a systemic dietary exposure can be encoded as spatially restricted memory within previously inflamed tissue. How brief HFD drives neutrophil accumulation before overt disease remains unresolved. Targeted lipidomics of skin before IMQ challenge revealed rapid remodelling of the cutaneous lipid environment (Extended Data Fig. 10e), while bulk RNA-seq identified increased expression of genes involved in fatty acid transport, lipid droplet formation and lipid storage (Extended Data Fig. 10f). Although these data do not identify the causal lipid species, receptor or stromal compartment, they nominate local lipid metabolism as an upstream process linking short-lived dietary change to neutrophil accumulation and transcriptional inflammasome priming. This interpretation is consistent with reports of rapid neutrophil recruitment and neutrophil-dependent inflammation after HFD52,53, lipid flux-dependent neutrophil recruitment in adipose tissue54, and FABP-dependent inflammasome and type 17 signalling in skin24,55. The dependence of HFD-amplified LPS-induced lung inflammation on neutrophils and T-cell-intrinsic IL-1R1 signalling suggests that a related acute diet-sensitive mechanism operates beyond skin, although durable inflammatory memory was established here only in skin.

The distinct requirements for memory establishment and recall suggest opportunities for intervention at different stages of disease. Dietary modulation around inflammatory onset may exert disproportionate effects relative to changes during quiescence. Targeting NLRP3 during the initial challenge or interrupting IL-1R1 signalling may prevent the establishment of a maladaptive resident memory program that amplifies recurrence. More broadly, transient physiological states may become embedded in local immune memory when they coincide with tissue inflammation.

Mouse studies were conducted at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). Mice were housed in specific-pathogen-free facilities in temperature- and humidity-controlled animal facilities, with ambient room temperature maintained between 19 and 23 °C and relative humidity ranging from 40% to 60%. Mice were maintained under a 12 h–12 h light–dark cycle, with lights on from 07:00 to 19:00, and were group-housed with ad libitum access to food and water. When required, mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory. By default, mice fed at UCSF were given irradiated PicoLab Rodent Diet 20 5053. For experiments requiring the use of special diets, diets were irradiated and purchased from Research Diets. The HFD was 60 kcal% fat (D12492), and the control LFD was 10 kcal% fat (D12450J). The MFD was 45 kcal% fat (D08091803). The 30 kcal% fat diet was D20072301. The Western diet was D18053102, and the matched control diet was D18053101. Mice designated as obese in this study were fed the HFD for at least 10 weeks, starting at an age of 6–7 weeks, and weighed at least 38 g (as an average within a cage). For short-term HFD feeding, 6-week-old mice were given HFD for 7 days before the IMQ challenge unless otherwise indicated. Unless otherwise indicated, mice remained on their assigned diets throughout IMQ treatment. For HFDin feeding, lean mice were placed on HFD starting 3 days before IMQ challenge and remained on this diet until 1 day after initiation. For LFDin feeding, obese mice were placed on LFD starting 3 days before IMQ challenge and remained on LFD until 1 day after initiation. For HFDout feeding, lean mice were maintained on LFD, except for two distinct periods when they were switched to HFD: first, from 7 to 3 days before IMQ initiation and, later, from 3 to 6 days after initiation during disease progression. For LFDout feeding, obese mice were maintained on HFD, except for two distinct periods when they were switched to LFD: first from 7 to 3 days before IMQ initiation and, later, from 1 to 6 days after initiation during disease progression. For HFDDODO feeding, mice were placed on HFD throughout the entire disease onset phase (spanning 7 days before to 6 days after IMQ initiation) and were then returned to LFD for the recovery and rechallenge phases. C57BL/6J (000664), B6.SJL-Ptprca Pepcb/BoyJ (002014)56, Rag1−/− (002216)57, Tcra−/− (002116)58, B6.129S2-H2dlAb1-Ea/J (MHCIIΔ/Δ) (003584)59, B2m−/− (002087)60, Tcrd−/− (002120)61, Cd4cre (022071)62 and Nlrp3−/− (021302)63 mice were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory. Il1r1fl/fl (ref. 64) and Cd4creERT2Ai14 mice65,66 were provided by the Scharschmidt Lab at UCSF. All of the mice used for the studies were male. All procedures involving animals were performed in accordance with protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of UCSF.

IMQ-induced acute type 17 skin inflammation was generated in mice at various ages fed with either the LFD or HFD. In brief, mice were anaesthetised using isoflurane, and 15 mg cream containing 5% IMQ (TARO) was topically applied to the dorsal and ventral sides of the mouse ear daily for 6 days (ref. 22). Ear thickness was measured daily with a digital micrometer (Mitutoyo). Then, 24 h after the last application, mice were euthanized, and ears were collected for flow cytometry, RNA extraction, histological analysis and other downstream applications. For rechallenge experiments, after the last day of IMQ treatment during the initial challenge, mice were allowed to recover. Ear thickness was measured weekly to evaluate recovery. Unless otherwise stated, after 25–30 days, mice were subjected to 15 mg cream containing 5% IMQ treatment for 4–6 consecutive days. To inhibit NLRP3 activation, MCC950 sodium (S7809, Selleckchem) was prepared in 50 mg ml−1 in water and 75 μg was given topically to each mouse daily in sync with application of IMQ. For experiments involving dorsal back skin, mice were anaesthetised with isoflurane 1 day before IMQ treatment, and an approximately 2.5-cm2 area was shaved and treated with Nair depilatory cream, which was promptly rinsed off with water. Under isoflurane anaesthesia, 50 mg of cream containing 5% IMQ (TARO) was applied topically to the prepared back skin daily for 6 consecutive days. For rechallenge experiments, shaving and depilation were performed only before the initial challenge and were not repeated before the second IMQ challenge.

Ear skin was collected and submerged in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) overnight. Tissues were then embedded, sectioned and stained with H&E by the Histology and Light Microscopy Core at Gladstone Institutes. Images were taken using a Zeiss microscope. The scale bar was added by converting pixels to μm using ImageJ.

Serum was collected and submitted to Eve Technologies for quantification using Luminex-based assays. For tissue IL-1β measurements, individual whole ears were collected and processed separately. Each ear was minced in 400 µl lysis buffer at 4 °C and homogenized using a Precellys Cryolys tissue homogenizer. Homogenates were clarified by centrifugation, and 100 µl of clarified lysate from each sample was submitted to Eve Technologies for Luminex-based cytokine quantification. IL-1β concentrations were calculated from standard curves and are reported as pg ml−1 of clarified lysate generated from one whole ear homogenized in a fixed volume of lysis buffer.

Fasting was induced for 2 h. Glucose (2.0 g kg−1, intraperitoneally) was injected and serum was collected for glucose measurements. Blood glucose was monitored using a Nova Max Plus glucometer.

Mice were administered semaglutide (Selleck Chemicals, S9697) by daily intraperitoneal injection at a dose of 120 µg per kg. Treatment was initiated at the onset of exposure to either HFD or LFD and continued daily until the end of IMQ treatment. Semaglutide was dissolved in a vehicle consisting of PBS:kolliphor:DMSO at a ratio of 18:1:1. Control mice received daily intraperitoneal injections of vehicle alone. Injection volume did not exceed 150 µl per mouse.

Dissected mouse ear skin was separated into dorsal and ventral halves and incubated in 1 ml of digestion buffer. Mouse skins were incubated in 1 ml digestion buffer (RPMI-1640 medium with 2% FCS and 1× penicillin–streptomycin–glutamine solution (10378016, Roche) containing 0.2 mg ml−1 liberase (05401020001, Roche), 0.2 mg ml−1 DNase I (DN25-100MG, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 mg ml−1 hyaluronidase (LS002592, Worthington). After incubation for 30 min, the skin samples were minced into fine pieces (1–2 mm3) and incubated for another 30 min. The suspension was then passed through a 40 μm mesh to remove undigested clumps and debris. The flow-through was centrifuged at 500 rcf for 5 min. The pellet containing the stromal vascular fraction was washed once in 10 ml RPMI, and the resultant isolated cells were prepared for fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) analysis directly or first stimulated with PMA and ionomycin in the presence of brefeldin A (Cell Activation Cocktail; BioLegend) for 1.5 h at 37 °C for subsequent intracellular cytokine staining and then prepared for FACS analysis.

The following antibodies were used: anti-mouse CD4 (BioXCell, GK1.5), isotype control for anti-mouse CD4 (rat IgG2b, BioXCell, LTF-2), anti-mouse Ly6G (BioXCell, 1A8) and isotype control for anti-mouse Ly6G (rat IgG2a, BioXCell, 2A3). For the anti-CD4 experiments: antibodies were injected intraperitoneally 2 days before, on the day of, and 2 days after the initiation of the IMQ challenge at a dose of 0.1 mg per mouse. For the rechallenge experiment, anti-CD4 or isotype control antibodies were injected intraperitoneally on days 29, 32 and 35 after the initial IMQ challenge using the same dosage. For the anti-Ly6G experiments: antibodies were injected intraperitoneally 3 days before, 1 day before, 1 day after, 3 days after, and 5 days after the initiation of the IMQ challenge at a dose of 0.1 mg per mouse. Injection volumes never exceeded 150 µl. For the LPS-induced lung inflammation model, antibodies were injected intraperitoneally 3 days before, 1 day before, 1 day after and 3 days after the LPS challenge at a dose of 0.1 mg per mouse. Injection volumes never exceeded 150 µl.

CD4+ T cells were isolated from the spleens of WT mice using the Mouse CD4+ T Cell Isolation Kit (StemCell) and 100,000 cells were transferred intravenously into Rag1−/− mice. After an 8-week reconstitution period, mice were fed LFD or HFD for 1 week. Mice were then subjected to IMQ treatment for 6 days to induce acute type 17 skin inflammation. Disease severity was assessed by ear thickness measurements, and immune responses were analysed by flow cytometry.

Fc Block (2.4G2, 553141, BD) was diluted in FACS buffer and added to each sample 5 min before performing surface staining. eBioscience Fixable Viability Dye eFluor780 was used to distinguish live from dying or dead cells. Cell surfaces were stained for 30 min at 4 °C. For intracellular staining, cells were treated with fixation and permeabilization reagents from eBioscience and labelled with the appropriate antibodies before being analysed. Data were analysed using Aurora Cytek (v.4.0.1) and FlowJo software (v.10 and v.11, FlowJo). Cells were sorted on the Cytek Aurora CS System. The following antibodies were used: CD45.2 (104, 109839, BioLegend), CD197 (4B12, 120120, BioLegend), CD11c (N418, 117322, BioLegend), CD11b (M1/70, 101224, BioLegend), CD44 (IM7, 103037, BioLegend), TCRγδ (GL3, 563993, BD), CD62L (MEL-14, 20-0621-U025, TONBO), CD69 (H1.2F3, 104506, BioLegend), Ly6G (1A8, 127672, BioLegend), CD3ε (145-2C11, 100349, BioLegend), CD4 (RM4-5, 100528, BioLegend), CD8α (53-6.7, 100744, BioLegend), Ki-67 (SolA15, 367-5698-82, Invitrogen), RORγt (Q31-378, 562684, BD), FOXP3 (FJK-16s, 46-5773-82, Invitrogen), IL-17A (TC11-18H10.1, 506914, BioLegend), IL-17A (TC11-18H10.1, 506925, BioLegend), IL-17F (9D3.1C8, 517008, BioLegend), CD121a (35F5, 564387, BD), CD121a (JAMA-147, 113505, BioLegend), IFNγ (XMG1.2, 505806, BioLegend), IL-22 (Poly5164, 516409, BioLegend). Antibodies against Fc Block, CD45.2, CD197, CD11c, CD11b, CD44, TCRγδ, CD62L, CD69, Ly6G, CD3ε, CD4 and CD8α were used at a 1:200 dilution; antibodies against Ki-67, RORγt, FOXP3, IL-17A, IL-17F, CD121a (clones 35F5 and JAMA-147), IFNγ and IL-22 were used at a 1:400 dilution. eBioscience Fixable Viability Dye eFluor780 (65-0865-14) was used at a 1:1,000 dilution.

CD4+ T cells from mouse ear skin were FACS-sorted, and mRNA isolation, cDNA synthesis and library preparation were then performed based on the protocol provided by PIPseq T2 3′ Single Cell RNA Kit v4.0PLUS (Fluent BioSciences). In brief, cells were sorted by FACS (sorting on live CD45.2+CD3ε+CD4+ cells on a Cytek Aurora CS System) in cell suspension buffer (provided in the kit) with 1 U μl−1 RNase inhibitor. Then, 4 μl cell suspension (5,000 cells maximum) with 20 U of RNase inhibitor was added to each PIP tube reaction, followed by vortexing to generate single bead to cell emulsion. We performed 16 cycles of PCR for cDNA amplification after cDNA synthesis, and 25% of each cDNA sample was carried into transcriptome library preparation. PIPseq T2 3′ Single Cell gene expression libraries were subject to standard Illumina paired-end sequencing targeting 20,000 reads per input cell using the NovaSeq X system.

Raw fastq files were mapped to the mouse transcriptome (UCSC mm10) using PIPseeker67 (Fluent BioSciences, v.3.2) pipeline that performs barcode whitelisting, alignment with STAR, and molecular index correction and generates barcode-feature counts matrices. After alignment and sensitivity calling (sensitivity_5 was chosen for all three samples), 2,103 cells were recovered from the LFD condition and 5,232 cells were recovered from the HFD condition—two T2 PIPseq reactions were used, labelled HFD1 and HFD2. Subsequent analysis was performed using Scanpy (v.1.10.4)68. The three datasets were concatenated into one AnnData object. Low-quality cells (number of genes < 200) and genes (expressed in fewer than three cells) were removed. Doublets were identified and removed using the scrublet function. Data were normalized to 10,000 reads per cell and logarithmized before clustering. Clusters were calculated using the Leiden algorithm and visualized using UMAP. Three clusters (clusters 8, 11 and 12) were excluded due to contamination (monocytes and stromal cells) or high mitochondrial content. Cell types were annotated based on the expression level of known genes and differential gene expression analysis, using the rank_genes_group function. After quality-control filtering (for doublets and non-CD4+ T cell contamination), 1,769 CD4+ T cells remained in the LFD condition, and 4,450 CD4+ T cells remained in the HFD condition, with over 1,500 median genes per cell. To assess TH17 pathogenicity, we calculated a TH17 pathogenicity score based on published gene signatures associated with pathogenic TH17 cells9,31. Gene sets from both studies, comprising key regulators and effector genes that define pathogenic TH17 cells, were curated and used to evaluate the pathogenic potential of TH17 cells in our dataset. Using the score_genes function in Scanpy, we calculated the TH17 pathogenicity score for each cell in the TH17 cluster. To compare differentially expressed genes in TH17 cells in HFD compared to LFD samples, differential gene expression analysis was performed using Scanpy’s rank_gene_groups function, with tie correction for Wilcoxon scores. To remove background noise of genes expressed by few cells, genes expressed in fewer than 100 cells were excluded. Genes with log2[fold change] > 1 and P < 0.0001 were displayed. Plotting was performed using matplotlib (v.3.9.3) and seaborn (v.0.13.2).

Total RNA was extracted from whole mouse ear skin before, at the end of or 26 days after IMQ challenge using the RNeasy Fibrous Tissue Kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol (74704, Qiagen). RNA quantity and quality were determined by NanoDrop spectrophotometers and Qubit 4 fluorometer. In total, 10 μg RNA from each sample was sent to Genewiz for library preparation and sequencing services (RNA-seq). Read alignment and junction finding were accomplished using STAR69 using UCSC mm10 as the reference sequence. Differential gene analysis and data visualization were performed in R using the DESeq270 package.

Single-cell gene expression libraries were generated using the Chromium Single Cell Fixed RNA Profiling (Flex) platform (10x Genomics) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Fixed single-cell suspensions were encapsulated using the Chromium Controller to generate barcoded gel beads in emulsion, followed by reverse transcription and library construction per the 10x Genomics Flex protocol. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X platform to obtain paired-end reads. Resulting raw fastq files were mapped to the reference genome (GRCm39) using the Cell Ranger’s multi pipeline71. Resulting matrix, barcodes and features files were analysed using Scanpy (v.1.10.4). A total of 27,738 cells was analysed (14,990 HFD and 12,748 LFD). The two datasets were concatenated into one AnnData object. Low-quality cells (number of genes < 200) and genes (expressed in fewer than three cells) were removed. Doublets were identified and removed using the scrublet function. Data were normalized to 10,000 reads per cell and logarithmized before clustering. Clusters were calculated using the Leiden algorithm (resolution = 0.5) and visualized using UMAP. Differentially expressed genes were determined using the rank_genes_groups function. Using the PanglaoDB database72 and decoupler’s OmniPath module73, cell type scoring was performed to help assign cell type labels. Using this, together with differentially expressed genes and expression levels of known markers, 17 different cell types were identified. Differentially expressed genes between conditions were calculated using rank_genes_groups. Plotting was performed using matplotlib (v.3.9.3) and seaborn (v.0.13.2).

snATAC libraries were prepared using the Chromium Single Cell ATAC v2 kit (10x Genomics) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Nuclei were isolated, transposed using Tn5 transposase and barcoded by droplet-based partitioning on the Chromium Controller, followed by library amplification and construction. Libraries were sequenced on an Illumina NovaSeq X platform to generate paired-end reads for downstream alignment and peak calling. Resulting raw fastq files were mapped to the reference genome (GRCm39) using Cell Ranger’s atac count pipeline71. Subsequent analysis was performed using ArchR74 (v.1.0.3). In the first step, arrow files were created from the fragment files using the barcodes that passed the cellranger pipeline. Analysis was performed using the mouse GRCm39 genome. After initial quality control, where fragment size distribution, TSS enrichment and number of fragments per cell were visualized, peaks were called using the addGroupCoverages function and addReproduciblePeakSet using MACS275. Initial clustering was performed using the addIterativeLSI and addClusters functions, and visualized using UMAP. Top markers for each cluster were calculated using getMarkerFeatures (using the GeneScoreMatrix) and significant markers were defined as markers with a false-discovery rate of <0.05 and Log2FC ≥ 1 or ≤ −1. To add imputation weights and smooth the signal across nearby cells for improved visual interpretation, the addImputeWeights function was used and data were visualized using the plotEmbedding function. Differentially accessible regions were calculated using the getMarkerFeatures using the PeakMatrix. Data were visualized using base R plotting functions or in-built ArchR functions, such as plotMarkers or plotBrowserTrack.

Acute lung injury was induced by intranasal instillation of lipopolysaccharide (LPS; Escherichia coli O111:B4, Sigma-Aldrich, L3012). Mice were deeply anaesthetised with inhaled isoflurane to achieve a reduced respiratory rate with augmented tidal breathing. LPS (60 μg in 50 μl sterile PBS) was delivered dropwise to the nares while the mice were held in an upright position. During deep inspiratory efforts, animals were gently rotated to alternate the orientation of the main bronchi and promote more uniform distribution of the inoculum.

Mice were euthanized 4 days after LPS administration. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and lung tissues were collected. Lung tissues were weighed before further processing. Dissected mouse lung was collected and finely minced in 1 ml of digestion buffer. Mouse lungs were incubated in 1 ml digestion buffer (RPMI-1640 medium with 2% FCS and 1× penicillin–streptomycin–glutamine solution (10378016, Roche) containing 0.2 mg ml−1 liberase (05401020001, Roche), 0.2 mg ml−1 DNase I (DN25-100MG, Sigma-Aldrich) and 0.5 mg ml−1 hyaluronidase (LS002592, Worthington). After 1 h incubation, the suspension was passed through a 40 µm mesh to remove undigested clumps and debris. The flow-through was centrifuged at 500 rcf for 5 min. The pellet was washed once in 5 ml RPMI, and the resultant isolated cells were stimulated with PMA and ionomycin in the presence of brefeldin A (Cell Activation Cocktail, BioLegend) for 1.5 h at 37 °C for subsequent cytokine staining and then prepared for FACS analysis.

Publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from psoriasis vulgaris lesions were obtained from EGA (EGAS00001007373 and EGAS00001005271; n = 15 samples) as reported previously76,77. Count matrices were loaded into R using Read10X (Seurat) and processed with Seurat78 to generate one Seurat object per sample. Putative doublets were identified and removed using scDblFinder79. Cells were filtered before downstream analysis to retain those with 100–6,000 detected genes, <20% mitochondrial transcripts and <50% ribosomal transcripts. Filtered datasets were merged and normalized in Seurat using standard workflows. Cell type labels were assigned by reference mapping to an annotated psoriasis immune atlas76 using FindTransferAnchors, TransferData, AddMetaData and MapQuery. Marker genes were identified using FindAllMarkers, and visualization was performed using FeaturePlot and VlnPlot.

Mice received daily intraperitoneal injections of 100 µl per mouse of FTY720 (1 mg per kg) or water (vehicle), starting 1 day before the IMQ challenge and continuing daily through its duration. This treatment was applied during either the initial disease onset or the rechallenge phase.

Tissue processing for 3D confocal imaging: after CO2 euthanasia, the dorsal back skin was excised and floated dermis side down in 2% PFA (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 1 h at 4 °C, then fully submerged in fresh 2% PFA for an additional 6 h at 4 °C. Tissue was subsequently cryoprotected in 30% sucrose overnight at 4 °C. One-centimetre-squared sections were embedded in OCT compound (Thermo Fisher Scientific), snap-frozen on dry ice and stored at −80 °C. Using a cryostat, 200-µm thick sections were cut, washed in PBS and blocked for 24 h at 37 °C in DPBS containing 0.3% Triton X-100, 1% host serum (matched to the secondary antibody) and 1% BSA. The sections were incubated with primary antibodies diluted in blocking buffer for 48–72 h at 37 °C, washed three times for 2 h each in PBS and incubated with appropriate secondary antibodies for 24 h at 37 °C. The sections were then washed three times for 8 h total and cleared using Ce3D clearing solution (40% n-methylacetamide) before imaging.

Primary antibodies used for mouse imaging included rabbit anti-dsRed (Takara, 632496, 1:400), rat anti-CD49f–AF488 (BioLegend, 313608, 1:200), rat anti-α-smooth muscle actin–CF405S (Biotium, BNC040665, 1:100) and goat anti-FABP5 (R&D Systems, AF1476-SP, 1:400). Secondary antibodies conjugated to Alexa Fluor 555 or Alexa Fluor 594 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were used as appropriate.

Cleared thick sections were imaged using the Leica SP8 upright laser-scanning confocal microscope equipped with a 405 nm laser and tuneable white light laser, using a 20× water-immersion objective. z-Stacks were acquired under identical acquisition settings within experiments to allow qualitative comparison across conditions.

Donor mice were anaesthetised with isoflurane. Anaesthesia depth was confirmed by toe pinch. The left dorsal back skin of the donor was shaved with an electric razor and disinfected with povidone-iodine and 70% alcohol. Using sterile scissors and aseptic technique, full-thickness left dorsal back skin was collected using blunt dissection at the level of the areolar connective tissue. After graft collection, the donor was euthanized by cervical dislocation. Under a dissecting microscope, connective tissue, fat and the panniculus carnosus were removed from the graft using fine scissors. Individual grafts measuring around 15 × 15 mm were cut and stored on sterile PBS-soaked gauze in a Petri dish on ice. A single donor yielded two grafts for two recipient mice.

Recipient mice were anaesthetised with isoflurane (induction at 3%, maintenance at 2%) and given bupivacaine (local) and Ethiqa XR (subcutaneous) for analgesia. The upper back (thoracic) region was shaved and disinfected with 10% povidone-iodine. A graft bed of matching size (15 mm square) was created by carefully excising skin while preserving the panniculus carnosus and its superficial vasculature. The donor graft was placed on the bed, aligned without folds and secured with eight interrupted sutures at the corners and midpoints of each edge. Once suturing was complete, the thorax was wrapped with an adhesive bandage. The bandage was adjusted to allow free breathing and thoracic excursion.

The recipient mice were returned to the housing facility after they could move freely. On postoperative day 7, the bandages were removed under brief anaesthesia by cutting only the ventral side of the dressing to avoid disturbing the graft. The grafts were inspected for signs of vascularization; contraction, scabbing or firmness indicated technical failure. For analgesia, Ethiqa XR was administered pre-operatively for sustained pain control. Additional analgesics were provided as required under veterinary guidance.

Statistical analyses were performed with Prism (GraphPad, v.10 and v.11). P values were calculated using Welch’s t-tests unless otherwise noted. Statistical tests were two-sided. When applicable, mice were randomly assigned to treatment or control groups. Experimental data were not excluded from the statistical analyses, except for exclusions due to technical errors or loss of confidence in appropriate controls. Measurements were taken from distinct biological samples, except for ear thickness, which was measured longitudinally in the same mice at multiple time points. The investigators were not blinded in the studies unless otherwise stated. No estimate of variance was made between each group. All in vivo experiments were conducted with at least two independent cohorts unless otherwise specified. Unless otherwise noted, data from one instance of the repeated experiments are represented in this Article. The recurrence experiment in which mice were allowed to recover for 6.5 months before rechallenge with IMQ was only conducted once. The targeted lipidomics analyses were conducted once. Bulk RNA-seq, scRNA-seq and snATAC–seq experiments were conducted once using multiple biological samples per group (as indicated in the figure legends). Histological analyses were performed on tissues from a single experimental cohort for each comparison. Unless otherwise indicated, at least five mice per group were examined; for each mouse, three serial sections were assessed at each of at least two separately cut tissue levels. Thick-section confocal imaging was performed once using two mice per group, with three 200 µm sections imaged per mouse.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

The raw and processed bulk RNA-seq data generated in this study have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession number PRJNA1212208. The raw and processed scRNA-seq and snATAC–seq data generated in this study have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository under accession number GSE287431. Publicly available human psoriasis scRNA-seq datasets analysed in this study are available from the European Genome-phenome Archive (EGA) under accessions EGAS00001007373 and EGAS00001005271. Sequencing reads were aligned to the UCSC mm10 or GRCm39 (RefSeq: GCF_000001635.27) mouse reference genome assemblies, as described in the Methods. Cell type annotation was performed using the PanglaoDB database and the OmniPath resource accessed through decoupler. Source data are provided with this paper.

Code used in this manuscript has been deposited at GitHub (https://github.com/bapatlab/RNAseq_scRNAseq_snATACseq).

a, Serum measurements of inflammatory cytokines (n = 4 LFD and n = 5 for 1 week and 10 weeks of HFD). b, Conventional T cells (Tconv) are defined as CD45+ CD3εInt CD4+ FOXP3−; regulatory T (Treg) cells are defined as CD45+ CD3εInt CD4+ FOXP3+; TH17 cells are defined as Tconv cells expressing RORγt, with competency for IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22 assessed separately; γδ T cells are defined as CD45+ CD3εInt γδTCR+; and neutrophils are defined as CD45+ CD3ε− CD11b+ Ly6G+. c,d, Quantification of TH17 cells (c) and γδ T cells (d) in skin of one ear (n = 10 per group). Data are mean ± s.e.m. Kruskal–Wallis tests were used in (a) with Dunn’s correction for multiple comparisons for each cytokine. No cytokines remained significant after Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the 18 cytokines. Brown–Forsythe and Welch ANOVA tests were performed, followed by Dunnett’s T3 multiple comparisons test to calculate P values in (c,d). **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001.

a,b, Glucose tolerance test tracings (a) and area under the curve measurements (b) in mice fed LFD or HFD for 1 or 10 weeks. c,d, Change in ear thickness (c) and frequency of TH17 cells (d) in mice fed diets containing 10, 30, 45, or 60 kcal% fat. e, Change in ear thickness in mice fed LFD or MFD (45 kcal% fat) (left panel) or control diet (CD) or Western diet (WD; 40 kcal% fat, 29 kcal% sucrose) (right panel). f,g, Ear thickness in mice fed CD or WD (f), or LFD or HFD (g), in the absence of imiquimod (IMQ) challenge.h,i, Experimental schematic (h) and change in ear thickness (i) in mice given control or 15% glucose water at the indicated time. j,k, Experimental schematic (j) and change in ear thickness (k) in mice maintained on LFD or subjected to HFDin feeding. l-o, Schematic and change in ear thickness depicting HFD feeding outside of the disease-onset window (l), LFD feeding outside the disease-onset window (m), HFD feeding for 1 week, switched to LFD at IMQ initiation (n), WT or ob/ob mice switched from LFD to HFD at the indicated time (o). Data are mean ± s.e.m. n = 10 (a,b,g,m,n); n = 5 (c-f,i,k,l,o); Ordinary one-way ANOVA was used, followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (b). #1474. After Robbie Fowler claimed the moon landing is 'bulls***' and dubious Joe Cole said he has 'questions' for Neil Armstrong... who makes our ultimate XI of football conspiracy theorists?

Published: 02:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 15:15 EDT, 1 November 2026

Robbie Fowler certainly helped to draw attention to his new podcast with his former Liverpool and England team-mate Steve McManaman this week by airing his views on the 1969 moon landing.

After answering fan questions ranging from favourite films, comedians and useless talents, Fowler responded to McManaman's prompt of the moon landing as a conspiracy theory.

'I think the moon landing is bulls*** to be fair,' with an excited McManaman declaring 'that is a massive one,' before declaring his subsequent reasoning made 'perfect sense'.

He is far from the only footballer to have doubts, with another ex-England international Joe Cole declaring he would like to sit down with Neil Armstrong – who died in 2012 – to get to the bottom of it.

Fowler later quipped he is 'not a flat earther' having been up on a plane. However, some former footballers are, while others have raised a wide range of conspiracies, ranging from the small scale to the more wild.

Here, Daily Mail Sport puts together our ultimate XI of football's conspiracy theorists.

Former Liverpool forward Robbie Fowler admitted this week he believes the moon landing is 'bulls***' Source: YouTube - We'll have a look podcast

For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist – so entrenched in his off-the-wall beliefs and so willing to share them publicly that he is more widely known as a crackpot than a goalkeeper.

Nevertheless, Icke turned out for Coventry City's youth set-up between the sticks in the late 1960s, and later played for semi-professional outfit Hereford United before hanging up his boots and pivoting to sports journalism.

While his playing career might have been small-fry, his commitment to conspiracy theories is Premier League. Among his often-cited beliefs is the idea that an inter-dimensional race of reptile-like shape-shifters – the 'Babylon Brotherhood' have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society.

Among the accused are the late Queen Mother, the Rockefeller and Rothschild families, and former Prime Minister Edward Heath, whose eyes, Icke alleged, he saw turn 'jet black' when the pair met in 1989.

Icke also believes that the 'Illuminati' at the top of the global food chain organised world events including Dunblane, 9/11, the assassination of John F Kennedy, the death of Princess Diana to prompt their subsequent responses. Less laughable is the thick seam of anti-Semitism which critics believe runs through his thinking, although Icke has denied this.

For many, David Icke is football's original conspiracy theorist, with one of his cited beliefs is the idea that reptile-like shape-shifters have infiltrated the upper echelons of global society

Javi Poves endured a similarly unmemorable professional playing career in Spain, but did at least register one La Liga appearance with Sporting Gijon. Then, he quit. It was a matter of principle: he had grown to believe that 'professional football is only money and corruption'. Not an unreasonable view point, from some perspectives, but years on from his 2011 resignation things become somewhat more surreal.

Poves joined lower-division Madrid club Mostoles Balompie in 2016 and later became the club's president. In 2019, he renamed the club Flat Earth FC, to draw attention to his primary cause.

'Football is the most popular sport and has the most impact worldwide, so creating a club dedicated to the flat earth movement is the best way to have a constant presence in the media,' he said that year.

'Flat Earth FC is the first football club whose followers are united by the most important thing, which is an idea.'

Although Poves has since moved to fellow amateur side CDC Moscardo, he remains passionately committed to the idea that the earth is flat and not round, and other environmentally-rooted conspiracy theories. These include viewing 'chemtrails' as a deployment of toxic chemicals, and refusing to believe that suncream can help prevent skin cancer.

One thread which runs through a number of players included in the XI is a scepticism of Covid-19. Some, like Sol Campbell, have suggested that the pandemic was in some way man-made. Icke is in the camp which believes that the lockdown and vaccination scheme was akin to governmental 'facism'.

Lovren was firmly in team Icke during the lockdown years, posting a number of his videos on social media. He also used social media to attack Microsoft billionaire Bill Gates, implying some kind of conspiracy with his comment: 'Game over Bill. People are not blind' on Gates's online tribute to health workers.

The Croatian defender seemed particularly swayed by Icke's theories around the links between Covid-19 and 5G technology in 'controlling' populations, with Lovren resharing clips with the caption 'we will not be censored'.

Dejan Lovren supported Icke's views during the pandemic and hit out at Bill Gates

Lovren took to Instagram to promote an interview with Icke during the pandemic

As mentioned in Lovren's section, Campbell also had his suspicions during the Covid-19 pandemic. Then managing Southend United, in May 2020, Campbell appeared to suggest that he believed the disease was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups.

'Was this virus a natural mistake or a designed mistake...?' he posted on social media. 'I wonder does this virus deliberately attacks a certain blood type.....?'

Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group. He later was widely derided for having no scientific evidence to support his argument.

Sol Campbell appeared to suggest in 2020 he believed Covid-`9 was made deliberately and designed to target certain population groups

Campbell shared his idea alongside a screenshot of an article citing an ONS report that showed Black people were four times more likely to die from Covid-19 than any other ethnic group

The former Manchester City defender has previously admitted to a conspiracy theory that has more sympathetic readers nodding in approval: he believes in ghosts.

Delph admitted in 2016 that he sees ghosts 'all the time', adding that 'genuinely' he had seen about 'four'.

'When I first signed for (Aston) Villa I stayed in a hotel there was lots of things moving in the room, a lot of bangs,' he told Man City's official YouTube channel.

'And about four months ago I saw, in my house in God's country (Yorkshire), I saw two ghosts in my bedroom.'

'I don't think they're there to harm me. But I've definitely seen them. It was just a split second and then they were gone.

'The one four months ago, that actually was carrying a body, it went out onto my balcony, then disappeared.'

Joe Cole admitted he is open to having his head turnedabout the moon landings and would be keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong to 'get to the bottom of things'

Compared to how some of the other members of Daily Mail Sport's XI have at times risked public safety or aired unpleasant and divisive views, Cole's position on the 1969 Moon Landings feels somewhat milquetoast.

Additionally, unlike many, he admitted that he is open to having his head turned, with Cole keen to sit down with Neil Armstrong, the first man on the moon, to 'get to the bottom' of things.

'I'm not sold either way and I need some convincing. I want to believe it, honestly,' Cole told FourFourTwo. 'But I've heard too much about it being fake - things like the flag waving and the footprints and all the rest of it.

'I would love to sit down with a man who actually went there and be convinced. I want him to tell me exactly how it all went down and some of the science behind my questions.

'I just want to put it to bed. If anyone could convince me, it's the first man to have apparently visited the moon. I don't mind being talked round to new ideas which is why I'd be more than happy for him to tell me how silly I'm being.

'That's what makes you evolve as a human being. You have to be open to different ideas in life.'

If Pove represents a distinctly Spanish-style conspiracy theorist, Marcos Llorente treads the well-beaten path, with his primary focus the benefits of sunlight – to the extent of snubbing suncream – and a suspicion of 'chemtrails'.

Llorente takes his theories on natural light and the sun to the extreme, however. A staunch advocate of the blue light-blocking sunglasses also favoured by stars including Erling Haaland, the Atletico Madrid midfielder also eschews unnatural light sources in his house after dark. Instead, Llorente works on soaking up as much red light as possible.

In the sun, Llorente takes it one step further, frequently sharing incorrect views on suncream's impact on Vitamin D and dismissing the connection between skin cancer and unprotected skin.

Marcos Llorente is a committed wearer of blue light-blocking glasses in a bid to boost his melatonin

Llorente has frequently endorsed the repeatedly debunked theory that 'chemtrails' are the result of government or corporate intervention

Llorente often does so in a tongue-in-cheek way: in April, he dressed up as a bottle of suncream, but with a twist. Written on the bottle in Spanish were messages reading: 'Protect against your biology' and 'Blocking Vitamin D since 1985'.

On the back of the bottle costume in lieu of ingredients, Llorente drew a graph of rising skin cancer rates and an accompanying message.

'Get in the shade when your body tells you, 'That's enough'. Get sun exposure year-round, not just three days in August,' the 'warning label' read. 'Use clothing as sun protection. Start in the morning and work your way up (don't start at 1pm).

'Build melanin gradually. Eat a balanced diet so your skin responds better. Stay hydrated and connect with nature.'

More recently Llorente, a bon viveur and lover of rare steak, 'bulletproof' butter coffee and good wine, has intensified his stance on other medical theories, including alleging that high cholesterol or 'bad' cholesterol does not have an impact on health.

Matt Le Tissier is no single-issue conspiracy theorist, with the Southampton icon borderline indiscriminate about the wide range of his causes.

Like many, his outpourings amplified amid the pandemic, with Le Tissier frequently opining on the efficacy of vaccines and painting 'big pharma' as a bogeyman. Then, in 2022, he was stood down from his role as Saints ambassador after peddling Russian lies that the massacre at Bucha, in Ukraine, had been fabricated. This came despite the fact that there was video, satellite, and photographic evidence that Russia had murdered over 320 people in the town.

Earlier this year, Le Tissier found himself in a spat with Grok, X's AI chatbot, over 'chemtrails', asking: 'Hey (Grok), why do some plane trails disperse quickly while others hang around and spread out to form grey blanket clouds?'

The bot had responded that the contrails lingered or didn't due to atmospheric conditions, much to Le Tissier's displeasure, with the former midfielder grumbling that Grok was 'spouting government propaganda'.

Matt Le Tissier, pictured taking a selfie at a Southampton game in February, has frequently raised conspiracy theories over social media

Former Wales international David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas.

Cotterill said in the incendiary post that 'false flag events are one of their go to methods of manipulating the public opinion to bring about change'.

He also alleged: 'America is the last major country that allows it's [sic] citizens to arm themselves. Which they can't really have with what they're planning to do in the coming months and years.'

Cotterill later stressed that the post had not been related to the Texas massacre, instead stating that his post was 'just about recent articles when you see some of the stuff about the pandemic'.

He similarly received intense criticism when he suggested that the retirement of Brighton's 24-year-old Enock Mwepu due to cardiac issues was linked to side effect of the Covid-19 vaccine.

Cotterill remains unrepentant however, recently appearing on a podcast where he admitted that he supports 'everything' Le Tissier says, and revealed his belief in 2016's discredited Pizzagate conspiracy, among other conspiracy theories.

'I've gone into so many rabbit holes. If you see lots of things happening in the world with the number 33, which is obviously massive for Freemasonry and symbolism,' he told Made in Brum Podcast. 'If you see a lot of things that happen in the world, 33 is not far from that. Some people think I'm f***ing nuts.

David Cotterill sparked widespread backlash in 2022 when he referred to 'false flag events' using 'crisis actors' at the whim of 'controllers' within hours of a fatal school shooting in Texas

Former Liverpool and Southampton star Rickie Lambert is among this cohort's Covid-19 conspiracy theorists, starting off on social media as a staunch vaccine sceptic - only to fall deeper into more fringe views.

Unusually, in 2023, Lambert claimed that he believed that one can change the molecular structure of water based on speaking to a glass of the substance positively or negatively.

'The one word where water responds in the most beautiful way, with the most beautiful crystals, is showing gratitude to water,' Lambert said.

More recently, Lambert has been an active supporter of the campaign against '15-minute cities', whose detractors believe is a government scheme to control the movement and rights of people, rather than an attempt to provide walkable goods and services.

Ahead of attending a protest in Liverpool in September 2023, Lambert's call to arms to publicise the event stressed that the scheme was 'a controlled tactic being implemented across this country' and that Merseyside was set to be put under permanent surveillance.

Rickie Lambert has claimed talking positively to water makes it clean

Like Cole, Fowler appears to have merely dipped a toe into the world of conspiratorial thinking, and has similarly alighted on the Moon Landing as the target of his suspicion.

Unlike the former Chelsea star however, there seemed to be little that would change his mind when he discussed the topic with his We'll Have A Look podcast with co-host Steve McManaman.

'I think the Moon Landing is bulls***, to be fair,' Fowler said. 'Because there was a race in the Sixties, between the Americans and the USSR.

'All of a sudden, the USSR were ahead of the Americans (after Yuri Gagarin became the first man in space) and all of a sudden, the Americans got there first.

'I think it's a bit far-fetched. I don't know, that is the general gist of what I'm saying - I just don't think it was real.'

#1473. Palmer and Rogers complete 12-minute rescue mission to save Chelsea

Xabi Alonso needed the cavalry – and referee Jarred Gillett – to stop Chelsea making a quick exit from the Carabao Cup and, boy, did they come up trumps for him.

Chelsea had looked to be heading out of the competition shortly after half-time, but, in Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, Alonso has a cheat code that is capable of masking even the worst defending.

Alonso’s side have shared 26 goals in the five games they have played this season. It has certainly been an entertaining start by Chelsea’s latest manager.

Palmer, Rogers and Pedro Neto stepped off the substitutes’ bench to complete a stunning rescue mission against Leeds United. Palmer scored twice, Neto once and Rogers helped himself to at least a hat-trick of assists. He claimed it was four, but the record books may say three.

When it was announced Palmer had been awarded the player of the match, Rogers responded by saying: “Mate, I got four assists. I can’t believe that! That’s mental. He scored a pen!”

"Mate, I got four assists!" "That is criminal!" Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer arguing over the POTM award! 🤣 pic.twitter.com/X2PkPnSGDk

Chelsea had looked down and out, when, just three minutes after Alonso’s quadruple half-time change, Leeds doubled their lead. But four goals in an incredible 12-minute spell turned the tie on its head and it was Alonso’s substitutes who Chelsea had to thank.

Palmer, with some help from Gillett, was the first to come to the home side’s rescue. Four minutes after Brenden Aaronson had put Leeds 2-0 up, Gillett pointed to the penalty spot after Daniel James had stood on the foot of Pep Chavarría.

It looked like a harsh decision on Leeds and proved to be almost as big of a game-changer as Alonso’s substitutions. Palmer stepped up to score the resulting penalty.

Cole Palmer pulls one back for Chelsea from the spot! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/BUv6h1wTPQ

“Nobody in the stadium, not one player was asking for a penalty and he gave the penalty,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, said. “All of a sudden their players came into the game. The momentum was on their side. Situations can change the whole momentum of the game.”

Stamford Bridge sensed a comeback and in the 55th minute, Rogers nudged the ball into the path of Palmer who produced a brilliant curling finish to beat Michael Zetterer, the Leeds goalkeeper.

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

Reece James then went close, before Neto completed the turnaround on the hour mark. Palmer found Rogers, who in turn picked out Neto and he sent Stamford Bridge wild by sending his shot into the corner of the net.

"This is a comeback of comebacks!" Pedro Neto scores and Chelsea have turned it around eleven minutes after going 2-0 down! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/FTPuWcFqEX

As Farke waited to make a quadruple substitution of his own, Danny Welbeck got in on the act by collecting the ball from Rogers, spinning and scoring.

Class from Danny Welbeck 😤 pic.twitter.com/FUFKxlzXDz

That should have been that and the atmosphere could not have been more different from half-time, when Chelsea fans had booed off their side after watching them fall a goal behind.

Reggie Watson, Chelsea’s 16-year-old debutant, Malo Gusto, Estêvão Willian and Jamie Gittens were hooked at half-time by Alonso, who said: “For sure, I take responsibility for all of them. No player to blame. It’s the decisions that we took.

“I know that probably I haven’t taken the right decisions for them to show their best level. It’s something that I will analyse and learn from. So it’s my responsibility and we had to make decisions at half-time. And we have seen another second half with another quality.”

Goalkeeper Mike Penders was one of the nine changes made by Alonso. He produced a superb double-save to first keep out Aaronson and then recover to tip Tarik Muharemovic’s header out from the corner.

Conor Coady was impressed with that Mike Penders double save in the first half 👏 pic.twitter.com/6NJqFDvnzk

But the Belgian flapped at the corner, which gave Harry Wilson a second chance to get his delivery right. And he did just that by finding Muharemovic at the back post to head the ball into the net.

Valentín Barco survived Alonso’s changes, but was partly at fault for Leeds’s second goal just after the break. He lost the ball and Ethan Ampadu galloped away from Rogers before crossing. Lukas Nmecha got the slightest of touches and Aaronsen smashed the ball into the net.

"Chelsea cut apart AGAIN !" Brenden Aaronson makes it 2-0 to Leeds 🔥 pic.twitter.com/LlJNpqXHav

The substitutes then took over, as Chelsea shocked the visitors before Leeds substitute Dominic Calvert-Lewin gave his team hope by reducing the deficit with 15 minutes remaining.

Any thoughts of a Leeds comeback were quickly erased, however, as Barco netted his first Chelsea goal from a Rogers pass, which may have taken a slight touch to deny him a fourth assist in the record books. Welbeck added a sixth in time added on.

Valentín Barco gets Chelsea a FIFTH! 🫨 pic.twitter.com/XnhgvhBpL9

On the defeat by Chelsea, Farke said: “The referee had the idea to give a penalty. No one in the stadium was asking for it, no one of their players was asking for it, but he spotted a situation where he thought he would give a penalty.

“All of a sudden they scored the goal, then their players came into the game at half-time, the whole stadium after being relatively quiet for 60 minutes they of course were there then. The momentum was all of a sudden on their side. In football small situations can change the whole momentum of a game and this happened.”

"100% I meant it!" 😅Morgan Rogers says he is really enjoying his football after he helped Chelsea beat Leeds 6-3 in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/7uUQb6eIla

Here’s a reminder of the assist in question. Did Rogers mean it? Let us know in the comments beneath this live blog...

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

"Mate, I got four assists!" "That is criminal!" Morgan Rogers and Cole Palmer arguing over the POTM award! 🤣 pic.twitter.com/X2PkPnSGDk

On the message from the manager at half-time, Palmer told Sky Sports: “Just up the intensity, play a bit more, become more alive because I think the first half was flat, everyone agreed in the changing room, so we stepped up.

Asked whether Alonso’s message was delivered calmly, he said: “At the start, but then he got a bit angry. But it was alright.”

On Chelsea’s half-time changes, Conor Coady said on Sky Sports: “I think the credit goes down to [Alonso]. He made a bit of a statement by doing that at half-time. Four subs is a lot to do at half-time but it was needed. Listen, we said about the first half that it was kind of like the players hadn’t played with each other, and then the big guns came on... They were electric at times.”

A crazy match which was decided by Chelsea’s superb substitutes. Alonso took action at half-time and was rewarded with six goals in a madcap second half. Palmer hauled Chelsea back into the game, Rogers collected a handful of assists and Neto scored the go-ahead goal. You wonder what this match will do for the likes of Estevao and Gittens, though.

Chelsea 6 Leeds United 3 (Welbeck) Pure reflexes from Welbeck, who diverts Barco’s wild effort beyond Zetterer.

Palmer has the hat-trick ball on his mind and attempts an audacious chip but just gets his angles wrong. Any guesses who laid on the chance? Rogers. Of course.

Fans in the away end have resolved they have seen enough and are now heading towards the exits. Stach attempts to launch a counter but his raking cross-field ball is far too heavy.

Rogers drifts out to the left and wins Chelsea a valuable corner. James walks over to take it to rapturous applause from supporters there.

Leeds look to break but Wilson mistimes his run and is caught offside.

There will be six minutes of time added on.

Chance! Okafor darts inside of Neto and spins in a teasing ball to the back post but neither Calvert-Lewin nor Tanaka are able to reach it.

Shouts for a Leeds penalty fail to pique the interest of referee Gillett. Gudmundsson was felled on the left of the box but the contact looked minimal.

A tap on Barco’s head from Wilson provokes some histrionics from the Argentine but Jarred Gillett calms all parties down.

Leeds are still pushing. Stach’s effort from eight yards out is closed down before Tanaka’s strike from the edge of the box is smothered by James.

Alonso goes into the book, apparently for straying too far outside of his technical area.

Chelsea 5 Leeds United 3 (Barco) Rogers lays on his fourth assist of the match, driving towards the byline before flashing a searching ball across the face of goal which Barco spears past Zetterer at the far post. That should be that, right?

Valentín Barco gets Chelsea a FIFTH! 🫨 pic.twitter.com/XnhgvhBpL9

Gudmundsson replaces debutant Bard down Leeds’ left.

Chelsea 4 Leeds United 3 (Calvert-Lewin) Game back on? Okafor is afforded far too much space down the left by a tiring Chelsea back line and his cross finds Calvert-Lewin who plants the ball past Penders to reduce the deficit to just one goal. What a tie this has turned into!

Leeds win a corner, which falls to Stach on the edge of the box but his effort is charged down.

It will be a source of acute anguish for Farke that Chelsea’s fourth goal came before he could make his four changes: Stach, Calvert-Lewin, Tanaka and Okafor eventually replace James, Nmecha, Longstaff and Aaronson. Conversely, it should be to Alonso’s credit that he took action early - his substitutes have decided this tie.

Chelsea 4 Leeds United 2 (Welbeck) Rogers gallops on to a simple ball down the right channel and his cutback (towards Palmer) is picked up by Welbeck who spins before firing beyond Zetterer, leaving three Leeds defenders sprawled in front of him. He cares not, and absorbs the love of the crowd in the near corner.

Class from Danny Welbeck 😤 pic.twitter.com/FUFKxlzXDz

Palmer goes close after having found a yard of space on the edge of the box. His strike spears through a thicket of limbs in Leeds’ box but Zetterer pulls off a strong save to deny the Englishman a quickfire hat-trick.

Chelsea 3 Leeds United 2 (Neto) Just 11 minutes after going 2-0 down, Chelsea find themselves ahead. Palmer threads a through-ball through the middle for Rogers, who slides in front of his marker to an open Neto who sweeps the ball beyond Zetterer. Leeds punished for leaving themselves two vs two at the back there.

"This is a comeback of comebacks!" Pedro Neto scores and Chelsea have turned it around eleven minutes after going 2-0 down! 🤯 pic.twitter.com/FTPuWcFqEX

Chelsea have got their tails up and Palmer almost lays on a go-ahead goal but James cannot turn in his cross from the left.

Chelsea 2 Leeds United 2 (Palmer) Wow! Palmer has turned this game on its head. And it’s so, so simple. Acheampong’s throw-in is knocked down by Rogers into the path of Palmer who works in from the right, passing the ball around a Leeds defender and past a rooted Zetterer.

TWO goals in TWO minutes for Cole Palmer and Chelsea are level! 🥶 pic.twitter.com/sgDd3YUgA6

Chelsea 1 Leeds United 2 (Palmer) Palmer makes no mistake. He goes right, and while Zetterer guesses the right way he cannot get there and Chelsea are back in business.

Cole Palmer pulls one back for Chelsea from the spot! 🎯 pic.twitter.com/BUv6h1wTPQ

Chavarria is caught by James in the box and the referee points to the spot. That came from nowhere.

Chelsea 0 Leeds United 2 (Aaronson) Amapadu deserves so much credit here. He steals the ball from Barco high, bursts beyond Rogers on the right and while Nmecha cannot turn in his cutback, Aaronson arrives late to stroke the ball past Penders and double Leeds’ lead.

"Chelsea cut apart AGAIN !" Brenden Aaronson makes it 2-0 to Leeds 🔥 pic.twitter.com/LlJNpqXHav

Alonso resolves he has seen enough and rings the changes at the interval. Palmer, Rogers, James and Neto enter the fray in place of Estevao, Watson, Gittens and Gusto.

Big cheers from the Chelsea fans at half-time, as Cole Palmer, Pedro Neto, Morgan Rogers and Reece James have all come on to warm up and are stripped off ready to play. Alonso is sending on the cavalry.

The delayed kick-off has knocked us out of kilter with tonight’s Champions League matches, but here are the live scores:

Liverpool 2 Atletico Madrid 1Paris St-Germain 4 Slovan 0Napoli 0 Arsenal 0Sporting CP 1 Galatasaray 1

Boos at half-time from the Chelsea fans. Their team were pretty awful, but booing so early in the season. Really?

There is only one minute of time added on and Watson earns himself a booking for a late challenge on Wilson before the half-time whistle is blown. It will be interesting to see how long Alonso waits before turning to his bench.

Justin, James and Wilson have got a lot of joy down Leeds’ right, rotating in Chavarria’s orbit. It has been difficult for Chelsea to pin them down and Gittens’ attacking threat has been blunted as he attempts to track their movements.

Better from Chelsea. Watson does well to regain possession high and Estevao takes over, darting towards the by-line. His cutback is directed towards Welbeck but he is beaten to the ball by a Leeds toe and it is played behind for a corner which comes to nothing.

Chelsea are really struggling to build up a head of steam, with individual mistakes proving costly.

Gittens and Estevao both end up on the left and the former works infield before firing a shot at Zetterer which the German parries behind for a corner. Perhaps Chelsea’s most dangerous moment of the half.

The corner is played short with the ball eventually falling to Barco on the edge of the box but his mis-hit effort trickles wide.

Gittens rescues an overhit Acheampong cross and finds Barco on the edge of the box, but the Argentine’s effort is charged down. Leeds spring a counter and their sweeping move up field earns them a corner.

Wilson floats another delivery to the back post to Muharemovic, but he cannot replicate his earlier goal.

Farke will be delighted with what he has seen so far. It is all well and good Chelsea allowing Leeds the ball, but they have to break incisively when openings arise, and they have not done that.

Big chance for Leeds! James bursts down the right and the Welsh winger dinks in a cross to the far post which Justin cannot get past Acheampong, but while Longstaff is first to the second ball, he can only sky the shot over the bar.

Leeds’ goal has stirred something inside them and they look motivated to score a second. Ampadu launches a long throw from the left which ricochets off a couple of players before rolling out for a Chelsea goal-kick.

Chelsea 0 Leeds United 1 (Muharemovic) Set-pieces have been a massive feature of Leeds’ game this season and here they take the lead with the simplest of corner routines. Wilson floats the ball to the back post where Muharemovic is waiting, unmarked, and he loops a header over Penders into the net. Such a shame for the Chelsea keeper as he had just pulled off a stunning double-save.

"The set-piece routine does it again!" Tarik Muharemović puts Leeds in front against Chelsea! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/UxeJ3xgL56

Barco slips on the far side and in doing so concedes a corner rather comically, to the delight of the travelling supporters. The delivery is met by Lacroix and Leeds are unable to create anything from the second phase of the set-piece.

There is an intriguing duel developing down Chelsea’s right as Bard looks to contain Estevao. The French wing-back has done a decent job so far.

Estevao attempts to free himself of Bard’s clutches and drifts inside, Chavarria then almost picks him out with a cross from the left but Leeds just about clear their lines.

Justin plays in a cultured through-ball from a wide-right position to James but Chavarria does well to snuff it out. Leeds are making the pitch as big as possible and spaces are beginning to open up as they did at Fulham on the opening weekend.

Although Penders’ shot-stopping has not yet been tested, he has shown some nifty footwork, sweeping up any loose balls that make it past Chelsea’s back three/five.

Big chance! Chelsea spring a surprise attack as Chavarria sets Gittens away down the left. He works the ball infield to Welbeck who lays on a great chance for Estevao but Justin darts back to take the ball off the Brazilian’s toes. A brilliant piece of last-ditch defending.

Gittens gets a shot away, a tame effort straight at Zetterer from 22 yards out as he cuts in from the left. The correct intent, though.

Leeds look to circulate the ball across their back line. As mentioned pre-match, Chelsea will not mind letting their opponents get on the ball as they set out-of-possession traps. Aaronson eventually dribbles off the pitch on the far side.

Chelsea’s Argentine midfielder, Valentin Barco, is being booed by the Leeds fans every time he touches the ball. Barco will already be used to getting that treatment, as it has even happened to him while he’s been a substitute this season.

In other news, there’s a real Borussia Dortmund vibe to this Leeds away kit.

Leeds supporters boo Argentina World Cup squad member Barco’s every touch, and another Leeds foul, this time Justin on Gittens, prompts a second Chelsea free-kick.

A couple of early touches for Watson who plays a neat pass around the corner. Ampadu then lands a late tackle on Lacroix and Chelsea earn a free-kick in their own half.

Although there are still some empty seats, we are finally under way. Chelsea in their customary all blue, kicking from right to left. Leeds in their yellow away strip.

Chelsea and Leeds emerge from the tunnel, led out by Colwill and former Chelsea defender Ampadu. Here’s a reminder of the teams in full:

Chelsea Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Substitutes Martinez, Hato, Fofana, James, Neto, Palmer, Quenda, Rogers, Pedro

Leeds United Zetterer; Justin, Bijol, Muharemovic; James, Ampadu, Longstaff, Bard; Wilson, Aaronson; Nmecha

Substitutes Trafford, Gudmundsson, Elvedi, Bogle, Tanaka, Stach, Okafor, Calvert-Lewin, Bahoya

Daniel Farke believes Leeds can go far in the Carabao Cup this year 💪 pic.twitter.com/26ueAAUHoZ

On the Brazilian winger’s opportunity tonight, Hasselbaink said on Sky Sports: “He has to find his place. This is his opportunity... It’s not really an out-and-out left-wing [position] or a No 10 as he can play, but [with] good players it doesn’t matter where you put them on the pitch. He will find his spaces and he will be direct as he was when he came in against Arsenal. He is going to play for his place because he wants to play week-in, week-out.”

"He deserves to be there because of what he has shown" Xabi Alonso speaks about Reggie Watson with the 16-year-old set to make his Chelsea debut in their Carabao Cup game against Leeds 🌟 pic.twitter.com/AAn4Av3iEh

Tfl has closed South Kensington station after a “customer incident” meaning parts of the District Line have closed. The decision was then made to delay the match to give supporters more time to get to the stadium.

Reggie Watson will become the fourth youngest player, aged 16, in Chelsea’s history. But he will have to wait a little bit longer for his debut as kick-off has been delayed by 15 minutes to 8.15pm.

There will be a 15 minute delay to kick-off for our Carabao Cup third round tie with Leeds United tonight. The match will now begin at 20:15 BST. pic.twitter.com/MdDXpxgW09

A couple of cracking strikes from the Dutchman. Some player he was...

"Good old days!" Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink reflects on his goals for Leeds against Chelsea 🎞️ pic.twitter.com/bYjyFYIVIK
