LeedsAug 22: Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds 1Aug 25: Nottingham Forest 0 Leeds 2Aug 30: Leeds 1 Brentford 1Sep 5: Brighton 1 Leeds 1

As recently as March, a giant mural of Estêvão Willian appeared on the side of a building outside Stamford Bridge as the teenager threatened to become Chelsea’s number one poster boy.

He may no longer hold top billing outside the club, following a summer in which Chelsea spent a club-record £117m on Morgan Rogers to complete a fearsome front three alongside Cole Palmer and João Pedro.

A giant mural of the Brazilian teenager appeared on the side of a building close to Stamford Bridge in March.

But inside Stamford Bridge, nothing has changed. Estêvão remains one of Chelsea’s star boys and is part of an “untouchable” group of players that also includes Palmer, Rogers and Pedro. Sources believe Estêvão is a player the club will look at rewarding with an improved contract in the coming months.

Having already earned his Chelsea “untouchable” status, the next challenge for the 19-year-old winger – once nicknamed “Messinho” – is to make himself undroppable.

Estêvão may not be a perfect fit for Xabi Alonso’s three-at-the-back formation that features two 10s – Palmer and Rogers – behind a striker. But the boy from Brazil is certainly not being squeezed out and Chelsea’s manager has spoken of the need to be flexible.

Chelsea Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Substitutes Martinez, Hato, Fofana, James, Neto, Palmer, Quenda, Rogers, Pedro

Leeds United Zetterer; Justin, Bijol, Muharemovic; James, Ampadu, Longstaff, Bard; Wilson, Aaronson; Nmecha

Substitutes Trafford, Gudmundsson, Elvedi, Bogle, Tanaka, Stach, Okafor, Calvert-Lewin, Bahoya

Much has been made of Chelsea’s willingness to let the opposition have the ball under Xabi Alonso, but tonight they will likely be forced to dictate proceedings. In Leeds, they face one of only two sides who have completed fewer passes than them in the Premier League.

1. Ian Hamilton in 1967: 16 years, four months and 15 days2. Kingsley Whiffen in 1967: 16 years, five months and six days3. Reggie Walsh in 2025: 16 years, six months and 11 days4. Reggie Watson in 2026: 16 years, seven months and 14 days5. Tommy Langley in 1974: 16 years, nine months and one day

Asked how he will approach the Carabao Cup this season, Daniel Farke said: “We’ll try to win it. That’s the quickest way to Europe and to some glory. Of course knowing that the Premier League will always have the priority and knowing that we are as successful as possible there, especially to reach our first goal to establish ourselves [at] this level.

“We are not the favourites to win the Carabao Cup, we know this. Challenging, difficult games, but of course we travel to London in order to go through in the next round without doing anything stupid at this stage of the campaign because you also have to rotate a bit more and integrate a few new players. Nevertheless, we want to be at our best and anyhow possible we also want to go through to the next round.”

Tonight represents an opportunity for 16-year-old Reggie Watson to announce himself at senior level. The central-midfielder caught Alonso’s eye during pre-season when the Spaniard said of him: “Reggie Watson, a great midfielder. He thinks, he’s very collective, he’s very generous on the effort, intelligent with the ball”.

“For his age, I’m really impressed with him.”

Dan James passes a late fitness test to make Daniel Farke’s starting XI.

📋 Tonight's Starting XI pic.twitter.com/MQKQtGZm8c

Reggie Watson, 16, son of former Wigan midfielder Ben (of 2013 FA Cup final fame), makes his full Chelsea debut and becomes the club’s fourth youngest player. Estevao, Jamie Gittens and Danny Welbeck replace Alonso’s thrilling forward three, who are on the bench.

Chelsea XI Penders; Gusto, Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill, Chavarria; Watson, Barco; Estevao, Gittens; Welbeck

Your Blues to face Leeds United in the #CarabaoCup! #CFC pic.twitter.com/636SOiUXVB

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of tonight’s Carabao Cup third-round tie between Chelsea and Leeds United. This is a rematch of last season’s FA Cup semi-final which Chelsea edged by a single Enzo Fernández goal, but plenty has changed since then. Xabi Alonso has taken over the reins at Stamford Bridge and made a promising start, reeling off three wins before losing to Arsenal in an absorbing contest last Sunday. Chelsea are not involved in European competition this season, so the domestic cups represent an avenue to silverware, as well as an opportunity to tinker.

In Alonso’s way, though, stands a Leeds team whose manager, Daniel Farke, told the media on Tuesday that his side are aiming to win the Carabao Cup. Farke has overseen an impressive run of form, having lost only two of their previous 16 competitive matches in a stretch that extends back to March. Two wins at Nottingham Forest preceded draws against Brentford and Brighton to keep Leeds undefeated this term. Farke has suggested he will rotate in west London to “integrate new players” having brought in seven new recruits during the summer.

If Leeds are to reach the next round, they must reverse a heavily one-sided head-to-head record against their hosts, who have won each of their past 10 cup meetings (three in the League Cup, seven in the FA Cup). In fact, Chelsea have lost at this stage of the competition just once in the past 15 years, and that was against Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City four seasons ago.

Alonso broke up the exhilarating “JP Morgan” band (João Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers) for Chelsea’s victory over Luton Town in the previous round, handing starts to Danny Welbeck and Estêvão. Players such as Jamie Gittens and Geovany Quenda are also waiting in the wings and may get chances to impress tonight. Mike Penders could also be in line for a start between the sticks.

#1472. Bradley Lowery's mum issues heartbreaking statement to condemn 'cruel' Coventry fan who used her late son's photo to taunt Sunderland fans as 14-year-old boy hands himself into police

Published: 10:02 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 18:17 EDT, 1 November 2026

Bradley Lowery's mum has released a heartbreaking statement after a Coventry fan appeared to use his photograph to taunt Sunderland supporters.

The deplorable behaviour came during the Premier League clash between the two sides on Saturday, which the Sky Blues won 3-1.

A video on social media showed a supporter holding up a picture of Bradley - who tragically died from a rare form of childhood cancer at the age of six in 2017 - smiling in the direction of Sunderland fans, with the individual pointing at it and seen smirking at the same time.

A 14-year-old boy 'handed himself in' to West Midlands Police on Sunday.

In a statement on Sunday morning after the behaviour of the Coventry fan went viral, Bradley's mum Gemma shared a heartbreaking message.

'My beautiful boy deserves to be remembered with love, not hate,' she wrote. 'Yesterday, a Coventry fan used a photograph of Bradley to taunt Sunderland supporters. As Bradley’s mam, this is heartbreaking, especially as it’s one of my favourite photographs of him. Just look at that smile.

A Coventry fan appeared to use a photograph of Bradley Lowery to taunt Sunderland fans

A fan held up a photo of Bradley, the Sunderland fan who tragically passed away aged six from a rare form of childhood cancer, and was seen smirking and pointing

'I remember that day like it was yesterday. He was so happy, having so much fun. Those moments were precious because they were few and far between. So much of Bradley’s short life was spent battling cancer and enduring treatments no child should ever face. To see such a beautiful memory used in such a cruel way really does make my heart hurt.

'We are a football-loving family who follow Sunderland home and away. I’m all for football banter, but surely mocking a child who died from cancer is not banter? I hope the club takes appropriate action and the young lad’s family help him understand how hurtful his actions were.

'I don’t want hatred directed towards him, so please please don't, just for him to learn from this. Behind that photograph is a little boy who was loved beyond measure and a family who miss him every day. Thank you to everyone who has defended Bradley and shown us so much love. It means more than you know.'

Gemma continued: 'What some people don’t realise is that Bradley’s story didn’t end when his life did. Because of Bradley, children’s lives are being saved, hundreds of families have received vital support, and children facing unimaginable battles are being given hope.

'Through Super Brad’s Pad, families can escape hospital life, spend precious time together and make memories that last forever. That is Bradley’s legacy. The difference my little boy continues to make in this world. No amount of cruelty will ever take that away.

'So rather than let this photograph be remembered for hatred, I want it remembered for what it truly represents. My beautiful little boy, enjoying one of the happiest days of his life, with the biggest smile on his face. That is how I want the world to remember him. #CancerHasNoColours.'

Bradley touched the hearts of football fans across the UK during his battle with neuroblastoma, and formed a touching relationship with then Sunderland striker Jermain Defoe

Confirming that a teenager had handed himself in to authorities on Sunday, West Midlands Police said in a statement: 'We are aware of a video circulating on social media showing an incident at Coventry City's Premier League match with Sunderland.

'A thorough investigation has been launched, and a 14-year-old boy has since handed himself in and will be spoken with in due course.

'We understand the upset and outrage this video has caused in the community and to the victim's family, and our officers are keeping them up to date with the progress of our investigation and working closely alongside both football clubs.'

Coventry condemned the shameful behaviour in a strongly-worded statement on Saturday.

It read: 'Coventry City FC is aware of footage circulating on social media in connection with an incident during our Premier League fixture against Sunderland.

'The club does not tolerate offensive behaviour and will liaise with the relevant authorities to determine the appropriate course of action.'

Since Saturday's clash, more than £1,000 has been donated to the The Bradley Lowery Foundation by Coventry City fans, with many supporters leaving heartfelt messages as they refused to let the actions of one person define them.

Bradley was previously used by a fan as a taunt back in 2023 when Sheffield Wednesday supporter Dale Houghton was seen holding up a picture of him at a match against Sunderland and laughing.

Houghton was subsequently handed a 12-week suspended prison sentence and ordered to do 200 hours unpaid work.

Bradley pictured with his mum Gemma at his sixth birthday party back in May 2017

Bradley touched the hearts of football fans across the UK during his battle with neuroblastoma, a rare form of childhood cancer, before he tragically passed away aged just six in 2017.

The Bradley Lowery Foundation was set up in his honour, with the charity aiming to help families who are fundraising for treatment or equipment that is not readily available or covered by the NHS, while it also supports research into various childhood cancers, including neuroblastoma.

Bradley, who was diagnosed with neuroblastoma when he was just 18 months old, also built up a touching relationship with Jermain Defoe, who later called him his 'best mate'.

Defoe played for Sunderland at the time, and speaking in 2023, he said: 'He will always be in my heart, for the rest of my life. There's not a day that goes past where I don't wake up and think about little Bradley, because his love is genuine.'

#1471. Mainoo looks primed for battle with Man City’s new-look midfield

This was Manchester United’s first foray back into the Champions League for 1,003 days, but even with hazy memories of the competition, they know full well they are unlikely to have it this easy again in Europe this season.

After an unconvincing beginning to their Premier League campaign and with Manchester City the visitors to Old Trafford on Sunday, Michael Carrick will have been grateful for a gentle start to life back among Europe’s elite.

Little-known Sabah of Azerbaijan have quite the story to tell, but the closest they got to making this an awkward evening for United came in the first half when, already trailing 1-0, Joy-Lance Mickels miscued an inviting header from close range. Otherwise, it was one-way traffic.

United’s biggest threat on the night was complacency, but there was none of that. This was a professional, unfussy display with a few nice flourishes. Kobbie Mainoo impressed again in central midfield and Carrick was able to substitute a number of his best players early with the derby in mind, as well as resting Luke Shaw entirely.

Goals from Matheus Cunha, Bruno Fernandes and Benjamin Sesko in the first half killed the game as a contest before Lisandro Martínez scored a fourth with just over 20 minutes remaining.

Matheus Cunha opens the scoring for Manchester United with his first ever Champions League goal 🏄📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/ZDQBbEfizq

“It’s nice to keep a clean sheet and obviously win the game,” Carrick said. “Some of the football we played was really good – dangerous on the transition. The result looks comfortable, but it wasn’t always like that but we did a lot of good things.

United probably could not have asked for a softer return to Champions League football. Atlético Madrid at the Wanda Metropolitano next month will certainly be a very different beast, but it was a rewarding first 45 minutes all the same that paved the way for Carrick to ring the changes ahead of the derby.

Already leading 1-0, two goals shortly before the interval changed the complexion of the game and effectively extinguished any flickering hopes Sabah had of a gargantuan upset.

Founded just nine years ago, Sabah had navigated four qualifying rounds that began on July 7 just to reach this stage.

Throw in the fact Valdas Dambrauskas, their Lithuanian manager, got his break in coaching with the Manchester United Soccer Schools 20 years ago, and it is quite the heartwarming tale.

But there is not much sentiment at this level and, given time and space, United punished their inexperience and carelessness.

Carrick will not read too much into the performance. City will be an entirely different proposition and it will be interesting to see whether he goes for a two-man midfield with Bruno Fernandes deployed as an advanced No 10, or perhaps operates with a midfield three and adjusts his attack.

Either way, Mainoo will be central to the game plan.

It is hard to believe the England midfielder missed most of pre-season after reporting back late following the World Cup, because he has barely missed a beat in his last three outings, even if his team-mates have not always hummed to his tune.

There is so much to like about Mainoo. His manipulation of space, how he never looks under duress, even when hounded, and his vision on the ball. There was one lovely angled ball over the top here, after United had worked the space well, that released Fernandes in behind. His cross was cut out before Sesko could tap in.

Mainoo’s work off the ball has improved enormously, too. There were numerous instances here of him making a timely intervention or nicking the ball away at the right moment to recover possession.United have spent £155m reconfiguring their midfield, but Mainoo will be a constant. “He’s a fantastic player, it’s pretty obvious to see,” Carrick said. “He has a massive influence on our games. He is a real joy to have, he wants to improve, he wants to listen and it’s great to see.”

Kobbie Mainoo completed 81/83 passes, 6/6 accurate long balls and 10 passes into final third on his full Champions League debut ⭐️ pic.twitter.com/NK9BIGvc4m

It will certainly be interesting to see how Carrick’s new-look midfield shapes up against City’s own revamped one in the form of Elliot Anderson, Enzo Fernández and Ayyoub Bouaddi.

“There are some good connections and we have played some good football through the middle of the pitch,” Carrick added. “A lot of it is on wavelength and understanding of where each other wants the ball. We haven’t had the perfect start but there are really good signs.”

Carrick was suitably confident to withdraw Youri Tielemans at half-time and bring on Mason Mount, who was having a good pre-season before his familiar injury jinx hit, and he will have been pleased to see Sesko on the scoresheet again. “He definitely offers a different kind of threat,” Carrick said. “There are not many who can give us what Ben does with his physicality, playing on the last line. It’s great to have him back.”

Sesko’s goal, rounding the goalkeeper to slot home from Bryan Mbeumo’s pass after line-breaking balls from Mainoo and Fernandes, capped off a quick-fire three minutes when Sabah were unpicked. Before then, Cunha had picked out Tielemans’s burst into the penalty area, from where he pulled the ball back for Fernandes to coolly finish.

Benjamin Šeško rounds the goalkeeper to make it three for Manchester United 🔄📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/tnslugsmZM

Bruno Fernandes and Youri Tielemans combine to double Manchester United's lead ✌️📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nZnkwLWJ00

United had taken the lead when Kaheem Parris paid the price for a misplaced pass straight to Mbeumo, from which the ball was moved at pace between Sesko, Fernandes and Patrick Dorgu to tee up Cunha to score.

Dorgu was starting here at left-back with Shaw rested with one eye on City. It was an early glimpse of how Carrick is going to have to manage the minutes of his only recognised senior left-back, who is not going to be able to play every few days.

Carrick prefers Dorgu further up the pitch and it remains to be seen if he trusts the Dane at left-back in bigger games than this.

With City having played in Porto on Tuesday and had a little extra rest time, the United manager will have been pleased he got the chance to withdraw several key players early. He was even able to give a rare run-out to Joshua Zirkzee and it was the Dutchman who helped to force the fourth goal.

Lisandro Martínez pounces on a defensive mistake from Sabah to make it four 🫣📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/eTAYgMmV9Q

Fernandes’s quick free-kick caught out Sabah and Zirkzee back-heeled the ball goalwards. It bounced off Aden McCarthy and from there goalkeeper Stas Pokatilov got himself in a dreadful spin, unable to locate the ball by which point Martínez had blasted it in from a yard out.

“Nice to have a clean sheet and obviously win the game. Some of our attacking play was fantastic. We were dangerous in transition, defended well in the most part. The result looks comfortable but it was not as easy as that. Kobbie [Mainoo] is a fantastic player, it is pretty obvious to see. He has a massive influence on our game and a real joy to have. Through the middle of the pitch, we have played some good football at times and we can get better. There are some good signs which we have shown tonight. The confidence is there, like at Everton on Sunday for large spells, just took a hit there at the end with the result. It is always nice to win. Another big one on Sunday.”

The final whistle is blown at Old Trafford and Manchester United claim a 4-0 victory on their return to the Champions League. Goals from Cunha, Fernandes, Sesko and Martinez give Michael Carrick’s side three points in their opening game of the competition. Debutants Sabah return home with nothing and no goals, despite some decent chances to get a goal.

A number of empty seats at Old Trafford are becoming visible as some home fans have seen enough, knowing their side is going to win.

Sabah have had a few chances to come away from their Champions League debut with a goal but have wasted some great chances, including one just now. Mickels delivers a lovely cross from the left, which perfectly picks out Mbina, but his header goes just over the bar.

Mickels wasted a glorious chance in the first half and he comes close to goal a now but drags his shot just wide of the far post from the left side of the box.

How on earth have the officials missed that one? Cunha catches Almeida on the leg and it should be at least a booking but the officials do not see it, despite the linesman being not far away. Cunha is very lucky as that was a nasty challenge.

Sabah would love to at the very least send their travelling fans back to Azerbaijan with a goal on their Champions League debut. You do wonder how different the game could have been had Mickels not missed a sitter that would have seen Sabah make it 1-1.

Michael Carrick is going to make his final two changes of the night as youngsters Lacey and Amass come on.

A bit of a soft goal for Sabah to concede. Fernandes clips in a free-kick into the Sabah box which picks out the run of Zirkzee. The Dutchman’s backheel is blocked and Sabah should then deal with the danger. However, Sabah make an absolute mess of things and their keeper Pokatilov has no idea where the ball is, allowing Martinez to nick in and smash the ball into the net.

Lisandro Martínez pounces on a defensive mistake from Sabah to make it four 🫣📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/eTAYgMmV9Q

Lepinjica is the first Sabah player into the book tonight for a cynical trip on Mount.

Zirkzee, only just on the pitch, shoots from range but it is straight down the throat of Pokatilov.

Puchacz takes the free-kick from just over 25 yards out and strikes it well but the effort is just off target.

Perhaps with the Manchester derby on Sunday in mind, Michael Carrick is going to make a double change. Zirkzee and Santos replace Sesko and Mainoo.

Dorgu is the first player into the book tonight. Lepinjica spots the run of Parris into the right channel and plays a clever pas forward. Dorgu cynically brings Parris down and is rightly booked.

The visitors are making a change as Parris is replaced by Isaev.

Manchester United come close to a fourth and Cunha his second. The home side work it well near the Sabah penalty area with a couple of clever flicks and passes before Cunha has an effort saved by Pokatilov to his left.

Mazraoui receives it out in space on the right and cuts inside onto his left. He comes across the face of the penalty area before getting his shot away but his effort is off target.

Sabah are enjoying a decent spell of possession but have not yet threatened Lammens’ goal in this second half.

Is Yoro lucky? Mickels appeared to turn him not far outside the Manchester United penalty area but Yoro is not penalised. It did on first viewing look like a foul and would have been at least a yellow card.

We are back under way at Old Trafford. How quickly might Michael Carrick make changes with Sunday’s Manchester derby in mind? Well, he has made one change at the break as Mount replaces Tielemans. It is Mount’s first appearance of the season. Sabah have brought on Mbina at the break.

That is game, set and match before half-time at Old Trafford as the dam has burst for Sabah. Sesko is played in behind by Mbeumo and is one-on-one with Pokatilov. Sesko takes it around Pokatilov before putting it into the empty net.

Michael Carrick’s side have their second of the night not long before half-time and it is a well-taken goal. Cunha, from the left side of the box, plays it inside to Tielemans. The Belgian takes one touch before, on the turn, playing it back into the path of Fernandes, who finds the net with a first-time finish.

Fernandes has an effort from the edge of the Sabah box but blazes his effort high over the bar.

That’s a warning there for United. Fernandes gives the ball away in the middle with a heavy touch and Sabah break through the tall, languid figure of Lepinjica. Parris’ cross loops the far post where Mickels should have done better than steer an inviting header into the side netting. Bit of a let off for Carrick’s side.

Sabah should be level as they miss a sitter. Parris, from the right side of the box, clips a cross to the back post that picks out Mickels. He should score but puts his header into the side netting. That should have been the equaliser for Sabah.

Dorgu clips in a cross from the left side of the box and picks out Sesko, whose hooked first-time effort goes just wide.

Half an hour in and United have been in command. It’s not scintillating but they warrant their lead and punished a misplaced pass by Parris brutally. Mainoo is orchestrating the game in the middle of the pitch. Best player on the park so far.

Parris’ shot from the edge of the box takes a deflection and goes behind for a corner. It is wasted though by Sabah as the inswinger is easily caught by Lammens.

Tielemans steps in with a crucial interception inside his own box to deny Mickels the chance of a shot on goal.

The Brazilian has his first Champions League goal but it is gifted by Sabah. The visitors are threatening a counter-attack but Parris inexplicably gives the ball away on halfway with a dreadful pass across the pitch. The ball is then moved out to the left, where Dorgu crosses. He picks out Cunha, whose first-time effort with his side foot hits the Sabah keeper Pokatilov and goes into the net. A sense of frustration had been growing inside Old Trafford but Sabah have rather gifted Manchester United the opener there.

Matheus Cunha opens the scoring for Manchester United with his first ever Champions League goal 🏄📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/ZDQBbEfizq

Sabah give it away inside their own half and Manchester United flood forward towards the Sabah penalty area. Mbuemo drives forward and cuts inside onto his preferred left foot before getting his shot away from the edge of the box but it is straight at Pokatilov.

That is outstanding defensive work from Dasdamirov. Mainoo plays a quite sensational first-time ball in behind into the right channel to pick out the run of Fernandez. The Manchester United captain has Sesko waiting in the middle for the cross but Dasdamirov steps in with an absolutely essential interception or else Sesko would have had a tap-in.

Sabah need to be careful as now a few times they have been caught in possession deep in their own territory.

Cunha sends in a corner from the left that threatens to go in at the far corner but Sabah keeper Pokatilov catches it near his own line.

Sabah are making their Champions League debut and so too tonight are Cesc Fabregas’ Como, who have just taken the lead at home against RB Leipzig. Manchester United will travel to Como in late October on matchday three. Manchester United play RB Leipzig at home on matchday six.

Sabah have to negotiate a couple of Manchester United corners in quick succession and they do so. The visitors’ starting XI tonight has a very international feel to it:

Sabah FC have named a starting XI featuring 11 different nationalities 🌍🇰🇿 Stas Pokatilov🇩🇿 Akim Zedadka🇦🇿 Rahman Dashdamirov🇿🇦 Aden McCarthy🇵🇱 Tymoteusz Puchacz🇺🇿 Umarali Rakhmonaliev🇭🇷 Ivan Lepinjica🇯🇲 Kaheem Parris🇷🇸 Veljko Simic🇳🇬 Christian Nwachukwu🇷🇼 Joy-Lance… pic.twitter.com/ih5Sf1aeie

Mazraoui, despite starting at right-back, has already had three shots in the game. Two have been outside the box that have been blocked and the latest hits the side netting from the right side of the penalty area.

Mazraoui plays a pass forward into Cunha on the right side of the box and the Brazilian tries to beat Pokatilov at the near post but the Sabah keeper makes the save and pushes it around the post for a corner.

Sabah are able to clear their lines from Mbeumo’s delivery.

Sabah seem content to take risks on the ball deep inside their own half and play out from the back. Will that be a masterstroke or is it asking for trouble?

Sabah make their first foray into the Manchester United penalty area and there are appeals for handball. It did hit Dorgu’s hand but it was right down by his side and that is not a deliberate handball. Sabah do win a corner, which Dorgu heads away.

Sesko, fresh off what he thought was going to be the winner at Everton on Sunday, has been given the nod to start up top for the home side tonight. He is very close to closing the Sabah goalkeeper Pokatilov down inside his own six-yard box and that was nearly a horrific moment for the Champions League debutants a matter of minutes into their debut in this competition.

Sabah started their journey through the qualifying rounds of this comeptition back in the early parts of July so they have already played quite a number of games so far this season, in comparison to Manchester United’s three competitive fixtures coming into tonight.

As has been the case at every Champions League game this week, there is a moment silence to remember the victims of the recent deadly floods in Nepal.

We are under way at Old Trafford. Manchester United, three-time winners of this trophy, return to the Champions League whilst Sabah make their debut in the competition.

It’s 1,003 days since the Champions League anthem has been heard at Old Trafford and, to be honest, it feels longer. There are about 500 Sabah fans here tonight.

Michael Carrick has made four changes for Sabah to the team that drew 2-2 against Everton. Benjamin Sesko is given his first start of the season with Marcus Rashford dropping to the bench. Luke Shaw was given an additional rest day on Wednesday and is left out of the squad. It makes sense with Sunday’s derby against Manchester City to come but it’s an early glimpse of the delicate balance Carrick will have to strike with his only recognised senior left back this season. Shaw can’t be expected to play every few days given his history of injury problems.

It looks like Patrick Dorgu will be operating at left back against Sabah. This is United’s 300th fixture in the European Cup, including qualifiers. On the subject of qualifiers, Sabah became only the sixth side to navigate four qualifying rounds to reach the European Cup proper, with their campaign starting back on July 7. That was the same day Argentina beat Egypt in the last 16 of the World Cup. The Azerbaijan club were only formed nine years ago so have had quite the ascent since.

At 8pm on Thursday night, Manchester United will kick a ball in the Champions League for the first time in three seasons.

It must mark the start of a permanent return to Europe’s premier club competition. If United are serious about once again challenging for the Premier League title and building a £2bn stadium, that must be the way forward.

This is only the seventh time in 13 campaigns that United have been in the Champions League and the implications have been significant.

Presenting your Champions League Reds 📋❤️‍🔥

Manchester United make their return to the Champions League as they host tournament debutants Sabah of Azerbaijan on matchday one at Old Trafford. It will be the first time that Manchester United have faced an Azerbaijani side in European competition.

Manchester United have one win, one loss and one draw to their name in their opening three Premier League games. They were seconds away from winning their second game of the season on Sunday but conceded a late equaliser at Everton. They last featured in the Champions League during the 2023/24 season, when they were eliminated in the group stage, and have won just one of their last nine games in the competition.

“It means an awful lot [to be back in the Champions League],” Manchester United boss Michael Carrick said. “Challenging yourself against the elite, the very best. This football club has been used to being the best. It is not something you can take for granted. We missed out on it for a number of years and now we are back. It is where we expect to be without getting ahead of ourselves. We have made huge steps to make it in, now it is about pushing into the next chapter and evolution if the squad and this is certainly where we want to be.

“I do not think it is a case of if we get to a certain stage it is a success and if we do not it is not. We have to embrace the new challenge that we are facing as a group and push to what we can push to. If we get further down the line in this competition then who knows? I am not writing anything off. But we are taking it step by step and we certainly are not getting ahead of ourselves. We have got a squad that is strong enough to compete.”

Sabah make their Champions League debut having been founded just eight years ago in September 2017. Back in April, they secured the Azerbaijan top-flight title for the first time in their history and also won the Azerbaijan Cup in May. They earned a spot in the Champions League group stages after beating Hapoel Be’er Sheva 6-4 on aggregate. In the previous three seasons, they have tried to reach the group stages of the Europa and Conference Leagues but failed to do so. They have won all three leagues thus far, including a 5-0 home win over Zira last Saturday.

Team news from Old Trafford to follow shortly.

#1470. Subcycle videography of Landau–Zener–Majorana transitions in graphene

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Strong light fields have unlocked entirely new possibilities to tailor coherent electron trajectories, engineer band structures and shape emergent phases of matter all-optically1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9. Unravelling the underlying quantum mechanisms requires a visualization of the lightwave-driven electron motion10,11 directly in the band structure. Although photoelectron momentum microscopy has imaged photoexcited electrons averaged over many cycles of light12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19, subcycle band-structure videography has been limited to small electron momenta8,20. Yet, lightwave-driven elementary processes in quantum materials often occur throughout momentum space. Here we introduce attosecond-precision, subcycle band-structure videography covering the entire first Brillouin zone and visualize one of the most fundamental but elusive strong-field processes: non-adiabatic Landau–Zener–Majorana tunnelling. The interplay of strong-field-driven acceleration within the Dirac-like band structure of graphene and periodic Landau–Zener–Majorana interband tunnelling manifests in a coherent subcycle displacement and distortion of the carrier distribution at the Brillouin zone edge. The extremely non-thermal electron distributions also allow us to disentangle competing scattering processes and assess their impact on coherent electronic control. Our panoramic view of field-driven electron motion enables a new quality of microscopic understanding of strong-field control of quantum materials.

According to the adiabatic theorem, a time-dependent, two-level quantum system remains in its ground state during a slow evolution21. By contrast, driving the system faster than its intrinsic timescale through an avoided energy crossing can create a finite occupation of the excited state by means of non-adiabatic transitions called Landau–Zener–Majorana (LZM) tunnelling22,23,24. This mechanism is central for strong-field light–matter interaction7,10,25,26. Yet, a direct observation of this foundational quantum effect in momentum space is still missing. The unique properties of graphene27 form the ideal test bed for observing LZM transitions. Its quasirelativistic electron dispersion and the robustness under irradiation with intense light have made this material a prime test ground for lightwave electronics26,28, including the demonstration of the first lightwave electronic logic gates7 and Floquet–Bloch states18,19. This has opened revolutionary prospects for quantum control, quantum sensing and quantum computation applications10,11,29.

Understanding and shaping the opportunities offered by lightwave control of electrons requires a direct observation of how LZM transitions dictate strong-field light–matter interaction. Attosecond spectroscopy has reached sufficient temporal resolution to access these dynamics30,31, and time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (trARPES) in combination with momentum microscopy32 has visualized electron dynamics directly in the band structure of quantum materials or in the orbitals of molecular layers12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,33. trARPES with subcycle temporal resolution8,20 has combined these approaches but offered only limited 1D momentum space access. To track coherent strong-field phenomena and scattering-induced momentum redistribution, observing carrier dynamics across the entire momentum space is imperative.

Here we expand subcycle band-structure videography to the entire first Brillouin zone (BZ). The new platform overcomes previous restrictions of momentum microscopy and subcycle ARPES, increasing the momentum area accessible with subcycle resolution by more than two orders of magnitude and the available field strengths by one order of magnitude. Exploiting few-cycle mid-infrared (MIR) field transients with large peak amplitudes, we drive coherent electron dynamics at the BZ edge of graphene. This approach reveals the simultaneous displacement and distortion of the light-driven electron distribution, uncovering the interplay between coherent intraband and interband dynamics underlying LZM transitions in graphene. Moreover, tracking the non-thermal subcycle distributions in 2D momentum space reveals how different scattering processes affect lightwave-driven dynamics.

When low-intensity, short-wavelength light interacts with electrons in a solid, it can induce perturbative interband quantum jumps in momentum regions in which the occupied and unoccupied bands are separated by an integer multiple of the photon energy (Fig. 1a). In graphene, the non-trivial pseudospin texture influences the dipole moments between the lower and upper halves of the Dirac cone, leading to a distribution of excited carriers only along the direction orthogonal to the light field34,35. Conversely, a strong low-frequency field transient can adiabatically accelerate carriers within their bands on subcycle timescales, deflecting the Fermi surface in momentum space according to Bloch’s acceleration theorem (Fig. 1b). During their excursion, electrons experience an energy gap, which, in graphene, varies linearly near the K point to form an avoided crossing. Thus, field-driven acceleration may drive prototypical LZM transitions, which leave a markedly different occupation in momentum space compared with Fig. 1a. If the driving field is periodic, the phase accumulated between consecutive non-adiabatic events—the Stückelberg phase—results in so-called Landau–Zener–Stückelberg–Majorana (LZSM) interference36,37.

a, Illustration of the fundamental electronic processes governing light–matter interaction in undoped graphene at the K point in the weak-field regime. Here electrons can be promoted from the valence band to the conduction band by absorption. In graphene, the optical selection rules favour transitions in the momentum direction perpendicular to the polarization of the electric field. b, In the strong-field regime, electrons can undergo ballistic acceleration by an electric field (dashed blue arrow). Simultaneously, the field can drive interband LZM transitions on subcycle timescales, allowing electrons to tunnel from the valence band to the conduction band (solid red arrows). This results in an elongated electron distribution in the previously unoccupied conduction band, with the weight of the electron population in the direction parallel to the field. c, In the experimental scheme shown in the bottom half, an s-polarized, phase-stable MIR pulse (red) drives a monolayer of graphene, and a p-polarized XUV probe pulse (purple) at variable time delay, t, provides snapshots of the induced dynamics with subcycle temporal resolution. The photoemitted electrons (blue) enter a photoemission momentum microscope. This enables the simultaneous detection of both parallel momenta, kx and ky, and kinetic energy for every individual electron. The upper half shows a femtosecond snapshot of the 2D band structure of a monolayer of graphene, recorded with the momentum microscope. The field of view extends over the entire first BZ, allowing tracking of the electronic occupation to slightly beyond the six K points.

To access this regime, we drive electrons in epitaxially grown monolayer graphene on SiC (ref. 38) with intense phase-stable MIR pulses (central frequency, 30 THz). After a delay time, t, extreme ultraviolet (XUV) pulses (central photon energy, 21.7 eV) photoemit the electrons with subcycle resolution. Their energies and momenta are detected with a time-of-flight photoemission momentum microscope (Fig. 1c and Methods). In equilibrium, the photoemission signal maps the occupied band structure. The high XUV photon energy and the large acceptance angle of the momentum microscope capture the electronic structural dynamics throughout the entire first BZ, including its six corners, in a single measurement with sub-10-fs resolution.

Figure 2a shows several momentum distribution maps in the vicinity of a K point at selected energies. The in-plane component of the p-polarized XUV radiation driving the photoemission process is set parallel to the kx-axis. Owing to the matrix elements in the photoemission process, the intensity exhibits the characteristic horseshoe-like distribution for energies far below the Dirac point39. The influence of the dark corridor at ky = 0 and positive kx − K values is suppressed for energies close to the Dirac point, ED, and the photoemission intensity forms a disc. To ensure that the relevant dynamics occur along a direction in which the two branches of the Dirac cone have equal photoemission intensities, we apply an s-polarized MIR field along the ky-axis. For large negative delays (t = −70 fs), a slice of the photoelectron intensity for kx − K = 0 (Fig. 2b) shows two linear bands with a slope of ħvF (with the Fermi velocity vF = 10.7 Å fs−1) and a Fermi level located 200 meV above the Dirac point. With increasing t, we observe an apparent shift of the overall band structure owing to momentum streaking20 of photoemitted electrons in vacuo by the MIR field. This effect can be used to retrieve the MIR waveform at the sample surface (Extended Data Fig. 2a and Methods). Compensating for this shift isolates the subcycle electron dynamics within the band structure.

a, Zoomed-in curvature-filtered (Methods) cuts through the band structure at a selected K point. The red arrow (top) indicates the MIR polarization. The dashed grey line (bottom) marks the BZ border. The solid black lines represent the integration range in momentum space used in the three panels in b. b, Streaking-compensated and curvature-filtered view into the band structure of graphene at the Dirac point before the arrival of the MIR pulse (t = −70 fs) and for selected delay times during the interaction with the MIR pulse, t = −13.6 fs and t = 6.3 fs (raw data, Extended Data Fig. 2b). The last two snapshots show how the electron distribution is accelerated along the Dirac cone away from the equilibrium Fermi level. c, Current extracted from the occupation imbalance in the photoemission maps (blue points) and MIR waveform reconstructed from the momentum streaking (red points). Dashed black lines mark the temporal positions shown in b. The lightwave-driven current is extracted by tracking the imbalance in the occupation for positive and negative momenta (red and green shaded areas) in the raw photoemission spectra (inset) and normalized on the total amount of carriers in both regions before the pulse arrives. The grey shaded area indicates the normalized population increase in the conduction band extracted from a similar measurement.

A corresponding femtosecond snapshot of the band structure for t = −13.6 fs shows a highly non-thermal lightwave-driven electron distribution (Fig. 2b). In the upper half of the Dirac cone (E − ED ≥ 0), the ky > 0 branch is occupied up to about 1 eV, whereas the ky < 0 branch is completely unoccupied. Half a cycle of the MIR carrier wave later (t = 6.3 fs), the field direction is inverted and the electron distribution is mirrored. The extreme carrier redistribution on subcycle timescales clearly proves the non-perturbative nature of the light–matter interaction. This scenario is expected for the small Keldysh parameter near the Dirac point (γ = 0.075; Methods). Still, it is notable that the few-fs timescales accessible with our experiment allow us to see lightwave-driven intraband acceleration despite the extremely fast scattering processes in graphene33,35,40,41,42,43,44,45. Asymmetric electron distributions in momentum space correspond to the excitation of an intraband current. By tracking the imbalance in the band occupation for positive and negative ky momenta (Fig. 2c, inset and Methods), we extract the lightwave-driven intraband current density and directly compare it with the MIR driving waveform (Fig. 2c). Although the current density shows a similar envelope and oscillation frequency as the MIR transient, there is a non-trivial phase shift between the two waveforms.

From Bloch’s acceleration theorem20,46, we would expect that, in the absence of decoherence, the momentum accumulated by electrons follows the integral over the MIR field, resulting in a phase shift of π/2 between the current and the field. A Fourier analysis (Methods) allows us to retrieve this phase delay with attosecond precision. Notably, the average delay of 4.9 ± 0.2 fs is much smaller than the value associated with a fully coherent evolution (8.3 fs). Simulations based on the semiconductor Bloch equations (SBEs)6 in the relaxation time approximation (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Methods) reproduce this phase shift for a mean scattering time of 9.0 ± 0.7 fs. As non-adiabatic LZM transitions rely on the coherent and unperturbed field-driven evolution of charge carriers, this sets the time and length scales relevant for lightwave electronics. Despite the short scattering time, electrons in graphene can travel almost 100 Å owing to their large velocity of vF = 10.7 Å fs−1.

Most notably, the current is accompanied by an ultrafast increase of the total conduction-band population within the strongest MIR half-cycles (Fig. 2c, grey shaded area). Perturbative interband transitions are too weak to become effective on subcycle timescales and, in equilibrium, straightforward vertical interband transitions are prohibited in the doped sample by Pauli blocking. Hence, the observed electronic structural dynamics attest to an interplay between strong-field-driven intraband and interband currents. Next, we unveil the microscopic mechanisms by imaging the full 2D momentum space. With this capability, unavailable in previous subcycle photoemission experiments8,20, we can directly target the coherent light–matter interaction regime and the subsequent relaxation dynamics.

Before the interaction with the MIR transient, the equilibrium carrier distribution in the conduction band (E − ED ≥ 0) of n-doped graphene can be approximated by a disc centred about each K point (Fig. 2a). If the electrons were solely subject to an accelerating electric field, they would, in accordance with Bloch’s acceleration theorem46, collectively move along the ky direction and we would merely expect a time-dependent centre-of-mass (COM) displacement of this disc. Although the streaking-compensated 2D momentum maps (Fig. 3a) indeed show pronounced oscillations of the COM displacement with the frequency of the strong driving field and a maximum amplitude of 0.078 Å−1 (Fig. 3b), they also reveal a further notable change of their shape (Fig. 3a,c). The observed deviations from the initial shape of the distribution are on the same order as the COM displacement.

The inset indicates the position of the evaluated window in momentum space and the arrow shows the MIR polarization. The grey lines mark the BZ borders. The Gaussian fits illustrate the width of the projection of the carrier distribution on the kx-axis (brown) and the ky-axis (green). The fits of the first panel are shown in black in the later snapshots as a reference. Under the influence of the field, the carrier distribution is displaced along ky (t = −43.6 fs). Owing to LZM transitions, the carrier distribution is elongated along ky, forming an ellipse (t = 3 fs). For later delays (t = 26.3 fs), scattering leads to a broadening also along kx. For vanishing fields, the electron distribution relaxes back to its original shape (t = 233 fs). b, Displacement of the COM of the electron distribution. The inset shows the Fourier transform of the oscillating electron distribution (green line) and the driving field (red shaded area). Dashed black lines mark the temporal positions of the momentum maps in a. c, Evolution of the change in the size of the electron distribution, Δσ, characterized by the width of the Gaussians used to fit the carrier distribution along the kx-axis (brown) and the ky-axis (green). The Fourier transform in the inset reveals oscillations in the width of the distribution along the ky-axis, with pronounced components at the second harmonic of the driving frequency during the initial half-cycles of the driving field (grey shaded area). The vertical orange lines in b and c are guides to the eye to relate the oscillation in the width of the electron distribution to the motion of its COM.

Already after the first MIR field cycles (Fig. 3a, t = 3 fs), the Fermi surface is strongly elongated from 0.054 Å−1 to 0.096 Å−1 in the direction parallel to the field, whereas the change in the orthogonal direction is only 0.014 Å−1 (Fig. 3a, Gaussian fits). The Fermi surface is no longer circular but takes on an elliptical shape. The time-dependent change in the ky width (Fig. 3c, green line) directly correlates with the field strength. Furthermore, this width oscillates at twice the MIR carrier frequency while the COM displacement tracks the electric field similarly to the current plotted in Fig. 2c. Because the maximum broadening coincides with the peak COM displacement, we can rule out motion blur as the origin of the elongation in the ky direction. Notably, the electron distribution encompasses the Dirac point at all delay times, even for the largest displacements.

All of these intriguing dynamics can be microscopically explained by a full quantum-mechanical solution of the SBEs6 (Methods), which account for intraband and interband transitions as well as LZM-type interband coupling, on equal footing. A systematic switch-off analysis pinpoints how specific aspects of coherent strong-field light–matter interaction manifest in the observed dynamics (Extended Data Fig. 4a). The periodic COM shift of the electron distribution is clearly associated with field-driven intraband motion of charge carriers. Yet, the distribution retains its circular shape and separates from the K point for large displacement if interband dynamics are switched off. Once interband coupling is included, the theory shows the same elongation of the carrier distribution as the experiment (Extended Data Fig. 4b). The theory also qualitatively reproduces the increase in carrier density in the conduction band (Extended Data Fig. 5), confirming that interband transitions at the K point act like a well that feeds electrons into the upper part of the Dirac cone on subcycle timescales.

These transitions originate from strong-field interband coupling, whereas conventional perturbative interband photoexcitation is suppressed by orders of magnitude under our experimental conditions (Extended Data Fig. 6). Owing to pseudospin selection rules34,35, photoexcitation would occur in momentum regions with |kx − K| > 0, located perpendicular to the polarization of the incident light (Extended Data Fig. 6a). By contrast, the coupled intraband and interband dynamics of the LZM scenario leads to the observed unidirectional elongation of the electron distribution parallel to the electric field (Extended Data Fig. 6b). Simulations with varying field strengths confirm that this feature is characteristic of the strong-field regime (Extended Data Fig. 7).

The region in which LZM-type tunnelling can occur is determined by the field strength, E0, and the energy gap, which increases linearly with |kx − K|. For E0 = 1.57 MV cm−1, the transition region is confined to momenta |kx − K| ≤ 0.08 Å−1 (Fig. 3a, t = 3 fs), corresponding to a Keldysh parameter of γ ≤ 0.63. Accounting for scattering and limited momentum resolution, this value is in good agreement with the original LZM formula \({P}_{{\rm{L}}{\rm{Z}}{\rm{M}}}=\exp \left(-2{\rm{\pi }}\frac{\hbar {v}_{{\rm{F}}}}{2|e|{E}_{0}}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\right)\), which predicts diabatic transitions in a momentum range |kx − K| ≤ 0.04 Å−1 (probability 1/e2 width; Methods). This confirms that the linearly dispersing Dirac cone of graphene is a perfect realization of the original model Hamiltonian23. And even Landau, Zener and Majorana’s assumption that the energy levels intersect at a constant speed holds true, as the strong driving fields propel the electrons past the intersection point in less than 1 fs—much faster than the MIR oscillation period (Methods).

The interplay between intraband motion and LZM tunnelling also explains the modulations of the width observed at twice the driving frequency (Fig. 3c). Because the region close to the K point features the lowest tunnelling barrier, electron injection into the upper part of the Dirac cone becomes most efficient in the few-fs time window between a field extremum and the nearest peak displacement of the pre-existing population, which occurs twice per optical cycle. Scattering shortens this time window, shifting the optimal injection time. This situation should result in a step-like increase of the population in the conduction band, with a phase determined by the interplay of Pauli blocking, the evolution of the field amplitude and scattering (Methods). However, a step-like increase can only be reproduced by simulations using extremely strong dephasing that destroys the quantum memory between successive LZM transitions (Extended Data Fig. 9). For realistic dephasing rates, the step-like character transforms into pronounced 2ω oscillations. Their presence in the experimental width of the electron distribution suggests interference of electrons owing to their accumulated phase between individual tunnelling events, emphasizing the role of quantum coherence in light-field-driven devices.

Although LZM dynamics dominate at early delay times, scattering limits the time frame for fully coherent light–matter interaction. At t = 26.3 fs (Fig. 3a), the initially anisotropic electron distribution broadens also along the kx direction and approaches a circular shape with a radius of about 0.065 Å−1, before it contracts to a more equilibrated and isotropic distribution (t = 233 fs). This ultrafast change of the elliptical distribution (Fig. 3c) reflects the interplay between field-driven acceleration, LZM transitions, scattering and carrier relaxation. Our SBE simulations (Extended Data Fig. 10 and Methods) predict distinctive momentum fingerprints for electron–electron and electron–optical phonon scattering. 2D mapping thus allows us to identify their signatures (Fig. 4a). Neglecting all forms of scattering results in a broadening (up to 0.053 Å−1) and displacement (about 0.107 Å−1) of the carrier density along the ky direction and the distribution remains elliptical after the MIR pulse (t = 233 fs), retaining the momentum hallmark of LZM transitions. Moreover, the phase delay of the microscopic current (Fig. 4b) is approximately π/2, as expected for undamped intraband motion. Introducing electron–electron scattering, the initially strongly broadened and displaced momentum distribution (t = 27 fs) partially thermalizes (t = 233 fs) and shrinks to a circular shape with a radius of about 0.038 Å−1. Still, the peculiar angular dependence of electron–electron scattering41,47 retains a large ellipticity on shorter timescales, and the phase delay is only marginally affected. This is caused by the reduced phase space for scattering imposed by the pseudospin texture of graphene.

The leftmost panels show how the carrier distribution behaves for intermediate and late delay times t, based on the SBEs without scattering. The light grey line marks the half-maximum contour, highlighting the shape of the carrier distribution. For comparison, the dark grey line shows the corresponding contour when also excluding interband coupling, emphasizing its role in reproducing the experimental observations. It is included in the other panels for reference. The middle and right panels show the carrier distribution including different scattering channels: electron–electron (ee) scattering and electron–electron combined with electron–optical phonon (ee + op) scattering, respectively. The cartoons in the insets illustrate the regions in momentum space accessible for an electron (small, blue sphere) through scattering (dark regions: accessible; bright regions: inaccessible). b, Time-dependent evolution of the extracted current for different scattering mechanisms (dotted purple line: no scattering; dotted light blue line: ee scattering; solid blue line: ee + op scattering). Without scattering (dotted curves), the distribution is broadened strongly only in the direction of the field. By including scattering with optical phonons (solid curves), it is possible to reach a qualitative agreement with the experiment. a.u., arbitrary units.

Simulations including scattering with Γ point longitudinal (LO) and transverse (TO) optical phonons reproduce the experimentally observed dynamics very well. For t = 27 fs, the electron distribution shows a substantial broadening in both the ky (about 0.051 Å−1) and the kx (about 0.041 Å−1) directions, associated with an isotropic redistribution of the charge carriers. This leads to a nearly circular distribution whose COM is shifted by only 0.008 Å−1 at t = 27 fs, much less than in the previous cases. This results from a large change in the phase delay (Fig. 4b), approaching a value of π/4. After the pulse (t = 233 fs), the distribution relaxes to a fully circular shape with a radius of approximately 0.031 Å−1. Both the phase delay and the time-dependent broadening of the electron distribution (Fig. 4c) are in good qualitative agreement with the experiment. We can, thus, identify the key limiting factor for coherent control dictated by the fastest momentum redistribution channel, which, in graphene, is electron–optical phonon scattering (Fig. 4b, solid blue line).

Our experiment opens the momentum horizon of subcycle photoemission over the entire first BZ of basically any quantum material. This universal tool enabled us to directly observe LZM transitions in the band structure of a solid. Attosecond-precision videography of graphene unravels how interband LZM tunnelling couples to field-driven intraband acceleration along the Dirac cone and how scattering influences and limits a fully coherent evolution. This platform may soon address other key questions of condensed matter physics and ultrafast information technologies, from optical band-structure engineering and phase transitions to light-field-driven sculpting of molecular orbitals.

The subcycle momentum microscopy setup (Extended Data Fig. 1a) is based on two ytterbium-doped potassium gadolinium tungstate (Yb:KGW) amplifiers (CARBIDE, Light Conversion Inc.). Each amplifier generates near-infrared light pulses with a duration of 250 fs, a centre wavelength of 1,030 nm and a pulse energy of 1.5 mJ, at a repetition rate of 50 kHz. In the probe arm, the second harmonic of the output of a four-stage noncollinear optical-parametric amplifier (NOPA; ORPHEUS-OPCPA, Light Conversion Inc.)48 yields carrier-envelope phase (CEP)-stabilized pulses centred at 400 nm with a pulse duration of 20 fs. These pulses are focused into a high-pressure argon gas jet to generate high-order harmonics (Extended Data Fig. 1b) in a vacuum beamline49. The seventh harmonic at a photon energy of 21.7 eV is spectrally selected by two multilayer mirrors (Extended Data Fig. 1b, grey shaded area). They feature a bandwidth of 0.9 nm around 57 nm and thus support a Fourier-limited pulse duration of less than 10 fs. The XUV pulses enter the experimental ultrahigh-vacuum (UHV) chamber, the momentum microscope32, through a 200-nm-thin aluminium foil, which also filters out the ultraviolet driving pulses.

Because the count rate in a time-of-flight photoemission momentum microscope is limited to only about one electron per laser shot, a high repetition rate is key for keeping measurement times at a reasonable amount while ensuring good statistics. In our experiment, this requirement entails the challenge of pushing the generation of the atomically strong, few-cycle phase-stable MIR pump pulses to new limits for a tabletop setup. Here the generated phase-stable MIR pulses feature, to the best of our knowledge, record-high average powers of up to 1 W and electrical peak field strengths of more than 200 MV cm−1. These field transients are obtained by difference frequency generation in a gallium selenide crystal between the outputs of two parallel (N)OPAs (ORPHEUS-MIR, Light Conversion Inc.)50. They feature pulse durations down to sub-50 fs and can be tuned between 4 µm and 15 µm. A small portion of the laser fundamental is picked off to pump a home-built single-stage NOPA. It is optimized to generate 10-fs pulses centred around 825 nm, which are used for electro-optic sampling (EOS) of the MIR waveforms. Extended Data Fig. 1c shows a typical MIR transient detected by EOS. A pair of wire-grid polarizers allows us to precisely control the polarization direction and power of the MIR pulses, which are then coupled into the UHV chamber through a diamond window.

The intense MIR pump (s-polarized) and the XUV probe (p-polarized) are spatially overlapped in the vacuum chamber with a custom-built off-axis parabolic mirror featuring a small aperture for XUV transmission and are focused onto monolayer graphene with an angle of incidence of 70°. A piezo-controlled delay stage in the excitation beam path allows us to set the delay between the MIR and XUV pulses with a temporal precision of 230 as. The emitted photoelectrons are detected by a time-of-flight momentum microscope (lens system: GST mbH; detector: HEX40, RoentDek)51. Multihit detection ensures linearity of the signal up to a repetition rate of 20 kHz. The combination of the 21.7-eV probe pulses with the large acceptance angle of the momentum microscope allows access to momentum regions up to ±2.14 Å−1, as compared with ±0.16 Å−1 in previous subcycle ARPES experiments8,20. The energy resolution is limited by the broad spectrum of the probe pulse. The bandwidth of the XUV pulse is tunable, setting a limit for the energy resolution of 180 meV. The momentum resolution is better than 0.01 Å−1. The custom-designed UHV chamber is shielded by a μ-metal liner and maintains a base pressure of 2 × 10−10 mbar. The samples were measured at room temperature.

Inducing field-driven dynamics in the monolayer requires a field that is parallel to the plane of the monolayer. To maximize the corresponding field component, the MIR pulse is s-polarized. The polarization of the XUV pulse is set to be perpendicular to the MIR pulse to prevent crosstalk between their fields that could introduce coherent artefacts effects in the observed dynamics. Finally, the rotation of the sample is chosen such that the MIR-induced momentum streaking in vacuum is minimized at one of the K points. This requires one K point to be at k∥ = 0, with k∥ being the momentum direction parallel to the electric field of the MIR pulse. This alignment also minimizes matrix-element-induced asymmetries along k∥ = 0 in the observed energy and momentum range. Although an asymmetry along the kx direction might persist, it is rather small at the observed energies. This is because the dark corridor only begins to set in at relatively high excitation energies, which do not occur along the kx direction in the experiment. This may also explain the slightly larger broadening observed in the simulations in which the matrix element was neglected.

For sample preparation, an n-doped 6H-SiC(0001) wafer was used as a substrate for growing an epitaxial monolayer graphene with 0° rotational alignment relative to the substrate lattice (0°-EMLG). The wafer was initially degassed in UHV at 880 °C for 30 min. The temperature was subsequently increased to 1,050 °C and maintained for 30 min under an external flux of Si atoms, resulting in a Si-rich (√3 × √3)R30° surface reconstruction. The sample was then further annealed at 880 °C for an extra 30 min, again under Si flux, resulting in the Si-rich (3 × 3) surface reconstruction. With this procedure, the oxide layer is removed from the SiC surface and atomic cleanness is achieved. In the next step, 0°-EMLG was obtained by annealing the sample at 1,400 °C for 30 min in borazine (B3N3H6) atmosphere with a partial pressure of 1.5 × 10−6 mbar. The borazine molecules act as surfactants on the heated SiC surface. They inhibit the formation of the conventional 30°-rotated graphene layer but instead force the homogeneous graphene layer in an unconventional 0° orientation with respect to the substrate lattice. For more details on the preparation of the 0°-EMLG, see refs. 38,52,53. Following growth, the surface morphology and crystalline structure were characterized using low-energy electron microscopy and low-energy electron diffraction. The average width of terraces on the SiC surface is approximately 160 nm and the surface is fully covered by 0°-EMLG. Subsequently, the sample was shortly exposed to air, transported in static vacuum (0.1 mbar) to the experimental chambers and degassed at 350 °C for 3 h before the measurements. The photoemission experiments reveal that the 0°-EMLG sample is n-doped, with the Fermi level approximately 200 meV above the Dirac point.

The acceleration of photoemitted electrons in vacuum allows for an in situ reconstruction of electric field waveforms20. In addition to acceleration within the sample, the s-polarized field also accelerates electrons after they have left the material. This causes a momentum change of the entire band structure parallel to the surface of the sample, Δk∥, that follows the vector potential of the field. The electric field waveform can thus be calculated by:

To extract Δk∥, the extracted photoemission data are shifted stepwise along k∥ and compared with a reference spectrum without a field. Within a fixed momentum window centred on the Dirac point, spanning +160 meV to −1.5 eV relative to the Fermi level (a range that, at equilibrium, encompasses predominantly the valence band), the sum of absolute pixel-wise differences between the measured data and the reference is computed at each iteration. The iteration with the smallest overall error gives the value for Δk∥. Repeating this procedure for every delay point, t, allows a reconstruction of the applied field E∥(t). To refine the retrieved waveform, a second method for extracting Δk∥(t) is used. Tracking the change in the number of electrons, integrated over all detected energies (+1 eV to −7 eV), with positive or negative momentum along k∥, yields a unitless quantity directly proportional to Δk∥(t), which is not subject to discretization caused by the binning of the data along k∥. The waveform that can be extracted in this way is then scaled by the peak electric field from the first method. The resulting waveform is shown in Fig. 2c.

The extracted Δk∥ is also used to compensate for the streaking in the photoemission spectra. As well as the trivial shift along k∥, a shift in energy, Δε, is connected to momentum streaking. The energy of every electron in vacuum is given by:
