Extended Data Fig. 2a shows band-structure snapshots taken without an applied field (left panel) and with a strong field applied before streaking compensation (middle panel) and after streaking compensation (right panel). The streaking-induced changes of energy and momentum were compensated for in all photoemission spectra before further analysis of the occupation of the band structure.

A parameter that is frequently used to distinguish between the weak-field and strong-field regimes of light–matter interaction is the Keldysh parameter

It was introduced by Leonid Keldysh in 1965 as the ratio between the carrier frequency of light ω and the tunnelling rate of an electron with mass \({m}_{{\rm{e}}+{\rm{h}}}^{\ast }\) through a barrier Δ, to show that tunnelling and multiphoton ionization in strong electromagnetic fields follow essentially the same physical laws54. This ratio scales linearly with frequency ω and the inverse of the electric field strength E0. Tunnelling dominates for γ ≪ 1, which holds for sufficiently strong fields and/or low frequencies. Equivalently, it can be expressed as \(\gamma =\sqrt{\Delta /{2U}_{{\rm{P}}}}\) by comparing the barrier Δ with the mean kinetic energy of a free electron in an oscillating electric field of amplitude E0, the ponderomotive potential \({2U}_{{\rm{P}}}={e}^{2}{E}_{0}^{2}/4{m}_{e+h}^{\ast }{\omega }^{2}\). Although similar considerations can be made for quasirelativistic motion of electrons in gapless graphene, it is more realistic for the present experiment to take the full Dirac cone with its distribution of barriers and effective masses into account (Extended Data Fig. 7a). In that case, we obtain a kx-dependent Keldysh parameter26

because both the gap, Δ = 2ħvF|kx|, and the effective mass at the gap, \({m}_{e+h}^{\ast }=\hbar |{k}_{x}|/2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}\), depend on the distance from the Dirac point. By identifying Δ with the MIR photon energy of 124 meV, we get γ = 0.075 for the peak electric fields of 1.57 MV cm−1. If we could switch off intraband acceleration, the relevant transition energy from the valence band to the unperturbed conduction band would increase to two times the doping energy of 200 meV, that is, to Δ = 400 meV. Even then, γ = 0.24 would comfortably place our measurements in the strong-field regime.

The microscopic intraband current density for each time instant, j(t), is directly extracted from the individual photoemission measurements, as in Fig. 2c. After compensation of momentum streaking, the photoemission intensity is integrated in two momentum regions with ky < 0 and ky > 0, respectively, and normalized by the total number of carriers in the two momentum regions at equilibrium. Subtracting the time-dependent number of counts with positive and negative ky components, we obtain a dimensionless value proportional to the microscopic current. To reveal the maximum amplitude of the current density, this procedure is performed for all carriers above the Dirac point (E − ED ≥ 0) within the momentum region |kx − K| < 0.15 Å−1. The result is then calibrated to physical values by multiplying with the Fermi velocity and carrier density in the conduction band of graphene with a Fermi level located 200 meV above the Dirac point, which can be computed from the density of states27. This yields a maximum current density of j(t) = 38.2 A cm−1. This value is very high, as it is even larger than in previous studies on topological insulators8,20, in which the scattering times were two orders of magnitude longer. Given the higher Fermi velocity and field amplitude, a higher current could be expected in the presented experiment. Yet, in a Drude-like regime, this would not be sufficient to compensate for the much higher scattering rate. This confirms that, in ballistic regimes, the current does not follow the Drude model. The same procedure is applied to the results of the simulations based on the SBEs.

To extract the relative timing between the microscopic current in the Dirac cone, j(t), and the electric field waveform, E(t), we apply a phase delay analysis. We compute the product between the Fourier transform of the field waveform, \(\mathop{E}\limits^{ \sim }(\omega )=F\{E(t)\}\), and the complex conjugate of the Fourier transform of the current, \(\mathop{j}\limits^{ \sim }(\omega )=F\{j(t)\}\):

The squared modulus of P(ω) peaks at the frequency of the pump field, whereas its phase corresponds to the timing difference (or phase delay) between the two oscillating quantities. We thus define the average phase difference as:

in which φ[P(ω)] is the complex phase of P(ω) and summations only consider frequencies at which |P(ω)| is larger than 50% of its peak value. To compute the phase delay, τi, we need to divide this quantity by the central frequency of the pump field. We then obtain the mean phase delay, τϕ, and the associated standard deviation of the mean over repeated measurements as:

in which i = 1,…, N runs over three different measurements performed on this sample geometry.

By performing a gated phase delay analysis, it is also possible to calculate a time-dependent phase difference, ϕ(t), which indicates the evolution of the scattering processes throughout the duration of the pulse. Here, however, the delay remains relatively stable over the first 100 fs of the driving pulse. We therefore use a single average phase shift, which we associate with a characteristic scattering time. In principle, however, this method could open new avenues for investigating relaxation dynamics across different samples with unprecedented temporal resolution.

To simulate the time-dependent MIR-driven electron dynamics in graphene, we numerically solve the SBEs6,55,56 for a two-band system:

in which k is the crystal momentum, t is the time, ħ the reduced Planck constant and e the elementary charge. fe(k, t) and fh(k, t) are the electron distributions in the conduction and valence bands, respectively, and peh(k, t) is the microscopic interband polarization. In these equations, E(t) is the MIR electric field, T2 = 5 fs is the phenomenological dephasing time of the microscopic polarization, εe(k) and εh(k) are the energy values of the conduction and valence bands and

are the dipole moments. \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}}}^{{\rm{e}}}\) and \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}}}^{{\rm{h}}}\) are the time-dependent and momentum-dependent scattering rates for electrons and holes, respectively, and will be discussed in the next section. In simulations without interband coupling (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Fig. 4), we set \({{\bf{d}}}_{{\rm{eh}}}({\bf{k}})={{\bf{d}}}_{{\rm{he}}}^{\dagger }({\bf{k}})=0\).

In the specific case of graphene, the Hamiltonian of a two-level system can be written as27:

and a = −2.46 Å is the nearest-neighbour lattice distance, vF = 1.072 × 106 m s−1 is the experimental value of the Fermi velocity and \(\gamma =-2\hbar {v}_{{\rm{F}}}/(\sqrt{3}{\rm{a}})\) is the hopping integral. From the Hamiltonian, it is then possible to compute the equilibrium eigenenergies and eigenfunctions:

The out-of-equilibrium dynamics shown in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 9 were simulated on a 250 × 250 2D square (kx, ky) grid in momentum space. The grid is centred on one of the K points with coordinates kx,K = 1.703 Å−1 and ky,K = 0 and it has a side length of 0.73 Å−1. The simulated time axis ranges from −100 fs to 300 fs, with a step size of 2 fs. The electric field, E(t), is parallel to ky and its temporal profile is analytically fitted to the experimentally measured field. At the initial time instant (t0 = −100 fs), we assume peh(k, t0) = 0, whereas the electron distribution corresponds to a Fermi–Dirac distribution. The position of the Fermi level compared with the Dirac crossing is set to εF = 0.2 eV to match the experiment. Simulations comparing the dynamics at other driving frequencies, varying field strengths or different Fermi levels sometimes used analytically modelled waveforms and smaller grid sizes to keep up with increased demands for spatial or temporal resolution.

In simulations including scattering, the grid was adjusted to 50 × 50 while maintaining the size in momentum space, to save resources. To reproduce the time-dependent electron distribution observed in momentum space, it is imperative to realistically model the scattering rates:

On these timescales, two physical phenomena mainly contribute to the scattering rates:

in which \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}},{\rm{e}}{\rm{p}}}^{\alpha }\) and \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}},{\rm{e}}{\rm{e}}}^{\alpha }\) are, respectively, the electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering rates.

Starting from the electron–phonon interaction, the scattering rate can be written as57:

in which v is the phonon mode considered and α, α′ ∈ {e, h} are the band indexes. The first term thus describes transitions from an occupied (k′, α′) state to an empty (k, α) state owing to the interaction with a v phonon, whereas the second term describes the opposite process. Whereas in the former the state (k, α) is empty and becomes occupied (thus, the rate is positive), in the latter, the rate must be negative. The probability of these transitions is associated with the electron–phonon transition rate:

in which \({G}_{{\alpha }^{{\prime} }\alpha }^{v}({{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{\bf{k}})\) is the electron–phonon coupling constant, δ is the Kronecker delta imposing energy and momentum conservation, q and \({\omega }_{{\bf{q}}}^{v}\) are the momentum and angular frequency of a v phonon, respectively, and \({n}_{{\bf{q}}}^{v}\) is the number of v phonons with a given frequency and momentum, which is described by the Bose–Einstein distribution.

To simplify our description, we assume that: (1) Umklapp processes are negligible and (2) the number of phonons \({n}_{{\bf{q}}}^{v}\) is constant and equal to its value at equilibrium (phonon bath). Moreover, previous works explained the dominating contribution of LO and TO phonons34,47. We will thus limit our model to LO and TO phonons and, because they have similar phonon energies (\({\omega }_{{\bf{q}}}^{{\rm{LO}}}\simeq {\omega }_{{\bf{q}}}^{{\rm{TO}}}\simeq 164.6\,{\hbar }^{-1}\,{\rm{meV}}\)) and matrix elements but their angular dependencies compensate each other, we will treat them together with an effective electron–optical phonon coupling constant57:

The effective matrix element is constant in momentum space and its value is adjusted to reproduce the experimental data. Owing to the isotropic angular dependence of this term, electron–optical phonon scattering will lead to a rapid spreading of the electron distribution around the Dirac cone.

In the same spirit, the scattering rate for electron–electron interaction can be written as57:

in which \(\alpha ,{\alpha }^{{\prime} },\beta ,{\beta }^{{\prime} }\in \{{\rm{e}},{\rm{h}}\}\) are the band indices. The first term, therefore, describes the scattering between a pair of particles in the initial states (α′, k′) and \(({\beta }^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} })\) to the final states (α, k) and \((\beta ,{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast })\), and the second term refers to the opposite process. The associated transition rate can thus be written as57:

and q = |k − k′| and \({q}^{{\prime} }=|{\bf{k}}-{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} }|\). The Coulomb potential between electron pairs is:

with A = 4π2/Δk2. The screening of the Coulomb interaction is given by the dielectric function \({\epsilon }(q)=1+{v}_{{\rm{c}}}(q)D({\varepsilon }_{{\rm{F}}})\mathop{\Pi }\limits^{ \sim }(q)\)57,58, in which:

and rS is the Wigner–Seitz radius of graphene, kF = εF/(ħvF) the Fermi wavevector and D(ε) the density of states close to the Dirac point. This approximation holds for n ≥ nth = 1012 cm−2, thus if εF ≥ 37.14 meV, as in our case.

In this form, the scattering rate for electron–electron interaction is computationally extremely expensive. Therefore, we assume that the electron distribution for the second particle can be approximated by the equilibrium Fermi–Dirac distribution of the carriers:

This allows us to write a simplified expression for the electron–electron scattering rate:

in which we use that \({S}_{{\rm{ee}}}({\bf{k}},{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast },{{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} })={S}_{{\rm{ee}}}({{\bf{k}}}^{{\prime} },{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} },{\bf{k}},{{\bf{k}}}_{\ast })\) and define:

In our simulations, we only focus on a small momentum space region around one of the six equivalent K points. In doing so, we neglect intervalley electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering processes, which are not expected to contribute notably in these conditions34. However, for electron–electron scattering, it is possible that an electron scatters from one state to another within the same valley by interacting with a charge carrier in a different one. For this reason, we effectively account for these processes by multiplying \({S}_{{\rm{ee}},\beta \beta {\rm{{\prime} }}}^{{\rm{eff}},1}\) and \({S}_{{\rm{ee}},\beta \beta {\rm{{\prime} }}}^{{\rm{eff}},2}\) by the number of equivalent K valleys, that is, six. To reproduce the experimental data, we assumed Veff = 4.386. It is important to notice that the dependence on the relative angle between k, k′, \({{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }\) and \({{\bf{k}}}_{\ast }^{{\prime} }\) determines the characteristic angular dependence of electron–electron scattering in graphene47, also termed collinear scattering41. Notably, at variance with the relaxation time approximation, our approach does not enforce any specific electron distribution at any time instant, while matching our experimental results.

To reduce the computational costs when relating the phase delay to an effective scattering time, a customary approach when solving the SBEs is to invoke the relaxation time approximation6,20,55,56. In this context, the scattering rate \({\varGamma }_{{\bf{k}}}^{\alpha }\) is assumed to be inversely proportional to a time constant, T1, associated with the mean free time between scattering events. Defining \({f}_{\alpha }^{(0)}({\bf{k}})\) as the equilibrium electron distribution in the α band, we obtain:

It is important to notice that, even though this approach allows us to extract an effective time constant, it is not enough to reproduce the experimental data. In fact, in this approximation, the scattering rate at a given point k in momentum space will only depend on the instantaneous electron distribution at that point and not on any other point in momentum space. This makes it impossible to reproduce any carrier redistribution dynamics in momentum space owing to, for example, the interaction with optical phonons.

The original works of Landau22, Zener23, Majorana24 and Stückelberg36 considered a two-state quantum system with an energy separation Δε = ε1(t) − ε2(t) = αt that changes linearly with time and undergoes an avoided crossing with a half gap energy δ. The diabatic transition probability is then given by26

with the diabaticity parameter \(\varGamma =\frac{{\delta }^{2}}{\hbar \alpha }\). This simple formula can be used to estimate the region in momentum space in which transitions occur in our experiment. The model is applicable under the condition that the characteristic sweep time through the transition, τ = 2δ/ε, is short compared with the oscillation period T = 2π/ω of the driving electric field. In this case, the field can be considered quasistatic during the transition and we simply have \(\alpha =2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}\hbar |{k}_{x}-K|=2{v}_{{\rm{F}}}|e|{E}_{0}\). With δ = vFħ|kx − K|, we obtain \(\tau =\frac{\hbar | {k}_{x}-K|}{|e|{E}_{0}}=\frac{\gamma }{\omega }\). Because γ ≈ 0.1, the crossing indeed occurs very fast (τ < 1 fs). For the peak electric field E0 = 1.57 MV cm−1, the diabaticity parameter \(\varGamma =\frac{\hslash {v}_{{\rm{F}}}}{2|e|{E}_{0}}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\,\cong \) \(210\,{{\rm{\mathring{\rm A} }}}^{2}{|{k}_{x}-K|}^{2}\) becomes smaller than 1/π for |kx − K| < 0.04 Å−2. In this region around the Dirac point, 1 − e−2 = 86% of the transitions from the valence band to the conductions band are expected to take place as long as Pauli blocking can be neglected. This region roughly coincides with the momentum area in which the conduction band of our doped graphene samples is occupied. This shows that transitions can only take place after the electrons have been accelerated away from the Dirac point. After several driving cycles, the observed dynamics of the doped and a hypothetical undoped sample are expected to be similar (Extended Data Fig. 8).

For an empty upper Dirac cone, we expect the carrier injection rate owing to LZM tunnelling to closely follow the magnitude of the electric field and the electron population to increase stepwise, with the highest injection rates occurring at the largest absolute field values. In an n-doped system and for high injection rates, as in the present experiment, Pauli blocking modifies this simple picture (Extended Data Fig. 5a). Electrons can only be injected when there is sufficient empty space in the conduction band near the K point. Consequently, intraband transport plays a decisive role in determining the injection timing. Carrier injection happens most efficiently during the intervals between the extrema of the electric field and the carrier displacement. Our simulations clearly show that this results in a phase delay between the population jumps and the field, which grows as more population has been transferred. Beyond the effects of Pauli blocking and scattering, the injection dynamics can be strongly influenced by quantum interference59. Here we find that they can cause a deviation of a step-like increase in the conduction band population (or electron distribution width) by transforming the plateau regions, following a strong injection phase, into local minima through destructive interference of electron wavepackets (Extended Data Fig. 9). Although the signal-to-noise ratio of the measured conduction band population does not allow us to resolve the jumps in the population during carrier injection experimentally, the dynamics of the increase of the carrier density can be well reproduced with the theory.

The simulations also show that the elongation of the conduction band electron distribution in momentum space is closely tied to the carrier population (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Notably, the weak oscillations in the width of the electron distribution, which are superimposed on the stepwise increase, become more pronounced with scattering (Fig. 4c). This effect is probably caused by a shortening of the effective injection time window. In the absence of scattering, the electron displacement follows the vector potential and is therefore phase-shifted by π/2 relative to the electric field. With scattering, the phase shift between the electric field and the displacement of the electrons shrinks, such that periods of rapid population increase occur only a few femtoseconds before an extremum in the displacement (Extended Data Fig. 5). Experimentally, the oscillation of the width of the electron distribution at twice the frequency of the driving field is clearly visible during the first three cycles of the electric field, that is, at times when there is still substantial carrier injection (Fig. 3c). The observed relative phase with respect to the electric field transient and the COM displacement agrees well with the simulations that include scattering. The data thus support the picture of a well that is periodically driven by the electric field and opened and closed by the oscillating carriers in the conduction band.

The new experimental platform presented here was developed to give direct access to strongly driven electron dynamics without relying heavily on theory or models. This philosophy also translates to data processing: our conclusions only rely on features present in the raw data. The previously described streaking compensation is the first and only step in the data analysis pipeline that is required to ensure that the observed dynamics can be attributed to processes that are happening in the solid and not the vacuum. Following that, the general strategy is that filtering is only used to remove technical noise and signals related to the matrix elements before the data are analysed or to enhance visibility in the figures. To ensure full transparency, the following contains a summary of all notable data processing steps for the presented figures.

The raw data from the delay line detector are binned with a spacing of 0.084 eV × 0.022 Å−1 × 0.022 Å−1 for the data in Fig. 1 and with a spacing of 0.084 eV × 0.011 Å−1 × 0.011 Å−1 for all other photoemission data.

The 3D data in Fig. 1c are symmetrized to remove the decrease in photoemission intensity caused by the angle of incidence of the XUV pulse.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 2a are obtained by integrating the 3D data within an energy window of 0.33 eV around distinct energy levels (0.25 eV, −0.25 eV, −0.75 eV, −1.25 eV, −1.75 eV). Before plotting, the data are further processed to enhance the visibility in the figure. First, a 1D simple moving average along both momentum axes (window size: 0.08 Å−1) is applied to the data four times. The filtered data are further processed by a 2D curvature filter described by equation (11) of ref. 60 with C0 = 0.2. Finally, a 2D median filter with window size 0.045 eV × 0.045 Å−1 is applied three times to clean up numerical noise.

The band structure cuts in Fig. 2b are obtained by integrating the 3D data within a momentum window of 0.08 Å−1 around kx − K = 0. Before plotting, the data are further processed to enhance the visibility in the figure. First, a 1D simple moving average along the energy and momentum axes with window sizes of 0.59 eV and 0.08 Å−1, respectively, is applied four times. The filtered data are subject to a 2D curvature filter with C0 = 0.2. Finally, a 2D median filter with window size 0.34 eV × 0.045 Å−1 is applied three times. The raw data are shown in Extended Data Fig. 2b.

The applied field transient and current in Fig. 2c are extracted from the raw data as laid out in Methods sections ‘Electric field waveform reconstruction and streaking compensation’ and ‘Current extraction and Fourier analysis of the phase delay’. Before plotting, a 4-THz high-pass filter is applied to the data to remove slowly varying offsets. The data showing the increase of the carrier population in the conduction band were acquired under almost identical experimental conditions in which special care has been taken to align the MIR polarization such that the electric field exhibits no perpendicular component leading to coherent oscillations of the integrated photoemission intensity.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 3a are obtained by integrating the 3D data for energies higher than 170 meV. This energy level is chosen to minimize contributions of the valence band caused by the limited energy resolution of the setup. Before extracting the COM displacement and width, a Gaussian filter with a small window size 0.02 Å−1 × 0.02 Å−1 has been applied to the 2D data. We applied the same filter to the experimental 2D data for a better comparison between experiment and theory. For the theory data, this is necessary to reduce numerical or binning artefacts. Owing to its small window size, the filter does not change or remove any of the features retrieved for data analysis.

To extract the COM motion and change of the width of the carrier distribution shown in Fig. 3b,c, the plotted 2D maps are integrated along kx and ky. For the data along ky, a Gaussian distribution with a constant offset (accounting for the background) is fitted to the integrated distribution. For the data along kx, the previously constant offset is modified with a linear decrease for growing kx values to account for the decrease in background caused by the photoemission matrix element. The mean of the extracted fit for the ky distribution is used to characterize the COM motion. Before plotting, a 15-THz high-pass filter is applied to these data to remove a slowly varying offset. The change of the standard deviation, Δσ, of the extracted fits is used to characterize the change of the width of the carrier distribution along kx and ky.

The 2D momentum maps in Fig. 4a are obtained by integrating the simulated population of the conduction band and applying a Gaussian filter with a small window size of 0.02 Å−1 × 0.02 Å−1 to the 2D data, as described above for the data shown in Fig. 3a.

The extraction of the simulated current density and change of the width of the carrier distribution shown in Fig. 4b,c follows the procedures outlined for the experimental data.

a, A Yb:KGW oscillator seeds two Yb:KGW amplifiers, each providing a pulse energy of 1.5 mJ at a repetition rate of 50 kHz. Half of the output of one amplifier is upconverted to 400-nm pulses with a pulse duration of 20 fs, which are then used to generate sub-10-fs XUV pulses by high-harmonic generation in argon (left side). In parallel, widely tunable, intense, few-cycle and CEP-stable MIR pulses are generated by difference frequency generation (DFG) of the outputs of a dual-branch OPA, which is supplied with the remaining half of the output of the first amplifiers (middle). The output of the second amplifier is used to almost exclusively pump the last amplification stage in the dual-branch OPA. Furthermore, a NOPA generates 10-fs-long NIR pulses (right side), which can be used to detect the MIR waveforms (EOS). Finally, all beams are guided into the UHV chamber of the momentum microscope, in which they are spatially overlapped. b, Generated XUV spectrum. The intense seventh harmonic order centred around 57 nm is selected by multilayer mirrors (grey shaded area) and is used as a probe pulse in the subcycle momentum microscopy experiments. c, Typical MIR waveform measured by EOS.

a, Photoemission spectra in different streaking conditions. The first two panels show a band-structure snapshot taken in equilibrium (left panel) and a snapshot with strong streaking along ky by the s-polarized MIR field (middle panel). The electric field is reconstructed by matching the streaked band structures to the equilibrium case. Once the electric field is known, the streaking effects can be compensated (right panel). The dashed black lines are a guide to the eye representing the equilibrium band structure. Applying the calculated shifts along energy and momentum, according to the extracted field from the middle panel, to the dashed black line yields the solid black line. b, Unfiltered version of the data shown in Fig. 2, showing the raw photoemission data after streaking compensation.

Simulations based on the SBEs in relaxation time approximation reveal how the phase delay between an applied waveform (central frequency, 30 THz) and the lightwave-driven current scales with the scattering time. For very small scattering times, the phase difference converges to zero, whereas for longer scattering times, it converges to π/2. The strongest change in the phase delay can be observed for scattering times on the order of a half-cycle of the driving waveform.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times without scattering. a, Interband coupling switched off. b, Interband coupling switched on. It causes a large elongation of the carrier distribution along the polarization of the driving light field, filling the gap between the displaced electrons distribution and the K point.

a, Normalized carrier density in the conduction band extracted from our theory model with electron–phonon and electron–electron scattering (black curve) and from experimental data (grey curve). The observed difference in the number of extra carriers between theory and experiment is to be expected, as the theory does not account for inherent constraints of the measurement itself, such as matrix element effects. The population rises fastest during the time window between a maximum of the field (red curve) and the COM displacement (green curve). b, During the first few cycles, the evolution of the width of the electron distribution (green curve) closely follows the population dynamics (black curve).

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times without scattering in the weak-field and strong-field regimes. The interaction regime is defined by means of the Keldysh parameter for an energy gap corresponding to single-photon absorption. a, The weak-field regime is reached by using fields that are 200 times weaker than in the experiment. Here the interaction is dominated by perturbative absorption, which is strongly affected by the selection rules owing to the pseudospin texture of graphene. By removing the doping, the first row highlights how this leads to a population increase in regions perpendicular to the polarization of the light pulse. The second row depicts the situation with the same doping level as in the experiment. Here no change in the population can be resolved, even when exaggerating the colour map by a factor of 2,500. b, In the strong-field regime, the interaction with light is characterized by a unidirectional elongation of the electron distribution parallel to the electric field as well as a displacement of the Fermi surface.

a, Illustration of the distribution of bandgaps Δ and the varying Keldysh parameter γ in graphene. b, Simulated 2D change of the population in the conduction band (blue curve) and aspect ratio of the carrier distribution (red curve) after interacting with the electric field for different field strengths in an undoped sample without scattering. For Keldysh parameters γ ≫ 1, the number of excited carriers scales quadratically with the field (grey curve), indicative of single carrier absorption. At the same time, the aspect ratio of the carrier distribution shows that the distribution is broader along the momentum direction perpendicular to the light field (left inset). In the strong-field regime (γ ≪ 1), the number of excited carriers is trending towards saturation, indicative of light-field-induced tunnelling as the transition mechanism. Simultaneously, the aspect ratio of the carrier distribution inverts, resulting in the elliptical distribution observed in the experiment with broadening in the direction parallel to the applied field (right inset). The extracted sub-quadratic scaling of the excited carrier density for the field strength used in the experiment (grey shaded area) indicates that perturbative single-photon or multiphoton absorption does not play a substantial role in the interaction.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times without scattering and different doping levels. a, No doping. b, Moderate doping. c, High doping. Intrinsic (a) and the moderately doped graphene (b, Fermi level 200 meV) closely resemble each other. Higher doping levels (c) reveal the difference between the intraband and interband signatures.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for different dephasing times. a, T2 = 0.1 fs. b, T2 = 1 fs c, T2 = 5 fs. d, T2 = 500 fs. The 2D carrier distribution is shown after the first (left panel) and second (middle panel) cycles. For very fast dephasing, the efficiency for LZM transitions decreases substantially, manifesting in a lack of additional carriers in the second panel of a. For very slow dephasing, signatures of LZSM interference emerge after the second cycle (fishbone pattern in the second panel of d). They manifest in a modulation at the second harmonic of the driving field in the elongation of the electron distribution along the direction parallel to the electric field (right panel), as highlighted in the inset by its Fourier transform during the first half-cycles of the driving field (grey area). The scale of the vertical axis is fixed across the insets.

Simulated 2D carrier distribution in the conduction band for selected delay times with different scattering contributions. a, No scattering. b, Only electron–electron scattering. c, Only scattering with optical phonons. d, Combination of electron–electron scattering and scattering with optical phonons.

Lightwave-driven dynamics in graphene. The video shows the subcycle dynamics of lightwave-driven graphene in the vicinity of the K point. On the left side, the electron population in the conduction band is shown, whereas the right panel shows a cut through the band structure at the K point. The field-induced asymmetry in the number of carriers with positive or negative momenta testifies to a macroscopic lightwave-driven current. Meanwhile, the emerging elliptical shape of the electron distribution in momentum space highlights the presence of LZM tunnelling into the conduction band. For late delay times, the electron distribution becomes circular again and relaxes back to its original shape by scattering.

#1469. Tottenham look set to deliver after so many disappointments but Roberto De Zerbi's side need a nasty streak if they are to build on their momentum ahead of a daunting festive period, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI

By RIATH AL-SAMARRAI, CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 06:52 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:31 EDT, 2 November 2026

It was late on Saturday evening when Roberto De Zerbi relayed a few of the comments he had shared with Tottenham’s players at half-time in their 2-0 win over Crystal Palace. One of those remarks was indicative of how quickly things can change.

In the knowledge that his side were 45 minutes away from a rare spot in the upper portion of the table, he reminded them: ‘We can't forget where we have been two weeks ago. Two weeks ago, before the Coventry game, we were last in the table and we can't forget.’

With Tottenham, it is always prudent to know calamity is never too far away, but for the first time in two years, there is a gathering excitement at the club - in the crowd and the dressing room.

The win over Palace was assisted hugely by Jean-Philippe Mateta’s red card after 13 minutes, but Spurs have an uncanny knack of slipping on the easier opportunities. Not this time – goals from Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke punctuated a dominant performance and a third straight win. Three managers and 616 days had expired since the last such streak.

But Spurs appear to be on the march and a promising season is belatedly taking shape. To finally deliver after so many disappointments, there are certain areas where improvements must follow…

Roberto De Zerbi reminded his players of where they had come from during their 2-0 win over Crystal Palace

That was De Zerbi’s own assessment of his frontline after a familiar shortcoming against Palace may have been concealed by the win. It was not lost on him that both of Tottenham’s goals were scored by defenders, nor that they had 34 shots to Palace’s two. As ever, Spurs had abundant creativity in their side but lacked a clinical edge.

De Zerbi said: ‘If we want to follow perfection, we have to be more nasty, no? That is an individual thing, because if I'm number nine, number 10, I want to score. But I can't say nothing.’

He later clarified that comment to encompass the whole side, but it was clear that the onus falls most on Dominic Solanke and Omar Marmoush.

In fairness to the pair, Palace defended so deep after Mateta’s dismissal that they had no space to operate, but one goal apiece this season is a poor return. Solanke, in particular, needs to do a better job of reading the movements and intentions of those around him – too often on Saturday he appeared a thought or two behind Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus, who both impressed in the more generous spaces out wide.

De Zerbi wants his side to develop a 'nasty' streak - particularly his attackers

Marmoush is an interesting case for De Zerbi. His mobility and technical ability are clear but he is yet to reveal his best position. On Saturday he was used as a No 10, having already been switched between roles on the left and up front. This experiment drew muted results.

It might be the case that a sustained run in one spot would be beneficial, but for now there appears to be confusion over where to use him. There is also a nagging thought that his best striking potential comes in a two-striker system, as shown in his most prolific period at Frankfurt, but that is not the way De Zerbi plays.

A significant improvement for Tottenham has come in midfield and, specifically, the pairing between Matheus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali.

Acquired at great cost, there was limited patience around the delivery of their impact, but time was always necessary, because De Zerbi’s system is notoriously complicated. In recent weeks, Fernandes and Tonali have shown signs that the penny has dropped on what they have to do.

This has been especially relevant in the instance of Tonali, who is very much the tempo-setter of the side on the ball and off it. On Saturday, he was excellent, or worth ‘double’ in the words of De Zerbi. There were times earlier in the season when he appeared disinterested, as if Tottenham was not the destination he had in mind, but his work rate was brilliant against Palace – he covered 12.3km, won all three of his tackles, and completed 93 per cent of his passes. He was all-action.

The same would be said for Fernandes, who covered 11.6km of ground and finessed a superb cross for Van Hecke’s goal. As a pair with Tonali, he was key to the pressing operation that limited Palace to a single counter-attack in the second half.

Mateus Fernandes (pictured) and Sandro Tonali have been huge boosts in the midfield

De Zerbi struck an interesting note after the game by alluding to the cohesiveness of his side and how it has changed on the pitch. Perhaps that relates to the recent team-bonding exercise in Marbella, but more likely they just needed time to understand the complexities of their manager’s demands.

‘I think even before the international break we were playing well,’ De Zerbi said. ‘We were playing maybe not 90 minutes, but many parts of the game we played very well. We didn't score. We conceded a stupid goal and then we lost energy. We lost spirit. We lost the right union between the players.

‘If we compare Tottenham before the international break and Tottenham after the international break, now we are playing as a team. Before the international break we were playing as many very good players, but not as a team.’

Archie Gray, for one, is getting to grips with the less familiar brief at right-back. The requirements to swap spots with Fernandes, overlap Kudus or hold the advanced position are mind-scrambling, but he has adapted well. His withdrawal at half-time against Palace was down to his first-half yellow card and doesn’t detract from a salient point – he can evidently be trusted to replace Pedro Porro, or at least give the latter scope for a breather.

Tottenham have an opportunity now. Their next four fixtures are Leeds, Ipswich, Sunderland and Fulham, with a nasty run waiting in December and early January.

If they can get something from Elland Road, the other three assignments present a rich opportunity for momentum before the tricky festive period.

One key area to improve in the short term will come against defensive sides who offer less space. That Spurs scored only twice from 80 per cent possession against Palace highlighted the issue.

De Zerbi said: ‘We are improving in the principle and the quality of play. Maybe we are not ready yet to play against such a low block but maybe in two or three months we will be.’

#1468. Xabi Alonso hits out at ‘soft’ Chelsea players

Xabi Alonso accused his Chelsea players of being “soft” after they failed to keep a clean sheet for the 20th successive Premier League game.

Chelsea threw away an early lead to draw 2-2 with Hull City and have conceded two or more goals in each of their four Premier League games.

Alonso has tried different systems and different players in those games, but suggested Chelsea’s biggest problem is mental.

The club’s dreadful clean-sheet record pre-dates him and is the first time in 65 years Chelsea have gone 20 league games without keeping the opposition out.

Hull’s first goal from Mohamed Belloumi came after the ball had bounced over Jorrel Hato and Alonso said: “We need to be aware that from any situation, any team in the Premier League can hurt you. Today it was from a long ball, two bounces, the way it happened. You need to be very aware, very ready that the danger can come from any situation. If you are soft or if you are not prepared, you will get punished and we have been punished that way.”

Chelsea have shared 30 goals with their opponents in the club’s six games in all competitions so far this season.

“Yeah, it’s all maybe entertaining, but I hope that one day you say it was a boring game and we win and we don’t give these entertaining moments,” he said.

“But, for sure, it kind of repeats some patterns that we are making. It will take time to... or it will take moments to fix them when we get the lead and you still need to be competing and not give the chance so easily for them to come back, especially in the first goal, we can do much better.

“It was too soft to give them this hope because until then we were controlling, we were creating chances. But that momentum that we had changed the mood and the score of the game, and it’s something that we need to be talking [about], we address and we will get better. But it’s having an impact on our performances at the moment.”

Asked if his players have a real desire to defend and keep clean sheets, Alonso said: “We can do better, we can do better for sure. We need to know that even when we have the lead, a very important part of the game is to hold together, to keep the distance, to go intense in the situations to defend. I’m sure that we can do better.

“Overall, I think that we are attacking better than defending in every part. We know that it’s a big topic and a big theme for us. For sure, it’s just four games. But the dynamic in terms of conceding, I don’t like it and we need to do much better. Open play, set-pieces, long balls, this toughness, this competitive sense, we can do better.”

Needing three goals or more to win games is not sustainable, as Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso is finding out.

This is not a problem of Alonso’s making, given Chelsea have now gone 20 Premier League games without a clean sheet. But he is certainly not improving the issue yet.

Chelsea beat Fulham with three goals and Brighton with four but left themselves far too much to do against Arsenal and were taken advantage of by Hull City, who will be slightly disappointed they did not leave Stamford Bridge with all three points.

Goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez has now conceded seven goals in three games since joining from Aston Villa, while central defender Maxence Lacroix, who joined for £52m from Crystal Palace in the summer, was relegated to the substitutes’ bench.

Martínez was at fault for Mohamed Belloumi’s second goal, but the Argentine did make a crucial save at his back post to stop substitute Mohamed-Ali Cho grabbing a winner that Chelsea could have had no complaints about.

Hull finished the game with more shots on goal than their hosts and a higher expected-goals rate. Chelsea are far too open and in some ways far too entertaining.

Defensive midfielder Moisés Caicedo cannot return from injury quickly enough, but this does not feel like a problem that will be solved by one man. Alonso needs to find a balance and instil a real desire in his team to defend.

Caicedo has that desire, but there are no defenders at the club who have shown that absolute desperation to keep the ball out of the net that Chelsea fans became so used to in the days of John Terry, Gary Cahill and César Azpilicueta.

None of this should diminish Hull’s performance. They were not only spirited and full of character but also showed quality and a threat. The joke is currently on those who laughed at their hopes of survival before a ball had been kicked.

It is now two wins and two draws for Sergej Jakirovic’s team and they are already a fifth of the way to 40 points. Jakirovic had promised his staff a week off in the international break if they reached eight points after five games. With that target already met, there may be a new reward if Hull can make it 11 points against Newcastle United next weekend.

“Before the season, I said to my staff that we will take seven, eight points in these first five and then I will give them seven days off,” Jakirovic said. “That was our target and now we are in a very good position, eight points.

“Especially today, it’s very, very difficult to play here, and now we will try to get even more. Of course, I’m a little bit worried about the international break because we have 13 national team players. But we will see who will come back and in what condition. So this is my concern right now.” Asked if his staff’s seven-day break will be extended if Hull can beat Newcastle, Jakirovic added: “I will tell them. But I know already.”

While his five-game target may need modifying, Jakirovic is not deviating from his goal for the season for Hull. “Our target is always to stay in the league and collect as many points as possible,” he said. “Forty points, 38 to 41, this is the average we need. Then it’s easier to play. You can play more relaxed, with more joy and happiness. So [get to] this as soon as possible, so that we are safe.”

Hull had not conceded a league goal before this and there had been predictions they might crumble when they finally let the ball into their net. They did so after just seven minutes but they kept their heads and came back stronger.

It was far too easy for Morgan Rogers to make a yard of space for himself to shoot after collecting the ball from João Pedro, and Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis may not have been happy to have been beaten at his near post.

Chelsea have now scored inside the first 10 minutes in all of their four league games, but Hull were in no mood to crumble and hit back with two goals in six minutes from Belloumi to take a half-time lead. Both Hull goals were shockers from Chelsea’s perspective. The first, in the 28th minute, came as a result of Jorrel Hato letting the ball bounce over him from a Ryan Giles cross and Belloumi finished brilliantly.

Belloumi’s second came after Martínez had flapped at a corner and Semi Ajayi had hit the bar with a header. The ball fell to Belloumi again and his shot was deflected into the net.

It was no surprise that Hato did not reappear for the second half, as he was replaced by Pep Chavarría at left-back. But Chelsea remained vulnerable and Martínez had to recover from spilling a Regan Slater shot to prevent Ollie McBurnie extending Hull’s advantage.

When Palmer and Pedro combined for Pedro to sweep the ball into the net and equalise with 24 minutes remaining, it seemed like it would be Chelsea who would provide the grandstand finish.

But it was Hull who got a second wind and Chelsea were indebted to Martínez for making a save to stop Cho securing all three points and sending the visiting fans home even happier.

I feel good. We have to be happy. It’s a huge result for us.

We had 2-1 at half-time and we had a 100 per cent chance with McBurnie but Martinez’s save was excellent. We have to control play better in the box because we can stop this [Chelsea goal]. We had an excellent chance for Cho – Martinez saved again. Player of the match.

We can be very happy. We took a point in a very demanding match.

Eight points against very difficult opponents. We have to continue like this.

There have been 12 Premier League games at Anfield in 2026, Liverpool have only won 4 of them to date. This was seventh draw and Fulham deserves their share of the spoils. This was very much a learning experience for Andoni Iraola.

Not a single home win in the Premier League, today.

Aston Villa 1 Nottingham Forest 2Bournemouth 2 Brentford 2Chelsea 2 Hull City 2Crystal Palace 2 Ipswich Town 3Liverpool 0 Fulham 0

What a result for Hull, who remain unbeaten and they have taken five points from fixtures against United, Villa and Chelsea.

That is the first really poor result of the Alonso era, points dropped.

What a thriller in SE25, both teams have been going for it in the closing stages, but Ipswich have surely score the winner through Zian Flemming.

Fulham were pointless before this game, but they have kept a clean sheet at Anfield with a disciplined display and they could well have score one or two. Underwhelming for Liverpool, who have not won just one of their first four games and their fixtures have not been the most taxing.

And as we predicted at the beginning of the game... Liverpool 0 Fulham 0. If this reporter ever gives you advice on a horse to back or a team to follow, make sure you take the opposite stance. Fulham deserve their reward and their fans are singing “We got a point!”

Villa are finishing the game with 10 men because Ian Maatsen pulled up after Emery had made his five substitutions, and Forest have punished them through Igor Jesus with just a few minutes of normal time to play.

Alexander Isak heads over the bar when he perhaps should have hit the target. Has time run out for Liverpool?

You might imagine Chelsea are battering down the door, but Mohamed-Ali Cho has just forced Emi Martinez into a save at the other end. Hull will remain unbeaten if they can hold out.

Strand Larsen has had his critics, but he has scored his first goal of the season to set up a grandstand finish with 15 minutes plus stoppage time to play at Selhurst Park.

Short corner, McGinn whipped in an inswinging cross that is glanced into the bottom corner by Alysson.

Liverpool continue to toil at Anfield, but no opening goal. Iraola has thrown on Frimpong, Mac Allister, Ngumoha and Gakpo in the second half. Fulham have had the chances to score at least one, and Josh King has just brought a save out of Alisson.

Hull are a little lucky they still have 11 men on the pitch. Already on a booking, my man Crooks bundled down Rogers. It could easily have been another yellow car but the referee let him off and now he’s been replaced by Iroegbunam.

Joao Pedro finds the smallest of gaps to be the goalkeeper and find the roof of the net with a brilliant, instinctive finish.

That had not really been coming for Chelsea. It all felt a bit easy for Palmer to get his low cross into the box and Pedro to sweep the ball in. The home fans have woken up again.

Martinez was lucky to get away with another slip up, there. He spilt Slater’s shot but reacted before McBurnie to stop the Hull striker scoring the rebound. Just a day after his nasty looking crash, Sorba Thomas is on for Hull.

This game is absolutely here for Fulham to win. Quietness has descended around Anfield, the hosts have no fluency in their play and Fulham are growing in confidence. Why wouldn’t they after getting to 65 minutes with a clean sheet?

Just like in the first half, four minutes after one of these teams taking the lead there has been an equaliser. Kevin Scahde is in a rich vein of form.

Bournemouth have have never beaten Brentford in the Premier League, but they might well be on their way to changing that record having trailed earlier in the game. Marcus Tavernier has just scored their second goal.

Matt Davidson Rider Crooks has just been booked for a very cynical foul on Rogers. It gave Chelsea a free-kick in a dangerous position Reece James had an effort tipped away. Chelsea have started the second half well

Within a minute of the restart, Villa lose the ball in midfield and Delap punishes them to the maximum. Cracking finish from just outside the box, and a much-needed goal by Delap. The Glasner curse striking for Emery again?

Liam Delap has just started paying back that £50m transfer fee with a fine goal.

Delap picked the ball up on the left and set himself up on the edge of the box before crashing a 25-yard shot past Zion Suzuki.

Unai Emery has made a couple of changes at half-time, taking off Nicolas Jackson who picked up a silly booking just before half-time.

Tammy Abraham is on in his place. George Hemmings is also off and replaced by Alysson.

Pep Chavarria on for Chelsea at half-time. He’s replaced Jorrel Hato, who had a bit of a stinker in the first half.

Andoni Iraola hasn’t hung about here. Milos Kerkez has come on immediately after half-time for Kostas Tsimikas and you can say with certainty that Liverpool will be shopping for a new left-back in due course.

So at half-time, Hull City are top of the Premier League and don’t their supporters know it? They were singing “we are top of the League” for the full two minutes of time added on for stoppages at the end of the first period. Alonso has some work to do at the break.

Forest did need a brilliant double save from Matz Sels to deny Victor Lindelof and have recovered to slow the match down.

Neco Williams wasted a decent chance for Forest from outside the penalty area shortly before the break.

Referee Andrew Madley has irritated both teams with a number of weird decisions - but that’s sadly par for the course with officials nowadays.

Villa 0 Forest 0Bournemouth 1 Brentford 1Chelsea 1 Hull City 2Palace 1 Ipswich 2Liverpool 0 Fulham 0

Palace in some trouble now, level with Ipswich and down to 10 men. Disasi was sent off in the 34th minute for a reckless challenge on Jack Clarke, caught him with studs on shin.

Things got worse for Palace just before half-time, with Leif Davis heading home at the back post to give Ipswich the league.

Apologies for the lack of updates, some technical gremlins at Telegraph Towers. A nip and tuck game as expected at at the Vitality: Kevin Schade gave Brentford the lead before Justin Kluivert equalised four minutes later.

One way to put it is that Kostas Tsimikas isn’t playing well. Another way to say it would be that his efforts are making Milos Kerkez look like Roberto Carlos. The Greek left-back is having a dreadful afternoon and Fulham are getting plenty of joy out of him. We suggested there was no chance of this game finishing goalless, and it’s anomalous that we have reached 40 minutes without score. Fulham, certainly, have a sense of adventure and have been into Liverpool’s 18-yard box plenty of times. Let’s see if the picture changes before the interval.

That’s now seven goals Emi Martinez has conceded in three games since joining from Villa to supposedly solve Chelsea’s goalkeeping crisis. Martinez won’t be pleased with Hull’s second goal, here. He was beaten to a corner by Ajayi. His header hit the bar and Belloumi’s shot was deflected past him. The Hull fans are in dreamland.

This is a turn up for the books. Chelsea undone by a long ball forward, and Hato lets the ball bounce over his head, and Belloumi finishes with aplomb.

That’s now 20 Premier League games Chelsea have gone without keeping a clean sheet. What an earth was Jorrel Hato doing, letting the ball bounce over him for Belloumi? Amateur stuff at the back from the home side. It was Hull’s first meaningful attack.

Emersonn has struggled in some games so far this season, but he has just planted a header into the corner from a Davis cross.

There is a VAR check for offside... but the goal stands.

5 - Morgan Rogers is the fifth different player to score or assist in each of Chelsea's first four games of a Premier League season, after Didier Drogba (2010-11), Cesc Fàbregas (2014-15), Diego Costa (2014-15 & 2016-17), and Eden Hazard (2018-19).Famous. pic.twitter.com/0cuThzH472

A sweet strike from one of Palace’s summer signings, recruited from Union Saint Gilloise, and that is his first Palace goal. The 22-year-old Israeli came through at Maccabi Haifa. Uphill task for Gary O’Neill and Ipswich.

Austin MacPhee, Chelsea’s flamboyant set-piece coach, just motioned for Xabi Alonso to sit down when the Blues manager momentarily got up from his seat when the home side were preparing to take a corner. It seems MacPhee wears the (correct length) trousers when it comes to set pieces.

An almighty let off for Alisson and Liverpool after pass from the goalkeeper played Gravenberch into trouble, but Jacquet cleared off the line to keep the game goalless. That was Fulham’s first foray forward.

A bright start in this game and there is no chance it will end goalless (famous last words). Andoni Iraola has made three changes from the team that beat Atletico Madrid on Wednesday and it’s a pattern of his early management that he is making the kind of decisions that supporters are nodding along in approval with. Liverpool should already be one up but Alexander Isak’s shot has just drifted across the face of goal but the signs are encouraging. It could be a long afternoon for Alvaro Arbeloa.

Wow. Unbelievable double save from Forest’s Matz Sels there to keep out Victor Lindelof.

The first was the most impressive, a reflex stop after a deflection.

Morgan Rogers is the first player to score against Hull City this season. Emi Martinez launched the ball forward after claiming a corner, and Rogers’ shot from the edge of the area crept under the goalkeeper Tzolakis. He will not want to watch that one again.

We’re past five minutes and it’s the longest Chelsea have gone without scoring in the league this season. Back on Matt Crooks – one of his middle names is Rider.

Although Rogers scored in the seventh minute...so the early goals continue for Chelsea. It will be difficult for Hull now.

Twelve seconds in and the chant “where were you in Istanbul” gets a very early airing from Villa’s home fans.

That is of course a reference to Villa’s 4-0 win over Forest in the Europa League semi-final second leg last season.

The early indications are that Reece James is playing in midfield with Malo Gusto at right-back in a conventional back four.

Xabi Alonso has made an encouraging start to life as Chelsea manager. But his trousers upset me. They are three inches too short and a bit baggy above the ankle.

We are under way in the five Premier League 3pm kick-offs. Goals and further updates from around the grounds as they happen.

Some early #analysis from Matt at the Bridge, about one of Hull’s midfielders.

One player who has really shone for Villa so far this season is teenage midfielder George Hemmings.

Unai Emery has been very impressed with the academy graduate, who made his Champions League debut on Tuesday night.

There is also a big buzz around £51m signing Johan Manzambi, who is on the bench today after recovering from a knee injury.

Will we get another fast start from Chelsea today? They have scored inside the first five minutes in all three of their League games this season. Hull are yet to concede.

Dominic King writes that there were signs of promise in the relationship between Barcola, Wirtz and Isak in Liverpool’s win over Atletico Madrid, and all three forwards start against Fulham. Timothy Castagne, Fulham’s right-back will need to have his sprinting boots on against Barcola, who is grease lightning.

Cole Palmer has 15 goal involvements in his 15 Premier League games for Chelsea against newly promoted sides.9 goals ⚽6 assists 🅰️ pic.twitter.com/PJIU0YxIhQ

I’m having real fun. I’ve got a smile on face and I’m enjoying my football. Playing with players like [Palmer and Joao Pedro] inspire you to be better and make you do better and do well for the team. We are in a good moment and we want to keep it going.

Hull are really tough to beat. They have played against some good opponents and they’ve kept them out - they haven’t conceded yet. It is going to be difficult because they are really organised but we are at home and it is on us to make the game about us.

We know it is always tough against Brentford. We can expect a tight game today, definitely. We both want to win so it’ll be a nice game.

We are very excited about our first European game coming up but we haven’t really spoken about it lately because we have just spoken about this game. This is a big game and we are looking for our first three points of the season. We have been close in every game so we hope to get it today.

Unai Emery is possibly the best coach in the Premier League but has found past encounters with Oliver Glasner very uncomfortable.

Since Glasner’s arrival in English football with Crystal Palace in February 2024, he has faced Emery’s Villa seven times and never lost.

With five victories and two draws, it is an impressive record albeit with a different set of players.

Aston Villa and Forest are two teams in transition, and meet for the first time since that two-legged Europa League semi-final last season.

Villa are building a new chapter after a summer of significant change, while Forest are implementing a totally different style of play under Oliver Glasner.

There have been signs of progress at both of the former European Cup winners. Villa secured an impressive victory over Club Brugge in the Champions League on Tuesday. Forest are improving under Glasner, with their best performance the 2-2 draw at Liverpool.

Returning to Villa Park will have some bitter memories for a number of the Forest players, after that 4-0 defeat in the second leg of the Europa League.

The Reds to take on Fulham 🔴 #LIVFUL pic.twitter.com/PpuyPkkNxU

Ollie Watkins and Emi Martinez departed for pastures new in the transfer window.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this afternoon’s Premier League three o’clock kick-offs, and home bankers would appear to be the theme of the day.

Liverpool will be strongly fancied to put Fulham to the sword at Anfield, with confidence low at the London club and new manager Alvaro Arbeloa (once a player at Anfield) already under pressure amid reports of dressing room unrest. Andoni Iraola secured his first Premier League victory as Liverpool manager at Ipswich last time out, and backed up that result with a come-from-behind win against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League.

Chelsea host Hull City, who are unbeaten after three games and have yet to concede a goal. It is a remarkable start to the season for Sergej Jakirović‘s side, who continue to defy expectations as well as the underlying data. For all their spirit and defensive organisation, keeping out Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro at Stamford Bridge promises to be a tall order, though.

Aston Villa’s rocky start to the campaign took a turn for the better with a 3-2 Champions League victory at Club Brugge, and as the weeks go by Unai Emery’s team should grow stronger as their raft of young signings bed in. Nottingham Forest could be obdurate opponents, although Villa swept them aside in the second leg of last season’s Europa League semi-final. Oliver Glasner’s Crystal Palace were a bogey team for Villa though, with the Austrian coach undefeated against Emery having notched up some resounding victories.

Glasner’s former club Palace could do with a home win against Ipswich Town, while there is cigarette paper between Bournemouth and Brentford, two of the league’s smartest operators who play at the Vitality Stadium this afternoon. Bournemouth qualified for Europe at Brentford’s expense last season, but Marco Rose is looking for his first league win despite some encouraging performances.

#1467. Jack Grealish can't turn down a good night out and his attitude is a problem. IAN HERBERT reveals how the magnetic maverick star sparked concern and now faces a tragedy of missed opportunity

By IAN HERBERT, DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 22:00 EDT, 29 October 2026 | Updated: 09:57 EDT, 2 November 2026

At the Pride of Britain awards a week back, we witnessed the brilliant and magnetic side of Jack Grealish, sprinkling stardust as he presented an award to a child of unimaginable courage who counts the Everton player as his hero. 'Footballers are classed as heroes – but these are the real heroes,' Grealish said that night. You could have heard a pin drop.

It was no different when he arrived back at Everton in September, to the delight of the kids awaiting him and his white Lamborghini in the country lane outside the club's Finch Farm training base. 'It feels so good. I think I'm at my best at everything in life when I feel loved,' Grealish said, articulating a very real sense that he was coming home.

He is popular around the club because it can be said without fear of exaggeration that he has a heart of gold.

Only on Thursday, an Everton-supporting father-of-three with a cancer diagnosis that gives him weeks to live disclosed that Grealish had put £10,000 his way. But within hours of that simple act of altruism coming to light, evidence of the other Grealish emerged, as Everton announced he had been excluded from the squad to face Newcastle in the Carabao Cup for failing to turn up for training last week.

It was by no means the first time. Everton sources say there had been similar causes for concern last season. Grealish reported sick ahead of last weekend's game at Arsenal, shortly after the Pride of Britain awards, and has breached Everton's disciplinary code through an unauthorised absence. The stated reason for his absence at Arsenal was illness.

Jack Grealish remains popular at Everton and has a heart of gold, shown by a £10,000 gift to a fan suffering from cancer, but he has since been dropped over a breach of discipline

There were similar causes for concern last season, with his return this summer going against David Moyes' better judgement

Everton's owners, looking for Grealish's glitz and glamour to gloss over their desperately poor and unambitious summer in the transfer window, were keen to bring him back. It was against David Moyes' own better judgement that he accepted his return as part of the deal that brought Iliman Ndiaye's unwelcome departure to Manchester City.

Moyes needed discipline in a thin squad where every player's contribution would count this season. It was an opportunity for the few star players to inspire and shine a light for the younger ones. And therein lies the tragedy of missed opportunity where Grealish is concerned.

He, the quintessential British maverick playmaker in the mould of George Best and Alan Hudson, could be a Goodison hero of these days, yet seems incapable of showing he is bothered, ridding himself of the acolytes and hangers on who are dragging him down, and appreciating what an opportunity football offers him.

Though he likes a drink, it's not so much booze as his attitude, and a struggle to turn down a good night out, which is contributing.

There is no doubt that he still has the skills to be a cherished player. That much was clear in the early stages of last season when he was providing more assists than any other Everton player until a broken foot requiring surgery brought a premature end to his season.

This season he has, as yet, no assists. He has perhaps been frustrated at the number of chances he has created not being converted, though not every winger has Erling Haaland as his support act.

Grealish's patchy attitude to a football life is affecting his game, as he is not taking his man on in the way he used to and does not emit such light on the wing

Look hard enough, though, and you'll see signs that his patchy attitude to a football life is affecting his game. He is not taking his man on in the way he used to and does not emit such light on the wing. Pep Guardiola, at Manchester City, was the first to see this and rapidly made it clear he wanted him gone.

It's not too late for the 31-year-old to become the totemic presence that so many fervently want him to be on Merseyside. Moyes, who sees the wasted potential, has given him abundant support and patience since City left him out in the cold, hoping that he can make him see the opportunity, here.

Thursday night's excellent Carabao Cup win over Newcastle United opens up the potential for an exciting Cup run, with Fleetwood Town awaiting in the quarter-finals. Everton have not won a trophy for 31 years.

The hope must be that the significantly public nature of Grealish's omission – very much a case of Moyes refusing to tolerate another breach – will shock him into action.

It was even the wish of Prime Minister Andy Burnham, present at Thursday night's match, that Grealish would be re-signed to Everton and the PM declared after meeting him at the Pride of Britain awards that the player was an example of the way people 'buy into Everton.'

The collective wish for him to thrive at the club could not be clearer. Only he can make that happen.

#1466. Molecular underpinnings of rheumatic diseases and emerging therapeutic concepts

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 658, pages 1141–1152 (2026) Cite this article

Inflammatory rheumatic diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus represent chronic inflammatory disorders that are caused by dysregulation of innate and adaptive immune responses. Here we review current advances in our understanding of the molecular underpinnings of these diseases and discuss consequences with respect to emerging targets and treatment strategies, which are increasingly enabling more robust disease control and the first prospects of a cure for previously chronic inflammatory rheumatic diseases.
