#1441. Blues Earn Solid Point Against United

Everton played out a goalless draw with Manchester United at Goodison Park on Saturday evening.

The Blues threatened throughout, with Yuka Momiki and Ornella Vignola both seeing strikes palmed away. At the other end, heroics from Courtney Brosnan kept the Toffees in it as they earned a solid point against the Red Devils on Halloween.

Brosnan and Clare Wheeler were presented with commemorative framed shirts prior to kick-off to mark the duo surpassing a century of appearances in royal blue.

Brosnan donned the captain’s armband in between the sticks, with a backline of Hikaru Kitagawa, Rion Ishikawa, Naomi Layzell and Hannah Blundell in front of her.

Ruby Mace and Wheeler sat deep in midfield, allowing Rosa van Gool – who scored in midweek against Sheffield United – to roam further forward.

Maz Pacheco started on the unfamiliar left-wing, with Momiki lining the opposite flank. Vignola shifted over to a central position to lead the line.

It was the hosts who threatened first as Momiki drifted inside and let fly from the edge of the box. Her effort had sufficient power, but whistled wide of the near-post.

The resilient Blues continued to show real spirit and battled hard throughout the opening 45, with neither side able to make the breakthrough.

Scott Phelan’s side emerged from the tunnel with an urgency about them – Vignola firing an effort in to the chest of Le Tissier from the edge of the box immediately after play resumed.

United reacted, with Brosnan called in to action to deny Dominique Janssen on 75 minutes. The Netherlands-international latched on to former-Blue Jess Park’s threaded through ball. With her first-touch, Janssen looked to catch the keeper off-guard, but Ireland’s number one was well-prepared.

Noemie Mouchon, who also netted against the Blades on Wednesday, replaced Momiki with nine minutes remaining as Phelan looked to his bench for a late goal.

After three minutes of injury time, the referee concluded the goalless affair to mark a solid point for the Toffees on home soil.

The Blues travel to face Chelsea in the capital next up, making the journey on Saturday 7 November (12pm KO).

#1440. Manchester United hounded off pitch by own fans

After a humiliating defeat by Grimsby Town in their previous League Cup campaign, Manchester United found a different way to exit the competition this time around. The jeers heard at the full-time whistle after throwing away a two-goal lead pointed to more worrying times a year on from Blundell Park.

For the first time in half a century, United lost a game at Old Trafford having led 2-0, highlighting the defensive problems Michael Carrick needs to solve after turning results around last season.

“What the f---ing hell was that?” shouted the home fans, in a chant that may have been aimed at the referee but equally applied to United’s players, who led through Shea Lacey and Mason Mount’s early goals.

Brighton cut through Carrick’s defence several times before staging their comeback with goals from Charalampos Kostoulas, Pascal Gross and Maxim De Cuyper. Carrick and his analysts will rewatch the footage of all three goals in horror at how they conceded.

Kostoulas halves the deficit! 🔵Brighton score on the stroke of half-time. pic.twitter.com/bGjN1w6s6c

“I totally understand the feelings of the supporters,” Carrick said. “We have to accept it. I totally accept it. It’s on me ultimately: as a team what we look like, how we play and what results you get. I take that. I’ll take the praise, I’ll take the criticism and the upset.”

Erik ten Hag used the domestic cups to taste success while struggling in the Premier League, but one of those opportunities is now lost to Carrick, who must be careful not to spiral from a poor start to the campaign into crisis. Sunday’s trip to Fulham before the international break now feels like a big game for United and Carrick.

“We’ve gone out of the cup and the feeling around the place feels bigger than that,” Carrick said. “I’ll be honest about that, that’s how it feels, but it doesn’t have to be like that. If we win football matches again, it can go in a different direction.

“We have a big game on Sunday that we have to prepare for. We’re out of this competition and we have to go back to winning football matches.

“It doesn’t feel good at the moment. It doesn’t feel good. We have to go back to winning football matches. We want to win and want to win quickly. The next game is Sunday. That’s all I’m thinking about right now.”

At the start of the evening it seemed that the tie would be remembered for Lacey scoring on his first start for United, the first teenager to do so since Marcus Rashford. In the week when JJ Gabriel, one of United’s great academy talents, asked to leave the club, a different United teenager was kissing the badge when he found the net.

SHEA LACEY ON HIS FIRST START!!! 🔴🌟What a hit from the 19-year-old to open the scoring for Man Utd! pic.twitter.com/Ex2ceXaUge

Mason Mount DOUBLES Man Utd's lead! 🤩 pic.twitter.com/c83ggCb8Bf

And after Mount’s strike it looked like United were cruising into the fourth round for their first knockout win in 19 months, since defeating Leicester City in the FA Cup last year. But Brighton’s way back into the game was to get Gross, 35, on the ball and the veteran German controlled the game.

Gross took his chance when United carelessly played the ball out of defence again, with Diogo Dalot’s clearance mishit. Luka Vuskovic’s header went straight into the United penalty area, with their centre-backs failing to react quickly enough.

Pascal Gross takes advantage of a gifted opportunity to level the score! 🔥 pic.twitter.com/Qu2E0B6060

The turnaround was completed a few minutes later when De Cuyper found the net, finishing off a counter-attack in which Diego Gómez and Kostoulas raided the left flank of United before cutting the ball back.

Brighton have turned it around!!! 🔵A sensational comeback as Maxim De Cuyper makes it 3-2 at Old Trafford. pic.twitter.com/Bfcr4N7mTL

Fabian Hürzeler’s side can be considered this season’s entertainers, with this comeback going with their seven-goal thriller against Chelsea, putting four past Aston Villa and five past Coventry at the weekend. Next for them in the League Cup is Manchester City or Norwich away, although they are unlikely to fear any opponents.

“We take it how it is. We want to go as far as possible but if you want to win something you have to win at the highest level,” Hürzeler said. “We have to stay very, very humble and get an understanding why we are at the place we are and getting the basics right and the small margins right. It is so vital we stay humble and then we can grow into the game.”

For Carrick, matches such as this can define a United manager’s reign if he cannot turn results around. The image of Ruben Amorim in the dugout at Grimsby was one of the lasting impressions of last season before Carrick was brought in to salvage the campaign.

“We can’t put ourselves in that position after being ahead in the game and the game finishing like it did,” he said. “So we’ve got to react to it. We’ve got another game on Sunday, we’ve got to react to it.”

"We can't accept that" ❌"I take responsibility for that" 🗣️ Michael Carrick reacts to his side's defeat👇 pic.twitter.com/OheT8yUK7y

2 league one teams and 13 premier league teams in a cup draw.. You couldn't write it Ridiculous 😡😡😡I give up on cup draws after 20 years waiting for one 😂

I think we’ve got to be a little bit careful on that one. He’s a 15-year-old boy. It’s more about the welfare and the care of JJ as a child really, or certainly a young man. The situation is what it is, but we’ve got to be a little bit careful of the exposure and how we jump on that.

The start of the game and the end of the game was completely different, didn’t feel like the same game or the same emotions at all. We had the game exactly where we wanted it and let it get away from us in a big way.

There’s a number of things we’ll look at, we’ll dissect and I know quite a bit of where it went wrong. We can’t accept that as a group. I take responsibility, the performance towards the second half that’s on me. We’ll have to get better, we have a big game on Sunday that we have to prepare for. We’re out of this competition and we have to get back to winning football matches.

We’ve got to keep evolving as a group. We have to keep learning and dealing with situations. Sometimes they come a bit easier than others. Tonight was a tough one. We didn’t find a way out of it. That’s up to me and the staff to help the players and guide them through it. I think we all know that in the end tonight feels like a big disappointment.

We’ve had small, little things that have gone against us in the last week or two and then it accumulates to feel that it’s a lot bigger. I think we have to be honest and say that. The late goal against Everton from outside the box. The [Manchester] City goal the other day. It can all of a sudden roll into something a bit greater but I understand the disappointment because we shouldn’t finish the game in that manner with the position we were in and we have to be humble and take that.

Fleetwood vs ArsenalMan City or Norwich vs BrightonEverton vs NewcastleSunderland vs BrentfordLiverpool vs ChelseaBradford City vs PeterboroughFulham vs Crystal PalaceBournemouth vs Aston Villa

Bradford City vs PeterboroughFulham vs Crystal PalaceBournemouth vs Aston Villa

Plenty of Carabao heritage in that one, they played in the 2019, 2022 and 2024 finals. That’s the glamour draw.

That promises to be a tight one. Many people fancy Brentford for this competition.

The team with a long trophy drought against the club who ended theirs in this competition a few years ago.

Brighton’s reward for a comeback is another trip to Manchester (or Norwich).

The first team out are Fleetwood Town! They will host Arsenal at Highbury, which feels appropriate.

Should be getting started in the next couple of minutes.

The Brighton man has now scored eight times against them, all for Brighton, which is quite amazing. The first of came back in May, 2018. He is not even a striker.

It was frustrating because it’s not the first time this season, it’s the third time this season where we started slow. We have to improve that because we always have to climb a mountain but today we did that.

We played here before last season a similar match that we won and that gives you belief in a stadium where you won before. The experience we try to give it to the lads. It was a really good performance and I have to say [Jason] Steeley’s save at the end was unbelievable.

His impassive demeanour was viewed as a virtue last season, bringing calm to a club that was a circus. Now some will be wondering if standing motionless on the touchline is indicative of a lack of answers. That is probably unfair, you can only be yourself, but we know the script. He’s on a slippery slope, like so many of his predecessors.

Boos ring around Old Trafford. Manchester United are out of the Carabao Cup, but of greater significance is that this defeat continues a poor start to the season and a general mood of deflation around the club. For the first time in 50 years, they lose a game at Old Trafford after leading 2-0. Another proud record falls in the post-Ferguson era.

Brighton have now won five of their last six games at Old Trafford, and are one of the best front-footed sides in the league on form.

As United push everyone forward, Heaven is penalised for a push on Vuskovic, and that is surely that now.

Mbeumo tees up Fernandes for a Hail Mary from 25 yards but he balloons the shot miles over the bar. Brighton fans can see the finish line and a place in the fourth round now.

Five minutes of added time to play, but Brighton have a corner after their press ensnares Tielemans on the edge of United’s defensive third. Dalot got a toe to the ball to prevent Rutter a sight at goal. Darlow claims the delivery, but some time has ticked away.

Tielemans slices his cross over the bar while off balance. This would be the first time since 1976 that United have led 2-0 in a game at Old Trafford and gone on to lose. At the moment, an equaliser does not look to be on its way.

Old Trafford growing impatient with how slowly United are moving the ball, a lack of options for the player in possession and they are being caught on it repeatedly by a sharp Brighton team.

Diego Gomez really should have sealed the victory, picked out by another clever Gross pass, but with so much time to take aim he blasted straight at Darlow. United still alive in the tie, but only just.

Lovely Brighton interplay again, Gross just keeps making the right decision around the box. This time his cut-back finds Kostoulas but Yoro blocks his goal-bound shot. Now Brighton make their fifth change: Rutter replaces Kostoulas.

Brighton still swinging punches. Costinha swings in a teasing cross to the back post, headed down by Gross, but De Cuyper cannot get over his volley. Carrick has made his final change: Cunha is on for Rashford.

Big miss by Rashford, but a big save from Jason Steele. It was a lovely touch by Fernandes while half stumbling that released Rashford, and he had so much time to think when through against the goalkeeper, but Steele stuck out a right boot to save.

Hurzeler making two more Brighton changes: Ayari and Kadioglu on for Hadjam and Boscagli, which probably makes their XI on the pitch even stronger. Kadioglu was voted Brighton’s player of the season for 2025-26.

Bruno Fernandes is stripped and ready to come on, Carrick calling for the man he would rather was resting on the bench. Fernandes replaces Mount.

De Cuyper, only on for a few minutes, scores the goal, but it was the off-the-shoulder threat of Kostoulas that made the goal. It looked as if the striker had the ball stuck under his feet, but he squeezed in a low cross that deflected off Mazraoui into the path of De Cuyper who had the simplest of finishes.

Brighton have turned it around!!! 🔵A sensational comeback as Maxim De Cuyper makes it 3-2 at Old Trafford. pic.twitter.com/Bfcr4N7mTL

Changes all round: Mainoo, Mbeumo and Zirkzee replace Sesko, Lacey and Andrey Santos.

For Brighton: De Cuyper and Diego Gomez on for Yalouye and Matt O’Riley.

He has been the scourge of United on so many occasions, and so it has proved again. United tried to play out from deep against Brighton’s press, hooked a longer pass around the corner towards Sesko but Vuskovic nipped in front of him to win a booming header back to Gross at the edge of the box. Nice touch to shift the ball left, before finishing across Darlow.

Pascal Gross takes advantage of a gifted opportunity to level the score! 🔥 pic.twitter.com/Qu2E0B6060

Short corner from United after good work from Rashford, but Tielemans could not keep his curling shot under the bar. Brighton break, but it is better defending from Heaven against Kostoulas this time. Carrick is preparing a triple sub.

Sesko with space to drive forward and look to pass or shot, but he dallies and dawdles before losing possession, much to the frustration of Old Trafford. Sesko has looked short of sharpness and confidence so far.

Delicious pieces of skill from Lacey, a Cruyff turn against the touchline when he was facing away from goal. Hadjam thought he had the winger boxed in, and dragged him down at the expense of a yellow card. Crowd enjoyed that.

Vuskovic with a shot from distance which is always rising; a number of Brighton players have tried their luck from range tonight, perhaps inspired by Lewis Dunk’s screamer at Coventry. This second half has a been a bit of a non-event thus far.

Matt O’Riley clips Heaven, which enabled the United defender to get out jail because he did not have control of the ball and was scrambling. Then Struijk very nearly sells Steele short with a back pass, had Sesko have won the first touch it was a red card or a goal, but Steele went to ground to win the ball well outside his area.

Rashford has been a bright spark for United, but he is having to do too much of the heavy lifting on his own at the moment. This time he finds Lacey on the overlap, but his cross is volleyed clear. Moments before that, the Old Trafford crowd were unhappy that Lacey was not awarded a free-kick. Looked like Hadjam took a swipe.

Brighton continue to apply the squeeze, but Kostoulas fouls Mazraoui to enable Darlow to boot the ball long and United to push up the pitch. Carrick’s team are still not exerting much control on the contest, though.

That is something of a rarity at this stage of the League Cup.

Plenty of entertainment for the paying punters at Old Trafford, with Shea Lacey and Mason Mount scoring twice in two minutes to put United in a commanding position. Given the JJ Gabriel story, the home fans enjoyed seeing a 19-year-old kiss the badge after scoring on his full debut.

Brighton have probably been the better team in general play though, and scored a deserved goal on the stroke of half-time.

United’s second-string back four looking very shaky, understandably.

Carrick and United wanted a foul on Sesko on halfway, but the referee said nothing doing. Hadjam then floats a diagonal pass over the head of Heaven to find the run of Kostoulas, but goalkeeper Darlow surely had the chance to come off his line and claim? Passive goalkeeping, and Kostoulas slips the ball under Darlow into the far corner. Game on.

Kostoulas halves the deficit! 🔵Brighton score on the stroke of half-time. pic.twitter.com/bGjN1w6s6c

Chema Andres, signed by Brighton from Stuttgart on deadline day and known by the moniker “Baby Rodri”, has just been booked for a reckless challenge in midfield. Then Rashford shows he still has plenty in the locker with a touch and shimmy to beat Costinha.

Tielemans with an important challenge on Kostoulas, after more unconvincing United involving Dalot misjudging a bouncing ball. Then Kostoulas fizzes a cross all the way through the six-yard box and Gross fires over at the back post. Brighton have had the chances to be level.

Yalcouye was very dangerous for Brighton against Coventry, and he is proving difficult to contain again. Gross’s through ball releases him into space behind Dalot, but his side-footed shot was shoved wide of the post. He tried to “Henry” one around Darlow with his right instep and failed to find the curl.

Clean hit from almost 35 yards from Boscagli, but his left-footed attempt whistles just over the bar. Yoro heads away a temping Gross cross when Brighton had three blue shirts in promising positions. Rashford then puts the ball through the legs of Chema Andres, and United have a corner.

Lacey goes down hoping for free-kick, anticipating the contact from Gross but it was not forthcoming. Since 2013-14, United have been 2-0 up at Old Trafford 145 times, winning 143 and drawing just two.

Brighton well on top now, and Ayden Heaven goes to ground hoping for a free-kick but the referee is having none of it. O’Riley’s cross is turned behind for a corner, which United scramble away. Feels like a Brighton goal is on the way, despite the comfortable scoreline for United.

Brighton’s corner swung in from the right was far too deep and loopy, drifting harmlessly behind for a United goal kick. Brighton are soon back on the front foot, and Gross picks out Kostoulas in the middle but the forward’s touch let him down. Edgy defending from Yoro but United clear their lines eventually.

Mazraoui is now back on the pitch but he does not look 100 per cent. Brighton enjoying some long passages of possession now, but you sense United are happy to drop off and let them have the ball. More promising build-up play ends with Mazraoui heading a cross over the bar for a Brighton corner.

There has been a lengthy stoppage in play while Mazraoui receives treatment for a bang on the head. United’s left-back looks a little shaken and is off the pitch now, and Mason Mount has dropped into the left-back position.

Sesko and Vuskovic are enjoying a good battle early on. Andrey Santos then sells Tielemans a little short in midfield and Brighton take advantage, but O’Riley does not have the pace to get away from Mazraoui.

There are usually chances at both ends when Brighton are involved and so it has proved so far. A pleasant surprise for any Manchester United fans who feared the worst arriving at Old Trafford tonight.

Shea Lacey is the first teenager to score on their full Man Utd debut since Marcus Rashford back in 2016. And they even got to celebrate together 🥺 pic.twitter.com/hBeXpCr4Tc

Brighton playing their way into trouble in their own defensive third, and it is great work from Rashford to drive into the penalty area from the left. Steele makes a save with his feet, but the ball runs kindly for Mount to power his shot into the ground and into the roof of the net.

Mason Mount DOUBLES Man Utd's lead! 🤩 pic.twitter.com/c83ggCb8Bf

The 19-year-old, sent off against Brighton in the FA Cup last season, has powered a left-footed shot from the edge of the box beyond Steele. That is a moment to lift the Old Trafford crowd.

SHEA LACEY ON HIS FIRST START!!! 🔴🌟What a hit from the 19-year-old to open the scoring for Man Utd! pic.twitter.com/Ex2ceXaUge

Really slick, one-touch football from Brighton through midfield, players bumping off passes blind around the corner knowing their team-mate has read the next move, but the move breaks down at the edge of the box. Brighton tend to have plenty of possession and they have made a confident start. Boscagli then tries to chip Darlow from about 70 yards but it was never really on.

Some sound early defending from Brighton right-back Constinha, just when it looked like Rashford was going to break into space down the left flank. Yalcouye with a flick around the corner in midfield but his touch gets away from him and he commits a foul.

Then Yalcouye’s directness causes Yoro a problem near the left touchline, with the French defender hacking him down.

Tonight promises to be a test for Ayden Heaven and Leny Yoro who are a young centre-back partnership for United. Looks a good crowd for a third-round League Cup game.

Meanwhile, some interesting news on JJ Gabriel’s future from our man at Old Trafford:

Barcelona are leading the race for JJ Gabriel after the 15-year-old requested to quit Manchester United.

Telegraph Sport revealed this week that Gabriel has told the club he wants to cancel his registration and move as a free agent, with Europe’s biggest club well aware of the teenager.

Gabriel travelled to Barcelona last season when he was shown around their training ground and met Wojciech Szczesny and club legend Sergio Busquets.

Sources at rival Premier League suitors believe that Barça have stolen a march in the race for the England Under-17 forward.

Should he move abroad, United may only get around £300,000 in training compensation as Gabriel has a European Union passport.

United would be expected to look into whether there was any influence from football agents before September 1 when Gabriel was allowed to have a representative.

They are the Premier League’s top scorers with 13 goals in four games and they also lead the division when it comes to expected goals amassed. Brighton have also won four of their last five visits to Old Trafford in all competitions.

We’ve got the squad to do it, we feel its important and the boys are desperate to play. We’ve got a very good team out.

We’ve moved on [from the Manchester derby]. On the day, you have to deal with it, I think there’s been enough said about it [the VAR decision] and we move on.

They’re a very good team, the way they play, you make you work for it, we’ll be ready for that. They play some very good football, and score an awful lot of goals.

Youri Tielemans has been given the armband for the evening in an interesting Manchester United line-up named by Michael Carrick. Karl Darlow gets his club debut and Mason Mount is back from injury. Shea Lacey gets a start too, a home-grown talent given his chance in the week JJ Gabriel, 15, has requested to leave Old Trafford.

Eight changes by Carrick, with Karl Darlow between the sticks. Mazraoui, Yoro, Heaven, Andrey Santos, Mount, Sesko and Lacey the other players to come in. No JJ Gabriel in the squad.

United starting XI: Darlow; Dalot, Yoro, Heaven, Mazraoui; Santos, Tielemans; Lacey, Mount, Rashford; Sesko.

Subs: Lammens, Maguire, Amass, Fernandes, Mainoo, T Fletcher, Cunha, Zirkzee, Mbeumo

Lewis Steele replaces Bart Verbruggen in goal, and O’Riley, Costinha, O’Riley, Chema and Hadjam are the other players to come in. With the Conference League not starting until after the international break, Brighton do not have a pressing need to rotate.

Brighton XI: Steele, Costinha Vuskovic, Struijk, Boscagli, Chema, Gross, O’Reilly, Yalcouye, Hadjam, Kostoulas

Subs: Verbruggen, Dunk, Georginio, Promise, Osman, Kadioglu, Gomez, Ayari, De Cuyper

TEAM NEWS! 🚨 Our starting XI for #MUNBHA. 👊 pic.twitter.com/gK5tUVYJ7L

Talents like Gabriel offer United fans hope of a brighter future after years of failure and underachievement.

No one can be certain he will fulfil the vast potential everyone in football circles can see. But United would love to have a good stab at helping him realise it.

The notion of him doing it somewhere else will send chills down the spines of the Old Trafford hierarchy.

Here are the numbers. Man City vs Norwich is tomorrow night, so their last-16 tie will be clarified then. Spurs, Leeds and Forest three Premier League teams who have already fallen by the wayside.

The joke goes that Michael Carrick has already bettered Ruben Amorim’s efforts by reaching the third round of the League Cup, but Manchester United will need to find a way past free-flowing Brighton if they are to go any further.

United were eliminated in the second round by League Two Grimsby Town last season, but start the competition a stage later because they are one of nine Premier League clubs playing in European competition.

Brighton knocked United out of the FA Cup in the third round, with Danny Welbeck scoring at Old Trafford, meaning the club played just 40 matches in 2025-26.

Carrick will want to make a better fist of the cup competitions, but he could really use a win of any kind after taking just four points from United’s first four league games of the new season.

The no-show at Hull and derby defeat by City’s 10 men were especially dispiriting, and the relationship between the club and supporters is becoming increasingly strained.

There were no flags on the Stretford End for the game against City, as fans voiced their opposition to what they view as a heavy-handed ticketing policy. The club says the measures are to stop ticket-touting but critics believe many innocent season-ticket holders are being caught in the crossfire and having their tickets revoked.

Discontent is never too far away given the continued presence of the Glazer family, and confidence is fragile regarding the club’s sporting direction under Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos.

The news that 15-year-old JJ Gabriel, possibly the country’s outstanding academy player in his year group, wants out (broken by Matt Law in a Telegraph Sport exclusive) nagged at some of those fears. Gabriel could have been in contention for a place on the bench this evening, but that is now surely out of the question even if United say they have not given up hope of persuading him to stay.Full team news on the way shortly.

#1439. Hibs boss insists his improving team are ready to upset the odds against Rangers in cup final

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 14:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 15:31 EDT, 1 November 2026

Marink Reedijk warned Rangers that they'll face an ever-improving Hibs team when they meet in the Premier Sports Cup Final next month.

The Dutchman created history by becoming the first manager of the Easter Road club to taste a Hampden victory over Hearts when they came from behind to win 2-1.

After recording just one draw in his four opening league games, Reedijk was starting to feel the heat ahead of the semi-final.

But having secured a date against Rangers on December 13, the Leith boss feels his side are now in a different place.

Asked what gave him the confidence that his side can now upset the odds and win the cup for the first time since 2007, Reedijk said: 'The performance of today and the performance we showed the week before.

'And if we have more progression, we can make every opponent's lives a little bit difficult or very difficult.

Hibs boss Marink Reedijk celebrates his team's 2-1 win over Hearts with Josh Mulligan

'And no matter which team it is, it's always another match to play.

'Finals are, again, special matches, but also finals are not only based on these special moments.

'It's also about teams with a plan and teams with an idea.

'And I think if we build on what we are doing now, keep on going - it will have ups and downs - I know I have a really good belief that we also can do something in the final.'

Behind when Claudio Braga struck on four minutes, Hibs responded brilliantly and deservedly went in ahead at the break thanks to goals from Martin Boyle and Jamie McGrath.

Reedijk was effusive in his praise for the way his players bounced back from the early blow to dominate the game.

'In the first half, I really enjoyed how we played football, how we dominated the game on the ball, how we made sure that we created chances and gave Hearts a big problem in defence,' he reflected.

'And in the second half, I really enjoyed the togetherness, the work rate, the energy, the desire.

The Hibs players start the party after reaching League Cup final by beating Hearts

'This is where we made a big step today. And also I'm so happy for the staff, the players, because they worked so hard for this. And that's really important.

'Not only those people, like the staff and the players, but also for the fans who kept on supporting us, not only during the match, but especially those matches where we didn't have the result like it was today. And that's really important to me.

Reedijk was asked if his first victory at the fifth attempt was the first real sign that the players had bought into what he was trying to do.

'Not the first sign,' he stressed. 'For me, I already saw glimpses and signs in the last matches, starting at Falkirk, where you see that we dominated the game, but we didn't bring the game home and lost by individual errors and moments.

'And then against Celtic and St Mirren also you saw that we can dominate matches, that we can make our way of playing a challenge for the opponent. That didn't lead to the result we wanted.

'However, today it did. So, it is not the first sign, but it is the first performance with a result.'

Jamie McGrath soaks up the acclaim after putting Hibernian in front at Hampden

At full time, the entire Hibs squad lapped up the rendition of Sunshine on Leith which was sung by their supporters.

Reedijk admitted that he felt more emotional at the scenes than his impassive demeanour suggested.

'I'm not always showing my emotions, but it's really touching,' he said.

'Maybe it looks like I'm an ice king, so to say.

'Normally in Holland we say ice queen, but therefore an ice king because I'm not a woman.

'But for me, it is really important that this happens and it comes close to my heart because this is what football is about.

'Guys who inspire people on the pitch with something people off the pitch and in the stands love to see.

#1437. Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment1,2. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis3,4,5, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood–brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood–brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin–CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

NEC remains a major cause of mortality and long-term morbidity in preterm infants1,2. NEC pathogenesis is multifactorial, involving the complex interplay of immature intestinal development, intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut dysbiosis and excessive inflammatory response3,4,5,6. The specific triggers of NEC and the mechanisms driving its rapid progression remain poorly understood.

The impact of NEC extends beyond the intestine. More than half of postoperative survivors develop brain injury and neurodevelopmental impairment7,8, with TLR4 inflammatory pathways implicated in this pathology9,10. Many insights are derived from experimental models that use hypoxia, cold stress and hyperosmolar formula feeding to increase intestinal vulnerability11,12. Although these models have been valuable for mapping inflammatory pathways, they may be less well suited to interrogating microbiome-driven early initiating events.

Gut microbiota are implicated in NEC susceptibility: NEC is associated with dysbiosis3,4,5, germ-free mice are resistant to NEC-like injury13 and microbiota-modifying interventions are protective14,15. Several studies identified enrichment of toxin-producing C. perfringens in NEC16,17,18, but causal virulence factors remain undefined.

C. perfringens is a ubiquitous, Gram-positive anaerobe producing diverse toxins19,20. Strains are classified into seven toxin types (A–G) based on toxin repertoire19. Type C strains produce Beta and Delta toxins, which are both pore-forming toxins (PFTs) that induce cell death by forming transmembrane pores21,22,23. While Beta toxin is well characterized, Delta toxin remains understudied. Here we identify C. perfringens Delta toxin as a virulence factor that drives intestinal necrosis and brain injury in a subset of NEC, providing an avenue for targeted therapeutic intervention.

To investigate the role of gut microbiota in NEC, we profiled faecal samples from 28 preterm infants without NEC and 16 preterm infants with NEC. 16S rRNA-sequencing analysis revealed an enrichment of C. perfringens in NEC samples (Fig. 1a), consistent with previous reports16,17. Two fatal cases of NEC showed high C. perfringens abundance (Extended Data Fig. 1a). To validate this finding, we performed anaerobic culture of faecal samples from 49 individuals without NEC and 17 patients with NEC (Supplementary Table 1). C. perfringens-positive cultures showed visible gas production and were confirmed by selective tryptose sulfite cycloserine (TSC) agar isolation and PCR targeting of C. perfringens-specific genes (Extended Data Fig. 1b–d). Overall, C. perfringens was more prevalent in patients with NEC compared with in infants without NEC (56% versus 18%), supporting its association with NEC (Fig. 1b,c).

a, 16S rRNA gene sequencing of faecal samples from infants with (n = 16) and without (n = 28) NEC. b,c, Summary (pie chart (b) and table (c)) of C. perfringens (Cp) and Delta toxin detection across the non-NEC (n = 49) and NEC (n = 27) cohorts as determined by anaerobic culture and serology. d, ELISA detection of anti-Delta toxin antibody in the serum (1:2,700 dilution) of infants without (n = 5) and with (n = 12) NEC. e, Clinical parameter fold changes between the Delta toxin+ (n = 2) and Delta toxin− (n = 5) NEC groups; the blue to magenta gradient indicates the change in magnitude. Mono%, monocyte percentage; T-CO2, total carbon dioxide; Neu%, neutrophil percentage; Lymph%, lymphocyte percentage. f,g, Representative T2W and T2 FLAIR brain MRI scans from the non-NEC (n = 3), Delta toxin− NEC (n = 4) and Delta toxin+ NEC (n = 2) groups (f), and quantification of the Evans index (>0.3 indicates ventricular enlargement) (g). h, Schematic of neonatal mouse NEC model induced by twice-daily intragastric gavage of formula containing C. perfringens. The representative image shows intestinal necrosis in a P11 mouse pup. i,j, Representative intestinal haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (i) and histopathology scores (j) of pups 4 days after infection with or without C. perfringens. n = 5 (NC), n = 6 (Delta toxin− C. perfringens) and n = 6 (Delta toxin+ C. perfringens). Scale bar, 100 μm. k, Survival curves of pups infected with Delta toxin− or Delta toxin+ C. perfringens. n = 8. l,m, Representative brain H&E staining (l) and quantification of lateral ventricular width (left; n = 4) and ependymal injury scores (right; n = 6) (m) of pups infected with Delta toxin− or Delta toxin+ C. perfringens. Scale bars, 100 μm (top) and 50 μm (bottom). Representative images from one of three independent experiments are shown. Data are mean ± s.d. P values were determined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA; j and m), two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (g) and the log-rank test (k). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001. The diagram in h was created using BioRender; Zhang, S. https://BioRender.com/o2lct20 (2026).

C. perfringens produces a repertoire of toxins, including Alpha, Beta, Epsilon, Iota toxin, enterotoxin (CPE), necrotic enteritis β-like toxin (NetB) and perfringolysin O (Pfo)19. We next examined whether specific toxin profiles correlated with severe outcomes. PCR-based toxin typing identified isolates from two deceased patients as type C C. perfringens strains containing the delta toxin gene (Delta toxin+ C. perfringens clinical-03 and clinical-15) (Extended Data Fig. 1e). Delta toxin production was further confirmed by western blot analysis of culture supernatants (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). We further detected anti-Delta toxin antibodies in two patients with severe surgical NEC whose stool cultures were negative, probably due to antibiotic treatment, indicating previous infection with Delta toxin+ C. perfringens strains. Expanded serological analysis of ten additional patients with severe surgical NEC identified five anti-Delta toxin antibody-positive cases (Supplementary Table 2). Thus, 7 of 12 (58%) patients with severe NEC showed serological evidence of Delta toxin exposure, whereas Delta toxin was not detected in any infant without NEC by faecal isolate PCR or serology (Fig. 1b–d).

Clinically, Delta toxin+ infants showed more prominent systemic inflammation, coagulopathy and brain injury, compared with Delta toxin− cases characterized by elevated C-reactive protein and D-dimer, decreased monocytes, platelets and haemoglobin (Fig. 1e). Importantly, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in these patients indicated more severe injury, including lateral ventricular enlargement (Fig. 1f,g).

To assess Delta toxin pathogenicity, we selected representative clinical isolates, the Delta toxin+ strain C. perfringens clinical-03 and the Delta toxin− strain C. perfringens clinical-01 for genomic analysis and animal infection studies (Extended Data Fig. 1e,f). Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the clinical-03 strain clustered with NCTC3181 (a known Delta toxin+ type C strain24), whereas clinical-01 clustered with CVCC1160 (a Delta toxin− type C strain), with the two clinical isolates sharing around 96% DNA identity (Extended Data Fig. 1h). Neonatal mice orally gavaged with these strains and formula for 4 days developed severe NEC-like intestinal pathology only after Delta toxin+ infection, including disrupted intestinal architecture, villus and crypt damage, inflammatory infiltration and mucosal fibrin clots, accompanied by increased mortality (Fig. 1h–k). During infection with the clinical-03 strain, Delta toxin was detected predominantly in the intestine, with lower levels in the kidney and lung, but was undetectable in the brain based on western blotting and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Extended Data Fig. 1i,j). Nevertheless, infected mice developed severe brain abnormalities, including lateral ventricular enlargement and ependymal cell damage (Fig. 1l,m). Reference strain comparison using NCTC3181 and CVCC1160 (around 99% identity) confirmed that Delta toxin+ infection caused more severe intestinal, brain and lung injury (Extended Data Fig. 1k–m). Finally, culture supernatants from Delta toxin+ strains induced cytotoxicity in HeLa cells, HT29 cells and intestinal organoids, which was neutralized by a Delta-toxin-specific polyclonal antibody (Extended Data Fig. 1n–p). These results support Delta toxin as a key secreted virulence factor responsible for cell damage.

Owing to technical challenges in performing some assays in postnatal day 7 (P7) neonatal mice, we included 4-week-old weanling mice for subsequent experiments. Intraperitoneal (i.p.) administration of purified Delta toxin caused dose-dependent lethality in both age groups, with neonates showing greater sensitivity (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 2a). We next quantified Delta toxin distribution in neonatal mice 4 h after i.p. injection of 10 μg toxin. Consistent with the infection model, toxin levels were highest in the intestine (around 61 μg per g), followed by kidney (approximately 15 μg per g) and lung (about 7 μg per g), with barely detectable toxin in the brain (Extended Data Fig. 2b). These levels were comparable to those in infected pups, supporting the physiological relevance of the toxin injection model.

a, Survival curves of P7 mice after Delta toxin challenge. n = 10. b, Representative images of neonatal mice after Delta toxin challenge (right), and the age-matched control mice (left). d, days. c,d, Intestine H&E staining (c) and histopathology scores (d) after low-dose (4 μg, analysed at day 5) or high-dose (20 μg, 4 h) Delta toxin challenge. n = 5. Scale bars, 200 μm (c). e–h, Brain (third ventricle and ependyma (e,f) and cerebral cortex and lateral ventricle (g,h)) histopathology scores (e,h) and H&E staining (f,g) from neonatal mice after Delta toxin challenge. n = 5. For f, scale bars, 100 μm (third ventricle) and 20 μm (ependyma). The black arrows show ependymal disruption; the blue arrows show periventricular vacuolation and oedema; and the red arrows indicate haemorrhage (f). For g, scale bars, 50 μm (cerebral cortex) and 100 μm (lateral ventricle). The black arrows indicate neuronal shrinkage with reduced volume, hyperchromatic cytoplasm and indistinct nuclear–cytoplasmic boundaries; the yellow arrows show neuronal degeneration; and the green arrows show inflammatory cell infiltration (g). i,j, Representative T2-weighted brain MRI images (i) and Evans index quantification (j) of 4-week-old mice after Delta toxin i.p. injection. n = 3 (control), n = 3 (20 μg) and n = 4 (100 μg). The yellow arrows indicate focal hyperintensity. k,l, In vivo photoacoustic imaging (PAI) of cerebral blood flow (k) and quantification of microvascular branching length (l) in the cortex of 4-week-old mice. n = 4. m, Schematic of the experimental design for the Evans blue assay to evaluate BBB disruption. D1, day 1. n,o, Representative whole-brain images after Evans blue perfusion (n) and quantification of Evans blue extravasation (o) in the brains of 4-week-old mice. n = 6. p,q, Immunofluorescence staining (p) and mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) quantification (q) of hippocampal ZO-1. The white arrows indicate a diminished ZO-1 signal. n = 4. For p, scale bars, 100 μm. Representative images are shown from one of three independent experiments. Data are mean ± s.d. P values were determined using one-way ANOVA (d, e, h, j, l and o) and a two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (q). The diagram in m was created using BioRender; Zhang, S. https://BioRender.com/o2lct20 (2026).

We next challenged P7 neonates and 4-week-old mice using either an acute high-dose model to mimic fulminant infection, analysed at 4 h, or a single low-dose challenge with prolonged follow-up to approximate residual toxin activity after antibiotic clearance, analysed at days 5–7. Across both age groups and dosing strategies, Delta toxin induced a severe NEC-like multiorgan pathology. Intestines showed mucosal disruption, villus destruction, epithelial detachment and oedema (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Concurrently, the brain exhibited haemorrhage, ependymal disorganization, periventricular oedema, ventricular dilation (Fig. 2e,f and Extended Data Fig. 2e,f), neuronal shrinkage and degeneration, and inflammatory cell infiltration (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 2g–i). We also observed intravascular coagulation within the cerebral microvasculature in the hippocampal region (Extended Data Fig. 2j,k). In 4-week-old mice, brain MRI further confirmed that Delta toxin caused brain injury and ventricle dilation (Fig. 2i,j), mirroring the neuropathology observed in patients with NEC. In vivo photoacoustic imaging of brains showed a significant reduction in cerebral blood flow, vascular density and branching index, indicating Delta-toxin-associated hypoxic–ischaemic injury and cognitive impairment (Fig. 2k,l).

Beyond the brain, Delta toxin induced widespread multiorgan pathology, with particularly severe injury observed in the kidney and lung. These tissues exhibited distinct signs of coagulopathy, haemorrhage and inflammatory cell infiltration, notably affecting the renal medulla, glomeruli and pulmonary parenchyma in both age groups (Extended Data Fig. 2l–o). Moreover, toxin-treated mice showed dilated ear vessels and increased Evans blue extravasation in the peritoneal lavage fluid, indicating vascular damage25 (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). Delta toxin further induced systemic coagulation abnormalities, including elevated red blood cell counts, reduced platelets and altered coagulation parameters, including prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time,  and reduced fibrinogen (Extended Data Fig. 3c–h). These findings recapitulate the severe disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) observed in Delta-toxin-positive patients with NEC (Fig. 1e). Inflammasome activation is known to drive coagulation through macrophage-mediated release of tissue factor26. Consistently, Delta toxin promoted tissue factor release from macrophages and Caco2 intestinal epithelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 3i), suggesting that both cell types contribute to toxin-induced coagulopathy.

To define the specific contribution of Delta toxin to neurological injury, we evaluated the effects of Beta toxin, which has been implicated in type C C. perfringens enteritis27. Beta toxin exhibited selective cytotoxicity for endothelial HUVECs but notably spared HT-29 intestinal epithelial cells and organoids (Extended Data Fig. 4a–c), aligning with a previous report that Beta toxin preferentially targets CD31+ vascular endothelial cells28. In vivo, it induced rapid, dose-dependent mortality (Extended Data Fig. 4d), but did not induce brain pathology at any dose tested (Extended Data Fig. 4e). These data demonstrate the specific pathogenic role of Delta toxin as a driver of NEC-like multiorgan pathology.

We next examined whether Delta-toxin-induced brain injury is associated with blood–brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and neuroinflammation. In 4-week-old mice, Evans blue extravasation revealed dose-dependent BBB leakage after Delta toxin challenge, with lipopolysaccharide (LPS)29 as a positive control (Fig. 2m–o). Acute high-dose Delta toxin (100 μg, 8 h) caused more-severe BBB disruption than either prolonged low-dose Delta toxin (20 μg, analysed at day 7) or acute LPS (1 mg, 8 h), indicating that Delta toxin rapidly disrupts BBB integrity. ZO-1 immunofluorescence in the hippocampus confirmed structural damage with localized disorganization and reduced signal intensity (Fig. 2p,q).

BBB disruption is often accompanied by neuroinflammation30,31 and intestinal CD4+ T cells migrate across the BBB into the brain, where they accumulate with microglia to trigger neuroinflammation32,33. We next characterized brain immune cell populations after exposure to Delta toxin. In both age groups, acute high-dose Delta toxin triggered an increase in total CD45+ cells (Extended Data Fig. 5a). This increase was largely attributable to a marked expansion of the microglial population, predominantly reflecting microglial expansion (Extended Data Fig. 5b,c), confirmed by increased IBA1+ immunostaining (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). Three-dimensional analysis revealed a shift of microglia from ramified to amoeboid morphology, characterized by shorter branch lengths and attenuated processes (Extended Data Fig. 5d–g). GFAP+ astrocytes also increased, with increased branching and cell volume (Extended Data Fig. 5h–k), indicating pro-inflammatory activation34. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells remained at similar levels at this timepoint (Extended Data Fig. 5l). In neonates after low-dose prolonged challenge, microglial expansion and activation (Extended Data Fig. 5m–r) were accompanied by increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Extended Data Fig. 5s,t), consistent with T cell recruitment 4 days after NEC induction32.

As patients with NEC exhibit a pronounced systemic and central nervous system inflammatory response1, we analysed cytokine profiles in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with NEC positive for C. perfringens Delta toxin. The results revealed abnormally high cytokine levels, including IL-6, IL-10, TNF and IL-1β (Fig. 3a,b). To examine whether Delta toxin contributes to this inflammatory activation, we administered Delta toxin to 4-week-old mice through i.p. injection and observed a significant increase in IL-1β levels in both the serum and peritoneal fluid (Fig. 3c), along with a dose-dependent upregulation of Il1b, Il18, Tnf and Nlrp3 mRNA levels in peritoneal lavage cells (Fig. 3d). IL-1β and IL-18 are major effector cytokines released after NLRP3 inflammasome activation35, and activated macrophages represent the principal cellular source of mature IL-1β36. The specific NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 suppressed Delta-toxin-induced Il1b and Il18 in peritoneal macrophages (Fig. 3e), improved survival rates (Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6a) and mitigated Delta-toxin-induced BBB disruption, as evidenced by reduced Evans blue extravasation (Fig. 3g,h). These findings suggest that Delta toxin activates the NLRP3 inflammasome to drive local and systemic inflammation as well as BBB damage.

a,b, Cytokine profiling of serum (a) and CSF (b) from Delta toxin+ patients with NEC. n = 2 (serum) and n = 1 (CSF). c, The IL-1β concentration in 4-week-old mice after Delta toxin challenge. n = 7 (control), n = 7 (20 μg) and n = 8 (100 μg) (left); n = 5 (right). d, Il1b, Il18, Tnf and Nlrp3 mRNA expression in peritoneal cells from Delta-toxin-challenged mice. n = 3. e, Il1b, Il18 and Nlrp3 mRNA expression in peritoneal macrophages treated with Delta toxin (0.005 μg ml−1), with or without MCC950. n = 3. f, Survival curve of 4-week-old mice challenged with Delta toxin treated with vehicle or MCC950. n = 12. g,h, Brain images (g) and quantification (h) of Evans blue extravasation in 4-week-old mice. n = 5 (no Delta toxin (−)), n = 7 (20 μg) and n = 6 (100 μg). i,j, Histograms (i) and quantification (j) of neonatal peritoneal macrophages (F4/80+Ly6G−) and neutrophils (F4/80−Ly6G+) after challenge with Delta toxin. n = 7 (control), n = 4 (20 μg) and n = 3 (4 μg). k,l, Histograms (k) and quantification (l) of neonatal intestinal macrophages and neutrophils after Delta toxin challenge. n = 5. m, Intestinal macrophage percentages (left) and numbers (right) in C. perfringens-colonized neonates at day 4. n = 4. n, MTT assay of primary peritoneal macrophages treated with distinct toxins. n = 3. o, Pro-inflammatory gene mRNA expression in peritoneal macrophages treated with distinct toxins for 24 h. n = 3. P values were determined using one-way ANOVA (c, j and m), two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-tests (h and l) and log-rank (Mantel–Cox) tests (f).

We next examined whether macrophages, well-established cells capable of NLRP3 inflammasome activation, are preferentially targeted by Delta toxin. In both neonates and 4-week-old mice, high-dose Delta toxin caused rapid, near-complete depletion of peritoneal macrophages within 1 h, and low-dose exposure resulted in reduced peritoneal macrophage numbers persisting for 5–7 days (Fig. 3i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). By contrast, neutrophils decreased at 1 h, accumulated by 4 h and persisted to days 5–7, suggesting a subsequent neutrophil-dominated inflammatory response (Fig. 3i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). In the neonatal intestine, Delta toxin selectively depleted macrophages, without significantly altering T cells, B cells, neutrophils or dendritic cells (Fig. 3k,l and Extended Data Fig. 6e,f). Consistently, neonatal mice infected with the NCTC3181 (Delta toxin+) strain showed both a reduced percentage and a reduced absolute number of intestinal macrophages at 4 days after infection, whereas infection with the CVCC1160 strain (Delta toxin−) resulted in no detectable change (Fig. 3m). To assess the inflammatory potency relative to other PFTs, we exposed primary peritoneal macrophages to Staphylococcus aureus α-haemolysin (α-Hla), C. perfringens Delta toxin, Beta toxin, Pfo or LPS. Macrophages were resistant to α-Hla, Beta toxin and Pfo, but exceptionally sensitive to Delta toxin (Fig. 3n). Delta toxin potently induced inflammatory cytokine mRNA at 1–5 ng ml−1, whereas Pfo and α-Hla required around 5,000 ng ml−1 and 50,000 ng ml−1, respectively; Beta toxin had a minimal effect even at high concentrations. Notably, Delta toxin was effective at approximately 100-fold lower concentrations than LPS (Fig. 3o). Consistently, IL-1β was detected in primary peritoneal macrophage culture supernatants after 10 ng ml−1 Delta toxin treatment (Fig. 3p).

To define the mechanism, we examined key inflammatory cell-death pathways in immortalized bone-marrow-derived macrophages (iBMDMs). Delta toxin induced a time-dependent increase in pyroptosis signatures, including accumulation of pro-caspase-1, cleaved caspase-1 and gasdermin D (Fig. 3q). By contrast, canonical apoptosis markers, BAX induction and caspase-3 cleavage37 were not detectably altered under the same conditions (Fig. 3r), supporting pyroptosis as the dominant cell-death program induced by Delta toxin in iBMDMs.

We next tested whether K+ efflux38, a conserved trigger for NLRP3 inflammasome activation after membrane permeabilization, mediates Delta-toxin-induced inflammation. Extracellular KCl, used to prevent intracellular K+ depletion, abrogated Delta-toxin-induced NLRP3 upregulation and caspase-1 cleavage (Extended Data Fig. 6g), identifying K+ efflux as a major upstream signal. Moreover, Delta toxin rapidly induced ERK phosphorylation (Fig. 3s), consistent with pore-forming toxin-induced calcium influx, which subsequently activates MAPK–ERK signalling39. In vivo, bone marrow cells from Delta-toxin-treated mice showed increased GSDMD cleavage (Fig. 3t), confirming pyroptotic signalling. Collectively, these findings reveal that Delta toxin drives potent inflammation through the NLRP3–Caspase-1–GSDMD pathway and activates MAPK–ERK signalling.

We next examined whether Delta toxin engages a specific host receptor to mediate cell binding and cytotoxicity. We first evaluated the sensitivity of various cell lines. HeLa and HT29 cells were found to be highly susceptible, indicating that they abundantly express receptor (Extended Data Fig. 7a). We therefore performed a genome-wide CRISPR–Cas9 screen in HeLa cells using the GeCKO v2 library40 against Delta toxin (0.01 μg ml−1) (Fig. 4a). Next-generation sequencing of surviving cells revealed Cd9 as the top hit (Fig. 4b). CD9 expression was confirmed across relevant cell lines, and higher CD9 expression was associated with increased sensitivity to Delta toxin (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7a). Although Delta toxin has been reported to bind to GM221, genetic disruption (UGCG knockout (KO)) or pharmacological inhibition (EtDO-P4 treatment) of GlcCer-derived glycosphingolipids (including most gangliosides such as GM2) did not change cellular sensitivity (Extended Data Fig. 7b,c). By contrast, CD9-KO rendered HeLa cells resistant to Delta toxin with toxicity reduced by around 40,000-fold (Fig. 4d). Moreover, CD9-overexpressing (CD9-GFP-oe) A549 cells showed markedly increased sensitivity (Fig. 4e). KO of other candidate genes (LRP6 and CLEC12B) did not alter toxin sensitivity (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7d). GST-tagged Delta toxin can bind to wild-type (WT) HeLa cells and CD9-GFP-oe A549 cells, but not to CD9-KO cells and A549 cells (Fig. 4f–h). Biolayer interferometry (BLI) assays confirmed specific binding between GST–CD9 and Delta toxin, but not Beta toxin (Fig. 4i). The measured interaction (KD) fell in the micromolar-range binding affinity, indicative of specific, low-affinity binding (Extended Data Fig. 7e,f). It is possible that a proper membrane environment is required for the high-affinity binding of Delta toxin on cell surfaces. Together, these data identify CD9 as a receptor for Delta toxin.
